Woctri. AUGUST. I Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store? Sometimes whoevevr seeks abroad may find Thee sitting careless on a granary floor, Thy hair soft-lifted by the winnowing wind ; Or on a half-reaped furrow sound asleep, Drowsed with the fume of poppies, while thy hook Spares the next swath, and all its twined flowers; • And sometimes like a gleaner thou dost keep Steady thy laden head across a brook; ! Or by a cider press, with patient look, Thou watchest the last oozings hours by hours. Keels.

A SUMMER LESSON. The brook, that threads the forest glade, Whispers, beneath the shade, His dream of love to listening flowers. Through the long summer hours; While myriad insects, in their festive round, Tune all the air to one rich harmony of sound. The leaves, which rustle in the breeze, Make music as they please, 1" ••• • And the soft zephyrs pass along Echoing the mystic son,, Till the whole woodland like a chantry rings, With antiphonal hymns, praising the kinglof kings. Here let us rest awhile, and dream Upon sweet Nature's theme,— The love of God in great and small, And mercy over all,— So fair a nursery garden still is ours, Fragrant with memories dropped from Eden's long-lost bowers. If Love can bear so long with sin, The heart of man to win, If Heaven its beauty thus can spend, Yet hardly reach its end, How shall we dare to weary or complain, Though all our toil and work should seem to be in vain? The palest flower that hides unseen Beneath its leafy screen, The smallest bird that sings on high Its gladness to the sky, The faintest whisper of the summer wind, Each has its special work in God's eternal mind. A life of sacrificed desire, A heart consumed with fire, Eyes that can read in every face Some lines of heavenly grace, Lips that dare only speak kind words and true, How shall they ever fail some heavenly work:to do? Rise, with the sunshine of the brook Brightening in every look, Fill thy hands full of God's dear flowers, Born of the springtide showers, Learn of sweet Nature how to work His praise, And take His summer world to gladden wintry days. —Sunday Magazine. GENEVIEVE IRONS.

Alexander the Great refused to see a beautiful woman whom he had made prisoner, for fear," said he, "I should be captivated by my captive." A SHARP LAD.—" Come here and tell me what the four seasons are?" Young prodigy answers: "Pepper, mustard, salt, and vinegar; them's what mother always seasons with." No serious argument to make wrong appear right would have half as much effect in sending a youth into evil courses as the careless word that depicts sin of any kind as a light and trivial matter. An old lady who had several unmarried daughters fed them largely on a fish diet, because, as she ingeniously observed", fish is rich in phosphorus, and phosphorus is the essential thing in making matches. Peter Macnally, a lame Dublin attorney, wanted to be enrolled in a volunteer corps. "You'd never do, Peter," said the officer to whom he applied for admission. "The more we told you to march, the more you'd halt." Mr. Ruskin, alluding to children, says :—" Make them try always who shall speak truest, both as regards the fact he has to relate and the precision of the,words he expresses it in, thus making ruth the test of perfect language." One of the difficulties of life—talking to a deaf person in an omnibus. One of the pleasures of life—taking off new boots and putting on old slippers. One of the rari- ties of life—a woman thoroughly satisfied with her daughter-in-law. Six days in drudgery's heavy wheel she stands, The seventh sweet morning folds her weary hands; Yes, child of suffering, thou may'st well;be sure He who ordained the Sabbath loves the poor! —Oliver Wendell Holmes.

There is a story of a wise monarch not contained in written histories. Two of his court damsels had a dis- pute as to precedence. The king looked kindly at them and said, "Let the oldest go first," and the damsels em- braced and went in together with entwinedlarms. Sir John Watson Gordon, who ultimately became President of the Royal Scottish Academy, used to tell this story of Lord Palmerston :—"I had exhibited for several years, but without any particular success. One year, however—the year before I painted The Corsi- cans '—Lord Palmerston took a sudden fancy to my pic- ture called Summer in the Lowlands,' and bought it at a high figure. His lordship at the same time made in- quiries after the artist, and invited me to call upon him. I waited upon his lordship accordingly. He compli- mented me upon the picture; but there was one thing about it he could not understand. 'What is that, my lord?' I asked. • That tfiere should be such long grass in a field where there are so many sheep,' said his lordship promptly, and with a merry twinkle of the eye. It was a decided hit, that; and having bought the picture and paid for it he was entitled to his joke. How do you account for it?' he went on smiling, and looking first at the picture and then at me. Those sheep, my lord„ I replied, 'were only turned into that field the night before I finished the picture.' His lordship laughed heartily, and said 'Bravo!' at my reply, and gave me a commis- sion for two more pictures; and I have cashed since then some very notable cheques of his, dear old boy!" MODES OF SALllTATlON.—Greenlanders have none, and laugh at the idea of one person being inferior to another. Islanders near the Philippines take a person's hand or foot and rub it over their face. Laplanders apply their noses strongly against the person they salute. In New Guinea they place leaves upon the head of those they salute. The inhabitants of the Philippines bend very ' low, placing their hands on their cheeks, and raise one foot in the air, with the knee bent. The Japanese take off a slipper, and the people of Arracan their sandals in the street and their stockings in the house, when they salute. Two nep.,To kings on the coast of Africa salufe by snapping the middle finger three times. If the Chinese meet after a long separation, they fall on their knees, bend their face to the earth two or three times, and use many other affected modes. They have also a kind of ritual, or "academy of compliments," by which they regulate the number of bows, genuflections, and words to be spoken upon any occasion. Ambassadors practice these ceremonies forty days before they:appear at court. The Dutch, who are considered as great eaters, have a morning salutation common amongst all ranks, " Smaakelyk eeten ?" (" May you eat a hearty dinner ?") Another is, "Hoe yeart awe ?" (" How do you sail ?") adopted, no doubt, in the early periods of the Republic, when they were all navigators and fishermen. 7he usual salutation at Cairo is, " How do you perspire?" a dry hot skin being a sure indication of a destructive ephemeral fever. Some author has observed in contrast- ing the haughty Spaniard with the frivolous Frenchman, that the proud, steady gait and inflexible solemnity of the former were expressed in his mode of salutation— " Come esta?" (" How do you stand ?") whilst the "Com- ment vous portez-vous ?" (" How do you carry your- self ?") was equally expressive of the motion and incess- ant action of the latter. Z7`,..."=VPIR/Itra,,aarks • THE BIRTH THROES OF THE Moow.—The tidal wave, set up on the earth by the moon, reacts to a certain ex- tent also upon the moon's orbital period. The moon is dragged forward in its path by the terrestrial tidal wave, as certainly as the tidal wave is drawn backward on the rotating earth by the moon, and this implies an enlarge- ment of the orbit of the MOOD, and a recession of the moon from the earth. This process must go on until the day and the month both meet in a common period of about 1,400 hours. But if this be the case the moon must have been once much nearer to the earth than it is now. Professor Darwin carries back his investigation in this direction to a time when the moon revolved about the earth in somewhere between two and four hours, and in a position when it was nearly in contact with the earth, and in which it was rotAing in the same period—a state which may be looked uMn as having been antecedent to the time when friction began its "work of grinding down axial velocity and expanding orbital range." The moon then started on its long spiral journey out from the earth. Professor Darwin calculates that this start oc- curred not less than 54,000,000 of years ago! But the most rapid rate of rotation in a fluid mass that would be consistent with spheroidal equilibrium is two hours and twenty minutes. One second of augmentation more than this in the rate of rotation would inevitably cause the rotating mass to fly asunder. The presumption is that the earth did fly asunder from overfast spinning, and that such disruption was coincident with what Miss Professor speaks of as the "birth throes of the moon." however, conceives that in all proba- bilityessother rw IDuanar-interrestrial system is an exception among the bodies swayed by the sun due to the circumstance that the moon is Proportionally by far the most massive satellite known, and that the influence of tidal drag has be en concomitantly great. o other satellite ever pos- sessed tide-raising capabilities at all comparable with the influence which is exerted by the moon. The separation of satellites from their primaries essentially depends upon the attainment of a disruptive rate of rotation— .= effect which may be prevented by the secondary effect of the additional tidal drag set up by the sun keep- I lug down the velocity of the rotation of the primary below the velocity that would correspond with the actual point of disruption. The earth just escaped this degree of retardation, and hence the existence of its solitary satellite.—Edinburgh Review. If clear views are necessary to discover right paths, heartfelt desires can alone give the energy to walk in them. There will always be a consonance between the workings of the mind and the nature of the hones and wishes. Together, not apart, will they influence the conduct and shape of life, while at the same time they act and react powerfully upon each other.l There is:no happiness in the world equal to that of blessing others. Not only by giving money to the needy, help to the sick, food to the hungry, is this blessing com- passed; we gain it as we give it, by sympathy, by affec- tion, by seeing that which is best in our friends and shutting our eyes to that which is worst.:bv taking joy in their good things even when our own portion is scant and poor. Just as the earth is ever receiving sunlight, air, and moisture, and at the same time giving out her blossoms, fruit, and fragrance, so our best interests demand a con- tinual taking in and giving out, a perpetual alternation between learning and doing, from the: earliest to tho latest years. Whatever tends to divorce these, or to limit them to different epochs,". banishing the one from youth and the other from maturity, mustbe detri- mental.

The sergeant-major of a Scotch Volunteer corps was to be presented with a long-service and good-conduct medal. All members of the corps who had won medals were ordered to wear them on the'occasion. When the battalion had formed into three sides of a square, the commanding officer glanced round the ranks, and spied one of the corps with an unusually large medal: on his breast. Galloping up to him, thel!officer called out, "Hallo, fellow, where :did you get that ;medal?" The private, saluting, answered, "At a plooin":match, sir !" While Miss Mary Anderson was rehearsing the part of Juliet, an eminent physician, an intimate friend, was present. The performance delighted him till towards the conclusion of the play, when his countenance wore a troubled expression. When it was over, he went up to the actress...." My dear young lady," he said, "you are wrong in one of your effects. Don't you know that a corpse doesn't stiffen for at least six hours after death?" "My dear doctor," responded Mary slowly, speaking in deep rich tones, and adopting a strong American twang, "do you think I'm going to keep my audience waiting for six hours while I stiffen?" _

The unsuccessful striver in any department of life may lose his property, his situation, his means of liveli- hood; all his plans may come to naught and all his efforts be frustrated; but, until he lose his courage, he has not lost ali.t4lnstead of sitting down idly to mourn over dead hopes, let him apply himself vigorously to the nearest duty, and his spirits and his fortune will alike rise triumphant from the ashes of the past. Even small disappointments and vexations, such as assail us con- tinually, lose half their sting by such treatment. The more we brood upon l them the more afflictive they be- come; but busily employed in the nearest duty, we for- get their sharpness and learn unconsciously to bear them with firmness.

STRAWBERRIES.—The different kinds of strawberry are natives of cold or temperate climates; but they meet the eye of the traveller also on the more southern hillsides of Asia and Africa. The wild strawberry grows abun- dantly in Swedish woods, and was considered by Lin- mous the most wholesome of all fruits. It is commonly carried about the towns of Sweden for sale, and the great botanist ordered his servants never to lose an op- portunity of purchasing the supplies, however large, that were hawked at his door. The Hautboy species was commonly cultivated in England as far back as the days of Henry VIII., and most of our readers will remem- ber the allusion in Shakspere to the strawberries in the London gardens of the Bishop of Ely. WINTER IN KANSAS.—We used to keep a pig in the house during the winter to cut from, a dead one. It used to hang in one corner of the room over the flour barrel, and was frozen as hard as a board. We used just to take a hatchet and cut off as much as we wanted to fry. It was a matter of no small difficulty to write a letter in the winter, as the ink was frozen in a solid lump, and had to be kept on the stove while in use. While sitting round the redhot stove at breakfast one's coffee would freeze in a very short time if placed on the table a few feet from the fire. Hot water thrown into the air out of doors would come down as hail.,'During weather like this we had to be mightily careful how we handled iron or steel, for the frost in an axe or hammer would cause it to cling to a damp hand. Ernigranti Life in Kansas.

THE PHILOSOPHY OF DIET.—" In matters of diet," says Sir Henry Thompson, "many persons have individual pecuiiarities ; and while certain fixed principles exist as absolutely cardinal in the detail of their application to each want's wants, an infinity of stomach eccentricities is to be reckoned on. The old proverb expresses the fact strongly but truly, 'What is one man's meat is another man's poison.' Yet nothing is more common—and one rarely leaves a social dinner-table without observing it —than to hear some good-natured person recommending to his neighbour, with a confidence rarely found except in alliance with profound ignorance of the matter in hand, some special form of food, or drink, or system of diet, solely because the adviser happens to have found it useful to himself." It is not only the good-natured com- panion of the dinner table who errs in this way. He were an ungrateful churl who would willingly say a harsh word about our Ministers of the Interior, so sym- pathetic, so patient, so courteous, so generous! Yet it must be owned that they are, some of them, a little apt to leave out of sight the varieties of the human constitu- tion, to take all human stomachs as framed on one fixed, ' primordial pattern; above all are they, as old Lessins complained, too likely to "bring men into a labyrinth of care in the observation, and unto perfect slavery in the endeavouring to perform what they do in this matter enjoin." Sometimes I think they do but flatter the weak- ness of humanity, and when they meet salute each other as the old augurs used. There are folk who will not so much as take a pill at their own venture, and never fulfil an invitation to dinner without a visit to the doctor next morning. He cannot afford to drive such inquisi- tive fools from his door; and so it may be that the heal- ing hand, like the dyer's, becomes subdued to what it works in. The answer given by his physician by Fal- staff, on his page's authority, is one it were hardly wise to risk to-day. In all these things, then, I believe a man must be his best physician. That is the life's experience of many and many a man who bears a cheerful front enough to his fellows. While he has health and strength, while the sun is still in the heavens, he can bear the bur- den, uncomplaining if unresting. But as the day wears I on, and the shadows grow, the question of the future grows 'with them—what shall be his fate when hand and brain can work no more? Happy as he may be in his work now, contented, prosperous, never can he wholly put by the thought, But there may come another day to me,— Solitude,o o canpapiunt off heart,of that d houristress y n , abndpoovheortlyid. Such an nay pass- times which to the idle man of pleasure are a mere weariness of flesh. But he can, so far as human will avails, put it off by hoarding his strength and health; and this he will most surely do by the observance of one simple rule, framed for man's conduct thousands of years before our wisdom discovered that the pancreatic juice converts starch into sugar, and that levulose is isomeric with glucose—the simple rule of moderation.—ffacmil- lan's Magazine. THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. A SEASONABLE ARTICLE. The poultry-keeper is now being reminded that.the period of moulting is approaching rapidly, and we pro- pose to devote this article to a consideration of the ques- tions which are pressing themselves, or ought to be, upon the attention of every poultry-keeper at the pre- sent time. First, then, as to the moulting period. This operation takes place every year, and is the casting of one set of feathers and the replacing of them by entirely new ones. It must not be thought, however, that it is at only one season of the year that this change takes place, for there is always more or less of it all the year round. But it is only in the autumn that there is any- thing like regularity in the process. Moulting makes a very severe demand on the system, and it is, therefore, necessary to make special provision to meet it. Chickens hatched during the first four or five months of the year usually cast their chicken plumage aboutlSeptember,:but this can hardly be called a moult. The first, moult proper takes Place when they are about nineteen or twenty months old, say the September of the year fol- lowing their hatching. Every year this becomes later and more protracted, and hence the wisdom of the plan often advocated for laying fowls, namely, to kill them off when they are about eighteen or twenty months old, that is, before their first or second moult. They are still fit for the table—an important consideration. It has already been said that the moulting period is a somewhat critical one for fowls, even for the hardiest, and especially so for such as are delicate in stamina and constitution. It is therefore necessary:to pay more than usual attention to them when they are moulting. This, unfortunately, is very often altogether neglected. Hens in the moult do not lay, at least, it is not natural for them to do so, and when they are not producing eggs some poultry-keepers do not appear to regard' it as necessary to give the same attention and food as when they are laying. This brings its own punishment very soon indeed. The fact is there should be even -nom attention and better food than is usually the case, to meet the demand upon the system. It must not be thought that there is'any very serious difficulty in bringing fowls safely through: the moult when they are of the hardier and more useful breeds, for unless there is some other trouble to complicate matters the time is simply one of cessation from laying, needing , a little better food and shelter. But with the more deli- cate and highly bred varieties it innore trying, and I , have known it so prolonged that the birds have died from sheer exhaustion. In-breeding has had much to do with this weakening of our domestic poultry, and we have noticed that closely-bred fowls get through the moult about the worst of all. The usual period of moulting for a strong bird in its first or second year is six to eight weeks, in which the old feathers are com- pletely cast and the new ones take their places, but weakly or old birds often take three months, with the result that winter arrives before they are through it, and they do not recommence laying until the following spring, so that several valuable months are lost, and just at the period when the produce is most valuable. This ,is an important consideration, and one that should not be lost sight of, as it, may have much to do with the suc- cess of the enterprise. Therefore, where profit is the object, it is necessary to see that the layers are not old fowls, or they will never give that profit which is de- sired. To hasten the moult there are some poultry men who always arrange to let the hens sit immediately prior to the moult. The object is to give the birds a needed rest, and it is found that this hastens the moult. Of course, it can only apply to sitters. In the case of non- sitters, they should be made to cease laying if it is felt that they are continuing too long. Generally, when the fowls are hardy and healthy, they naturally cease with- out any of this needing to be done. It may be taken for granted that it is most advan- tageous to get the moult over as early as possible in the autumn, so that the fowls may have their plumage fully grown before the winter sets in. The cocks and hens should be separated at once, if they have not already been attended to, and it is better to put the gentlemen into moderate-sized pens in warm houses. An empty stable or loft is very good for this purpose. The evil effects of the cement or brick floor of the one, and the wooden floor of the other, can be obviated by covering them deeply with sand or dry earth. It is much more difficult to make the house in which the hens are con- fined warm, especially upon a large farm, and it is neces- sary to depend more upon the food supplied to them. This should at first be rather sparing, and by no means stimulating in its nature, so as to stop laying. That secured, it may be more generous. During the:moulting season we have always given more warm soft food than usual, and have found the plan to answer. A little meat can also be given every day, but in this, as in many other things, the care must be not to overdo it. To the drinking water may be added a little sulphate of iron and sulphuric acid, say two pieces of the former about the size of nuts, and ten drops of the latter, to:a gallon of water. This must be renewed every day, for fresh water is a most important thing in poultry-keeping. Whore there is a running stream at hand, and it is not needful to provide water at other seasons, we should suggest that there be a fountain of water during the period of moult. The ordinary farmer ought ever to see that his fowls are of a healthy strain, and he will he well advised if, discovering this not to be the case, he gets rid of what he has and makes a fresh start. But there are times when, for some temporary reason, the ?Moult does not progress properly. Under these circumstances the first thing to do would be to administer an aperient, either a small quantity of Epsom salts or of Turkey rhubarb in the soft food. We have often known good result from giving a little boiled linseed twice a week during the time of moulting. This must be properly prepared, which is best done by putting a pan upon the fire con- taining a quart of water, and when thelwater: boils throw two handfuls of whole linseed into it. In about fifteen or twenty minutes the water will have become thick with oil, and the seed will be soft and digestible. This should be mixed when hot with the meal,-which will need no other moisture. Green food should also be given freely to birds in the moult, and when the process is very- much prolonged, it may be necessary to give doses of calomel or jalap ; but these are seldom needed, except when the fowls are delicate, and, as already advised, in that case it is better to get rid of them altogether. Where it is intended to get rid of any of the old stock, this should be done as speedily as possible,l for if the birds get into the moult, of course no one will buy them. Therefore both the adult stock and the chickens should be overhauled, so as to have determined what shall be retained and what shaU be sold or killed. Even now the thoughts should be planning the work of the next breed- ing season for in thinning out the stock it must be determined what are the most likely birds to be retained either as breeders or as layers. There can be nothing gained by retaining such fowls as are not likely to be used in either of these ways, except what may be wanted for killing and supplying the table. Therefore, it is most desirable to consume every surplus fowl, or sell it, and so reduce the stock, which is generally far too large at this season of the year. We have known poultry-keepers fail through inattention to this one point. They have been most attentive to everything else, but from dislike to get rid of birds which they have reared, or from a wish to secure better prices than others were willing to give, they have gone on keeping a large stock, to the serious injury of their balance sheet.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886
GENERAL NEWS.
The Earl of Elgin has been appointed Lord Lieutenant of the county of Fife.

The late Miss Gamble, of 66, Portland-place, London, has left Girton College, Cambridge, a legacy of £19,000. The man Boyle, who is alliged to have murdered a man named Maloney in the streets of Listowel, was arrested on Tuesday morning in the outskirts of the town. _

A waggonette-, full of excursionists, descending Seale Hill, Seven Oaks, on Monday night, overturned. One man was killed, and others were seriously injured. The Lord Lieutenant has commuted to penal servitude for life the sentence of death passed at the last Cork Assizes an Mary Brophy for the murder of her brother. Owing to the closing of ironworks in West Cumberland, great distress prevails. The outlook in the iron-producing districts of Cumberland was never so gloomy. An explosion of coal gas occurred on Taesday aboard a Norwegian barque lying in East Bute Dock, Cardiff. The vessel was partially wrecked, and six men badly injured. Three of the boy inmates of the Greenock Industrial School have been apprehended in connection with the recent fire at that institution, and committed on the charge of in- candiarism.

H.M.S. Orlando was successfully launched at Messrs. Pal- mer's shipbuilding yard at Jarrow on Tuesday afternoon in the presence of a large concourse of people. The Orlando is a new type of warship. Lord Lonsdale was fined 40a and costa at the Newcastle City Police Court, on Monday, for assaulting Mr. David de Bensande, tbe husband of Miss Violet Cameron, actress, whose operatic cempany was last week performing at New- castle.

TIE ARMSTRONG CAM—ACTION AGAINST THE "PALL MALL Geznrrn."—The London Evening .lVeles says that pro- ceedings have been commenced in the Queen's Bench Divi- sion by Mr., Mrs., and Eliza Armstrong against Messrs. Thompson and Lambert, proprietors, and Mr. Stead, editor, of the Pall Mall Gazette, and Mr. Bramwell Booth, and Mrs. E. Smith, for libel on all the plaintiffs, and assault on the girl hliza. Damages are laid at £B,OOO. MYSTERIOUS STABBING CASE.—A man named Thomas Martin is lying in a crit,cal condition in Carlisle Infirmary, having been stabbed under circumstances of much mystery. Martin and another man named McLaughlin were out poaching at Castle Shields. The latter says that at about midnight he beard Martin crying for assistance. Ano- ther man was struggling with him. Martin said he bad been stabbed. McLaughlin has been arrested and re- manded.

SUPPOSED MURDER AT BRADFORD.-011 Sunday, Jame- Craig, an Iriah labourer, was apprehended by the bradford police on suspicion of having caused the death of hisjwite on Sunday night. Craig quarrelled with his wife, and during the course of a violent altercation is reported to hays dealt her a blow on the neck. The woman reeled out of the house and fell dead on the pavement. The body has been taken possession of by the police, and awaits a post-mortem examination.

ASSAULT BY A VICAR.—At Doncaster, on Saturday, the Rev. C. W. Manwaring, vicar of Stainton, and Mary Wright, his housekeeper, were charged with assaulting a boy named George Jackson, aged nine, cn July 13th. It was alleged that the boy took a card with "No Primrose dames need apply here" on it to the clergyman, who ordered the house- keeper to tie the boy's legs ; he then thrashed him with a knob stick. For the defence, it was denied that the boy's legs were tied, but the assault was admitted. Wright was dismissed, but Manwaring, who was convicted in 1877 of as- saulting a boy, was fined £5. A NOTORIOUS BURGLAR.—On Monday, before the Mac- clesfield magistrates' Henry Johnson, who has a number of aliases, was charged with breaking out of several houses, and stealing jewelry, lwearing apparel, and other things. Prisoner took lodgings at the respective places, under the pretext that he had got work in the town, and got up early in the morning, ransacked the houses, took whatever ha thought be could coin into money, and decamped. This he has been doing in a wholesale way up and down the country. being "anted" at several places in Lanca- shire, Cheshire, and Staffordshire.—Prisoner was committed for trial. THE KIRICHAM TRAGEDY.—BLIGH RESPITED.-0/1 Sat- urday morning, the Acting Under Sheriffs had received a communication from the Secretary of State for the Home Department informing them that her Majesty has been pleased to respite the capital sentence passed upon Alfred Bligh, late a constable in the Lancashire County Force, who was condemned to death by Mr. Justice A. L. Smith at the Lancaster Assizes on July 13th far the murder of his three children at Kirkham. The culprit received the news with the greatest coolness and indifference. He had previously stated to his father and sister, when on a visit to him in his cell, that he bad no desire to live. THE VIVIAN Roawacz.—" Dr. Vivian," alias Thomas Barnett, was charged before the Whitchurch magistrates on Friday with stealing £7 in money and 20 Roman coins from the Victoria Hotel,Whitchurch. The case excited consider- able interest on accaunt of the prisoner's antecedents. It was alleged that in April last Barnett was discharged from Chatham Prison after undergoing 10 years' penal servitude. By some means he had since become possessed of a consi• derable sum of money, and had been living in great style, and had married a young lady in Birmingham, to whom he represented himself as an American doctor travelling for pleasure. He was committed for trial at Shrewsbury Quar- ter Sessions. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A PIT-BROW GIRL.-0/1 Saturday, Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at Platt Bridge, near Wigan, on the body of Margaret Platt, aged 20, who was killed at the Fir Tree House Colliery, belonging to Messrs. Crompton and Shawcross. The jury, after a lengthy adjournment, returned a verdict of "Accidental death," adding that they thought Mr. Howarth, general ma- nager, Was censurable for allowing a female to lower wag- gons ; they also censured a man named Hilton for giving an order to a girl named Radcliffe without exercising personal superintendence and stated that they considered the system which :flowed females to lower the waggons was reprehensible. The coroner censured both Howarth and Hilton. _ _

Na; HONOITII9.—The Queen has conferred the honour of knighthood on Mr. Serjeant Simon, M.P.; Dr. B. W. Foster, President of the Council of the British Medical Association, and late M.P. for Chester; Mr. J. D. Weston, late M.P. for Bristol ; Mr. C. E. R. Kortright, formerly H.M. Consul at Philadelphia; Mr. E. C. Buck, redresenting the Indian Government at the Colonial and Indian Exhibition; Col. E. B. Sladen, lately political agent in Upper Burmah ; Mr. P. Magnus, the Head of the City Guilds Technical Institu- tion at South Kensington; Mr. John Tomes, F.R.C.S.; Mr. Douglas Maclagan, M.D., Inspector Medical Jurisprudence, University of Edinburgh; Surgeon-General ThoThas Long. more, C. 8., Professor of Military Surgery, Netley ; Mr. Samuel Lewis, late Director of Victualling for the Navy; Mr. Richard Howard, Mayor of Weymouth; Mr. Edward Sievkeing, M.D., Physician Extraordinary to the Queen; Mr. Horace Jones, Architect to the City of London. Lord Monson is to be created a viscount.

ELECTION PETITIONS.-A short time ago it was rumoured in Chester that a petition against the return of Mr. R. A. Yerburgh (Conservative) would be lodged. A couple of well-known lawyers have been engaged upon the matter, and after full inquiries it has been decided not to proceed with the petition.—Although efforts have been made to ob- tain evidence to lodge a petition against the return of the Hon. Elanbury-Tracey, M.P. for the Montgomery Boroughs, the investigation has been of no avail, and no petition will he made. The time expired on Saturday.—Mr. David Davids, ex-M.P. for Cardiganshire, will not demand a scru- tiny of the votes of Mr. Brown Rowland, M.P., who was re- turned by a majority of nine.—Messrs. Rollit and Sors, solicitors, of London and Hull, on Tuesday paid into court he sum of £l.OOO as a guarantee in connection with the pe- tition of Mr. Christopher Sykes (C) against the return to Parliament of Mr. W. A. McArthur for the Buckrose Divi- sion of Yorkshire, on the grounds of incorrect counting of votes, voting by unqualified persons, and other breaches of the Ballot Act.

Charles Lamb was once riding in a stage coach in company with one of those sympathising souls ever on the look out to compassionate affliction. "What a bad cough you have, sir 1" said his companion, after Lamb had recovered from a violent fit of coughing. "I know it," replied Lamb, "but nevertheless it is the best I can do."

Beware of Imitations.— much t RIC 0 the horror of Mrs. Miggles, who shouted to Advt. !niggles to separate them. This feat was at last accom- plished, and the birds were placed in the coop and shut up for the night. At daybreak in the morning, Miggles was aroused by noises proceeding from the coop, and he started out to investigate. He had hardly opened the door when the black hen flew out in an effort to escape, and dashed right in his fare With a wild yoll of alarm tend rago, Mr. Miggles tumbled out of doors and swore until he could have been heard a block away. Mrs. M. rushed to his assistance, aad having got her good man upon his feet and brushed the feathers and dust from his eyes, she looked into the coop; only to find the black rooster dead and the two speckled ones fighting like mad. "Bring me my revolver," roared Mr. Miggles, "and I'll shoot the head off the goldarned nuisances." But Mrs. Miggles was too busy trying to catch the fugitive black hen, which had got into the parlour. It had tried to perch upon the hot stove, and finding it warmer than comfortable was sailing and running around the room, sweeping off ornaments, breaking glasses, and acting as a very mad hen will act when it gets into a tight corner and is chased by a woman and a lap-dog around a room filled with bric-a-brac and nicknacks. Just then Mr. Miggles dashed in to the assistance of his wife, and seizing a porcelain cuspadore, hurled it at the misguided hen, which was struggling to get under a what-not. He missed the bird, but hit the window, and the frightened bird had just sense enough left to see that a hole that was big enough for a cuspadore was big enough for her, so she took it. Marius standing amidst the ruins of Carthage wasn't a circumstance to Mr. Miggles standing amid the ruins of his neat sitting-room, and there was a dangerous glitter in his eye as he reached his revolver out of a drawer and sallied out into the yard. Two shots were fired, and then the angry man came back into the house and threw himself into a chair. "Did you kill the nasty things, dear ?" said his wife, wiping away her tears and referring to the poultry. But before Mr. Miggles had time to answer, the door was thrown open, and the man in the next house stalked in to ask what in thunder Mr. Miggles meant by shoot- ing his dog. One of Mr. Miggles' bullets had done more than it was intended for; it had not only killed one of the birds, but had flown off at a tangent and finished the dog in the next yard. Explanations were made, apologies offered, and Mr. Miggles would willingly pay for the dog. He owned to being mad and reckless, and pleaded that he had been so exasperated that he did not, know what he was doing. "If you doubt it, my dear sir, just look at this cyclone- stricken apartment, andthenaskyourself if you wouldn't have been mad. And this is the work of only one of the feathered fiends." The neighbour took in the situation at a glance, and sympathised with Miggles. Said he: "But I can't understand how it happened that all the birds should have been fighting. Let us go and look what is left of them." They went out and examined the three dead birds. , "Arid are you sure that the bird which went through the window was a hen?" asked the neighbour. The Miggleses hadn't a doubt about it. "Well, I'm glad you'd one hen in the lot, for these ' three stiff uns are all roosters." " What? " "Fact, I assure you. The two speckled roosters have first of all killed the Spanish gentleman, and then were comfortably fighting it out to see which should marry his widow, when you happened in. When you opened the door she dusted, and the two speckled onescontinued their light until you shot them, and a dog .for which I paid 2 dollars 75 cents last Thanksgiving. That's about all there is to it." But Mr. Miggles said that was not all. He was going to break the head of that wretched caitiff on Eight Rod Way, who had palmed upon him a couple of roosters under the pretence that one of them was of the egg-producing persuasion: and seizing a heavy cane, he started off. If the police find any poultry fancier in that district with his head stove in, they may get a hint from the foregoing as to who is responsible for the vengeful deed. His other name will be Miggles.—Fall Riper Ad- vance.

VEGRTABLB MARROWS. Though these have made ample growth, the weather has not been favourable to betting the fruit, except for a few days between the 201-h of last month and the 4th of this, when there was a chance of setting any that might be in flower at that time, and by this the fruit will be fit to cut. If they are to be used young, and if there are no other fruit set on the same shoot, we would cut it out at the same time as the marrow, in order to let more light and air into those left. Marrows that grow on a quantity of decomposed vegetable matter are furnished with bottom heat, and have a more agreeable root run, and they consequently make rampant growth if aupplied with plenty of moisture, which nature has done this week and last In a liberal manner, In the event of the plants becoming crowded, the weakly shoots and those not showing fruit blossom should be cut out. STRAWBERRIRS.—How TO SHCTIRR FRUIT FROM ONE- THAR-OLD PLANTS.—Layer the plants at once in small pots filled with good soil made moderately firm, or on pieces of turf two or three inches square, and two inches thick; in either' case secure the runners down with a small hooked peg or a stone, and supply them with water in dry weather. In about a fortnight they will be well rooted and fit to plant out. Another method ot layering—but not so satisfactory—is to loosen the soil with a small fork or trowel under each runner, and re- place it with a stone on the top. The obvious disad- vantages of this plan are that in taking the plants up many of the roots must get broken, and the plants ex- perience a check. After the plants are rooted, the sooner planting is performed the better, and the ground should be in good condition, either from manure that has been applied to a previous crop, or by digging in half- decayed dung at once, in order to hasten further decay. The way we generally proceed to plant is to stretch the line in the direction the rows are to run, choosing a dull day for the work, so that the roots of the plants may not suffer by being exposed to the rays of the sun, when lifted from their growing place and laid at the right dis- tance in front of the line ready for planting. A con- venient method of planting small numbers would be to make a bed 4ft. wide, with three rows of plants, if t. dis- tant in the row, with an alley on each side for conveni- ence at fruit-picking times. Large breadths may have the rows 18in. distant, still preserving the same space between the plants in the rows, and in this case half the plants—i.e., every alternate one—should be cut out as soon as the fruit is gathered, allowing the re- maining ones to bear a crop the following year. Plants in their third year, according to our experience, rarely pay for their room, and still people persist in allowing them to remain longer than that even.

THE FRONT GARDEN.—Pansies: The cool.",moist season has suited these admirably, and masses of them are flowering freely. Those intending to exhibit must not, however, depend on these kind of plants for winning flowers in good company. They may secure a place if the shoots are thinned out, leaving from two to six of the strongest according to the strength of the plants, and then mulch them with a mixture of soil, decayed manure, and sand, pressing it moderately firm round the stem to prevent oscillation in windy weather, as well as encouraging the growth of surface roots. If after this the plant exhibits signs of swaying, thrust into the ground on either side small twiggy branches such as may be found in a cast-off birch or ling besom. Watering is an important operation in dry weather, but it must not be applied over the flowers, especially in the morning, for some days before the show. All flowers must also be moved as they make their appearance until about three weeks to the time they are wanted, so that the plants' energies may not be prematurely exhausted. Success- ful exhibitors, however, do not depend even on these expedients, but propagate their plants annually, and those that are rooted in August and September produce flowers in April and May, and another batch of cuttings is put in in either of the two latter months, to supply flowers for August and September. The best stimulant for them is soot and guano water applied alternately, and some growers prefer this method of feeding to applying a quantity of decayed manure, as they contend it has a tendency to shorten the existence of the plant, but as this is not the season for planting we will not stay to discuss the question of compost. _ THE REPORTED DISTRESS AT LABRAffiOR. NEW YORK, SUNDAY—It is almost certain that the La- brador horrors are a cruel hoax. A correspondent, whom I know to be trustworthy, telegraphs from Halifax :—" The Rev. Moses Harvey, one of the best informed and most ti unworthy men in Newfoundland, telegraphs that the re- ports of starvation in L4brador and aorthern Newfoundland are false. l`do such reports have reached St. John's, al- though vessels are arriving from these places daily. The fiBheries are improving." A despatch to the "Halifax Herald" from the Attorney-General of the colony says :- 1. The telegrams representing great destitution in Newfound- land are utterly false. Give the same an unqualified con- tradiction. Though hitherto the fisheries have been unsuc- cessful, Newfoundland has no destitution requiring extra means of assistance. There is no such person as the Hon. Mr. Widdell, who has, as alleged, been soliciting aid in Canada. The whole of the statement is a disgraceful canard, ci-culated widely to the detriment of the colouy.—Daily IVews SUPPRESSION OF AN EGYPTIAN PAPER. Cidao, MOND/LY.—EI Zaman, an Arab journal which has supported the English policy, has been suppressed by the Egyptian Administration at the instigation of Moukhtar Pasha. This is a most inconsiderate, ill-advised measure. THE SOUDAN. _ _ _

CAIRO, SATURDAY.—The military authorities regard the state of affairs in the Soudan as promising for the restoration of order and the revival of trade in that region. FRANCE.—THE ELECTIONS.—DISASTROUS FIRES. PA.RIS, SUNDAY NIGHT.—The village of Villard, in the Department of the Hautes Alpee, has been completely destroyed by fire, nothwitbstanding the strenuous efforts of the villagers to extinguish the conflagration. Sixty houses have in all been destroyed, the families of which are with- out shelter. PARIS, MONDAY, 10-45 Aat —Up to the present 1,043 results of yesterday's elections to the Councils-General are known. The candidates returned include 638 Repablicans and 300 Conservatives. Second ballottings will be neces- sary in 107 cases. 14NTES, MONDAY.—A fire, attended with loss of life, oc- curred last night on the fourth floor of a house in Quai de la Fosse, in this town. A child thrown from the window by its mother to save its life died from the effects of the fall, and the charred remains of five persons were found to-day. THE EASTERN QUESTION. VIENNA, MONDAY NIGHT.—The Novae Vremya says that in Russian Government circles some distrust is felt re- specting the inte. view est, Prince Bismarck and Count Kai- noky. It is supposed that the result of their nerotiations will not he completely made known to the Russian Govern- ment, and that some points will be altogether kept secret. The mission of Archduke Karl Ludwig must therefore have a somewhat undecided character, and his declarations can only form the basis of further negotiations between M. de Giers and the Austrian and German ChancVlors. The writer advises Austria not to follow the saggestions of England, which, he says. would derive the greatest advantages from an Austro-Russian war. To come to an agreement upon the future of the Balkan peninsula would be the hest course for both empires to adopt. KISSENGEN, SATURDAY.--Prince and Princess Bismarck left to-day for Munich OR their way to Gastein. SPAIN.—RESIGNATION OF THE FINANCE MINISTER. _

MADRID, SUNDAY.--fe-Ht-e-rd-a—y -afternoon, after Senor Sagasta had read in both Houses of the Cones the Royal Decree suspending the sittings for the usual summer recess, it became known that Senor Camacho had in fact written a letter to denor Sagasta tendering his reeiguation. As in 1883, he retires because his vigorous system of financial reforms has aroused the political opposition of powerful factions, which oppose his policy of retrenchment. 7BE UNITED'STATES AND MEXICO. WASHINGTON, SATURDAY.—Mr. Bayard, Secretary of State, has ordered an investigation to be made into the case of Arresares, the naturalised American citizen from Eagle Pass, Texas, who is alleged to have been shot in Mexico. The excitement od the frontier between Texas and Mexico is incteasing. UNITED STATES AND CANADA.

WASHING-TON, TUESDAY.—A bill has been introduced in the House of Representatives by Mr. Collins, member for Massachusetts, authorising the President to exclude from the United States all Canadian railway cars and vessels. The proposal is intended as a reprisal for the stringent action of the Canadian authorities against American fishing vessels. FOREIGN LANDLORDS IN THE UNITED STATES. PHILADELPHIA, MONDAT.—The House by 20iil votes to six passed the Alien Landlord Bill, affecting the foreign ownership of real estate. It provides that no non-resident alien or foreigner nor any resident alien or foreigner who has not declared his intention to become a citizen of the United States, nor any corporation or association where at most one tenth of its stock or right of property is owned or controlled by aliens or foreigners, shall acquire or own, hold or possess, by right, title, or descent accruing hereafter any real estate in any of the territories of the United States, provided that the provisions of this Act shall not apply to real estate necessary for the construction or working of any railroad.—Later : The Alien Landlord Bill which passed the House, will not be acted upon by the Senate this ses- sion, and will probably not be considered at all. The belief is that the effect of so large a vote in the House will pre- vent the formation of any more United States land or cattle companies in Europe, this being the object of the bill.
TURKEY. ATTEMPT TO ASSASSINATE IHE GRAND VIZIER.

CONSTANTINOPLE, TIIESDAY.-At noon on Sunday last, as the Grand Vizier was stepping from his carriage to enter the Porte for the purpose of presiding at the Council of Ministers, a Mussulman fired three shots from a revolver at His Excellency. He also attempted to fire two others, but tha cartridges did not explode. The three buliets went through the side of the carriage, without, however, touching Kiainil Pasha. The perpetrator of the outrage was immedi- ately arrested. He was found to be a inouhadjir from Adrianople, that is to say a refugee, of the time of the lest Russo-Turkish war, and is a cloekmaker by made. He de- clared that he wished to kill Kiamil Pasha on account of the injustice which he had suffered at the time of Kiamil Pasha's direction of the Ministry of Justice, during Heiman Felimi Pasha's mission in London. THE CHOLERA. _ _ _

- TRIESTE, WEDNESDAY.—During tbe last 24 hours 7 cases of cholera and four deaths have occurred here. Fwars, WEDNESDAY.—Tbere have been two deaths from cholera here during the last 24 hours. ROME, WEDNESDAT.—The cholera returns for the past 24 hours report 16 cases and 13 deaths at Ravenna, 11 cases and 5 deaths at Bologna, 1 case and 1 death at Treviso, 25 cases and 3 deaths at Castlefranco, 9 cases and 4 deaths at Monte- helluna, 14 cases at Caerano' 14 cases and 6 deaths at Ve- rona, 3 cases and 1 death at Padua, 16 cases and 4 deaths at Piazzola, 6 cases at Venice, Pelves and 4 deaths at San Michele Tagliamento, and 3 cases and 1 death at Chioggia. AMERICA..—DEATiI OF MR. TILDEN. NEW YORE, WEDNESDAY.— Mr. Samuel icnes Tilden, the well-known leader of the Democratic party, died this morning at his residence, Greystone, on the Hudson, near this city. He expired peacefully at a quarter to nine o'clock, only his niece and two physicians being present.
ANTI-VACCINAT lON .-ANOTHER FINE.

Before Colonel McCorquodale, Mr. T. J. Gilles- pie, C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, Michael Cannel was summoned for neglecting to have his child vaccinated. Mr. Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, deposed to having served the necessary notices, and he had informed Mrs Cannel that if the child was ill she was to get a certificate from Dr. Wat- kins. Mrs Cannel (who appeared for her husband) told the Bench that the child, had been suffering from an abscess under its arm, and she was quite willing to have the child vaccinated when it re- covered. She had previously had two children vac- cinated. Dr. Patterson had told her on the previous day (Friday) that the child was not fit to be vaccin- ated. The case was postponed for a month.— Patrick McDermott was summoned for a similar offence, and Mr. Cooper said defendant had re- peatedly promised to have the child vaccinated, hut it had not been done. The defendant said the child was very ill.—Colonel McCorquodale (chair- man): Have you brought a doctor's certificate? Defendant: No ; I have not had any doctor to it. —Chairman : Are you willing to have the child vaccinated? Defendant: Yes, I have had two done alreadv.—This case was also adjourned for a month. --Robert Taylor, for whom Mrs Taylor appeared, was summoned for failing to carry out a magis- trates' order to have the child vaccinated. Mr. Cooper said he saw Mrs Taylor on the previous Tues- day morning and she then said her child was not vaccinated, and she added that if she could have her own way she would not have it done. The Chair- man (to Mrs Taylor) : Why is he not vaccinated? Mrs Taylor: I don't believe in it. If it did the child any good thele would beno need to bebrought here, because I should be glad to have him done. But I have seen the fruits of vaccination, and I would sooner serve a week in gaol than have him done.—The Chairman: Will you tell your husband that the case has been heard and that you were . told the law requires a child should be vaccinated, and. we are bound to inflict a fine in the case of every child unvaccinated? Your husband will, be fined 2s 6d and costs.

FATAL ACCIDENT.—At noon on Thursday a mason, about 28 years of age, was working on the first floor of the new rown Hall at Burnley, when a staying supporting a derrick gave way. The alarm was given, and the deceased ran to get out of the way, when he fell headlong into the cellat beneath, a distance of about 25 feet,•and was killed almost instantaneously. Some fine batting was shown on the part of Lancashire by Barlow, Lancashire, and Rob- inson, who made 71, 64, and 73 respectively, repeated changes of bowling by six of the Cheshire men having little effect upon them. Mr. R. H. Moss, of Huyton, played for the county for the first time and scored 9 not out. For Cheshire, Mr. C. H. Parr, of Chelford, made his first ap- pearance. Cheshire made a very poor show in batting en Tuesday, and were defeated by an innings and 140 runs. On the previous day :they bad lost four wickets for 31 runs, and on Tweslay the other six fell in half an hour for the ad- dition' of 22 rune. In the second innings, owing to Ow fine batting of Davenport and Pointon, wlao between them made 100. NOTES BY THE WAY.

On Saturday, at Bennington Oval, Surrey gained a splen- did victory over the Australians by an innings and 209 runs. This is the most severe defeat ever sustained in England by an Australian team. At the drawing of stamps on Friday evening the game stood—Australians, first innings, 185; Surrey, first innings, with only three wickets down, 427. Surrey's innings was completed at a few minutes before one o'clock for 501. Abel was out before a run had been added to the over-night score, and Maurice Read was dis- missed at 469 by a wonderful catch at mid-on. Abel's 144 included 14 fours, seven threes, and 20 twos; while Read's 186—a record score against Australian bowling in England —comprised 23 fours, 12 threes, 10 twos, and 38 singles. On the Trent Bridge Ground at Nottingham on Saturday there was a good batting performance shown on the part of the Notts batsmen. No fewer than 319 runs were scored for the loss of but three wickets. The hero of the achieve- ment was Barnes, who went in first wicket down at 51, and was out third at 304, having scored 156 out of 253. In all he was batting for four hours and 25 minutes. His figures weie 11 fours, 11 threes' and 21 twos. Gunn hit finely for his not out 80, in which were five fours, four threes, and 13 twos; while in Shrewsbury's 66 were three fours, seven threes, and eight twos. In all 664 runs were scored for the loss of 13 wickets. Lancashire and Yorkshire met again at Dewsbury on Satut day, when the play was thoroughly interesting, and was followed with attention by a large number of spectators. The three outstanding Yorkshire wickets fell in less than half an hour for the addition of 15 runs, the innings clos- ing for 112. Lancashire scored 21 for one wicket in three- quarters of an hour before lunch, and afterwards raised their total to 40 with only one man out. Briggs then had to leave, and so complete a collapse then ensued that in three- quarters of an hour the innings was all over for 13 more runs. In the second innings of Yorkshire Bates scored 30 by brilliant cricket, and Ulvett, too, hit well. At the finish Yorkshire with three wickets to fall had a lead of 166 runs, so the draw was distinctly in favour of the home connty„ At Derby on Wednesday, after an interesting contest, Gloucestershire defeated the hone county by 47 runs. o vernight each side had completed an innings, and Glou- cestershire besides had lost three wickets in their second attempt for 30 runs. Thus on continuing the visitors. with

An hour and twenty minutes on Wednesday finished off the match at Canterbury, the Australians again being badly beaten—this time by ten wickets. The last four Austr,lian wickets put on 35 runs in three•quarters of an hour, and then Kent, who wanted 32 to win, got the runs in 35 minutes without losing a wicket. There were no features ef intermit in the play, but Kent must be congratulated on 4 brillioat victory, thoroughly well earned by excellent all-1 sound cricket. A victory for Kent was certain when play ceased en Tueri-1 day evening, for against the Kent total of 171 the Austra- lians had finished a first innings of 79, and following on in a minority of 92 had lost six wickets for 88, so that with , only four wickets to go down the Colonists were still fouri rune behind. The Surrey men did not succeed in their efforts to save the match against Notts at Kennington Oval, and were ' beaten by seven wickets. Altogther it was a capital match, and the Nottinghamshire men are to be congratulated on their victory.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. it,,berts (chairman), Messrs. Brown, Clarke, Forster. Gibson, William Houghton, John Houghton, Ratcliffe, Isherwood, Jolley, Har- rison, Balharry, Kashall, Owen, Grsnge, Heaton, Strange, Broadbent (ex-officio), J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. NORSE COMMITTEE. The committee reported that the usual leave of absence had been granted Mrs. Mackey for 14 days, and recommen- ded that steps be taken to get the boy John Warrington on the ship Clio.—On the motion of Mr. CLARE, seconded by Mr. FORSTER. the minutes were passed.

SCHOOLS COMMI TIME. The minutes of the Schools Committee stated that atten- tion had been called to the cost of the fiAtt supplied far the use of the officers, and it was explained by the t.,tiperinten- dent that although it occasionally occurred that the cost of the fish exceedtd the cost of buteht-rs' meat, it was other- wise on the average. The superintendent reported the chil- dren to be ell well.—On the motion of the Cuantmart, se- conded by Mr. JOLLEY, the minutes wore confirmed.

SCHOOL FEES AND OUT RELIEF. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in a total of 79 cases, 60 of which were old and 19 new cases.—Mr. Bnovers moved, and Mr. HARRISON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. RATCLIFFE asked how the amount of fees allowed corresponded with those allowed twelve months ago.—Mr. Bnower said there was a very considerable increase.—Mr. ISHERWOOD wished to keow upon what basis school fees were allowed.—The CLERK said that was a difficult matter to explain, but he would advise Mr. Isherwood to attend one of the meetings of the committee, and he would there gather far more informa- tion than any one could give him.—Mr. BROWN said that in dealieg with school fees they could not have one fixed line. They had an imaginary line with which they endea- veured to square everything, but there might be very many surrounding circumstances of a case, welch they had to take into consideration. Up till within the present year they had gone on very economically in granting these fees, but during the last six or nine months things had been going from bad te) worse, and, he was sorry to say, they had had te increase their fees continually. There were families they were sorry to have to allow for.—Mr. BROADBENT said the Boatel would no doubt be anxious to know whether the in- crease of fees was the result of increasing poverty in the town, or whether it arose from the easiness of the com- mittee in allowing fees.—Mr. BROWN: Not the latter.—The Outwears thought that the increase of the number of per- sons out of employ accounted for the increase of school fees.—Mr. JOLLEY said the gist of the whole matter was that people had less employment, if not totally out ef em- ployment. The committee did not grant fees where there was the slightest possibility of the people paying for them- selves.—Mr. ISHERWOOD remarked that his experience showed that many people got school fees who did not de- serve them.—Mr. HARRISON mentioned that the committee before graoting fees always fortified themselves with the opinion of Mr. Shearer, who, in his opinion, was a most in- defatigable and conscientous officer. (Hear. hear.) They might rely upon it that the increase in the number of cases did not arise from any relaxation of stringency on the part of the committee.—The CLERK mentioned that there was a considerable increase in the number of people in the Work- house, and in the amount of out-relief, as well as in school fees —Mil BROWN thought the out-relief allowances of money •ught to be regulated by the price of provisions. Now, when the cost of provisions was so low, they ought not to give the same amount as they did when provisions were high, but he was not aware that they had seduced it. —The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Brown should bear in mind that the judgment of the committee which administered relief was given as IO each ease, and the question of the value of the money given was gone into.—Mr. BROWN said his ex- perience did not lead him to think that. It was much easier for their officers to give money than to give relief in kind. —The CHAIRMAN said that sometimes when he had sugges- ted relief in kind the officer present said he really could not find time.—Mr. Baowee : Time used to be found.—The CHAIRMAN thought when there was a doubt as to hew the money would be used it was best that goods should be eiven.—The subject then dropped, the minutes of the School Fees Committee having been approved.

div.head: FATAL RIOTS IN BELFAST.
div.p: FATAL RIOTS IN BELFAST.

Rioting was renewed at Belfast on Saturday night. 1 Between eight and nine o'clock a band passed up to- 1 wards the disturbed quarter. Some Sunday School excursion parties had passed by a few minutes before, and there was much excitement. The result was that stone-throwing was soon freely indulged in on both sides. Many persons were injured. Colonel Forbes, RAI., and three policemen, were taken to the Royal Hospital at the close of the disturbances and had their wounds dressed. Several civilians were also suffering from wounds inflicted by stones. William Wallace received a bullet wound through the thigh. A lad, named Knox, was carried in dead, shot through the chest and right leg. Many shots were fired, and it is stated that the police fired on the mob twice. In ad- dition to the lad who was shot dead a great many policemen and civilians were wounded. Many arrests were made. On Sunday evening the police were distributed in parties through the disturbed parts of the town, several magistrates being with them at the most dan- gerous points. Three or four public-houses were wrecked and looted in the oeurse of Saturday night's rioting. The military, both horse and foot, were out on duty in the streets. Amongst the public-houses attacked was one belonging to a man named Riordan. Shots were there fired. The police were ordered to fire upon the mobs two or three times. A number of the persons injured were treated by medical men in the vicinity of the Old Lodge Road and Shankhill Road and not taken to tho hospital. The police were badly stoned. They at first used their batons freely, but in consequence of the violence of the mobs they were obliged to use their rifles. The disturbance, which commenced in the vicinity of Carlisle Circus and Clifton-street, extended towards the more dangerous and disturbed districts of Shankhill RoAd and Old Ledge Road, and it was there that it was maintained to an advanced hour. On Monday morning the streets in the disturbed districts had assumed their normal aspect, but the wrecked premises were being proteeted by armed police. The injured persons at the Royal Hospital were reported to be doing well. The most serious oases were those of Thomas Lemon and Thos. Mcßurney, who are suffering from gunshot wounds in the forehead and chin respectively. No less than 107 cases were disposed of at the Belfest Police Court on Monday in connection with the disturbances. The Rev. R. Kane, Grand Master of the Orangemen of Belfast, issued an ad- dress congratulating the members of their body on their not being implicated in the disorders, although a hostile " press" had spoken of Orange riots. He counsels the members of that body to abstain from atone throwing, and not to depart even in sympathy from respect for constituted authority, and to assist in the restoration of tranquility. Rioting again took place at Belfast on Monday night. In York-street and adjoining thoroughfares abets were fired with fatal effect by the police. A young man named George Williamson was wounded by a bullet in the chest, and died while being conveyed to Dr. Gault's surgery. A man named Thompson, tailor, was shot while tbe police were facing a riotous mob in Little George-street. The premises of Mr. Sharman and Mr. Stephen McKenna, publi- cans, in Little George-street, were wrecked. Two detectives were severely beaten, and one badly stabbed in the face. On Wednesday the disturbed districts in the town re- sumed their normal aspect. The ab.ence of an', serious rioting on Tuesday night was attributable to the vigilance of the authorities and to the reinforcements of military and police. There was no perceptible change is the condition .of the wounded at the hospital.

div.head: SPOOPENDYKE'S SUSPENDERS.
div.p: SPOOPENDYKE'S SUSPENDERS.
..,,a "Now, :my dear," said Mr. Spoopendyke, as he stretched himself and drew on his pantaloons, "syou're cleaned these trousers up first rate. This is what I call co

inomy. It saves money. If I'd taken 'em to the tailor's it would have cost a couple of dollars at least, and you've saved just that amount" And Mr. Spoopen- dyke went to his ablutions, and then pulled on his shirt.

"I'll clean your coat, too, if you like," said Mrs. ftoopendyke. "Leave it at home some day and I'll take this spot out of the sleeve." And Mrs. Spoopen- dyke bustled around and looked delighted with the idea of pleasing her husband. "Where's my suspenders?" asked Mr. Spoopendyke, screwing himself around and looking down his back. "You didn't clean the suspenders clear out of sight, did you ? " "They were there when you put on your pants," said Mrs. Spoopendyke. "I havn't touched them. What did you do with them?" "Oh, yes, certainly, I did something with them What d'ye s'pose I did with them? Think I set 'em up in business somewhere, don't ye? Got an idea I gave 'em a vacation to go fishing, haven't ye? Well, I didn't, and mor'n that I didn't send them away to be educated for the ministry. Where's my suspenders? Where'd you put 'em? &pose I'm going around holding these pants up all day? Think I got no business interests be- side holding on my breeches with both hands? What did you do with the measly things?" "I know I didn't take them off the pants," said Mrs. Spoopendyke, pulling open the bereau drawers and hustling things round in a vain endeavour to find the missing articles. "Maybe I can fix your pants so you won't need any suspenders to-day, and I'll find them before night," sug- gested Mrs. Spoopendyke. "That's it. You've got it," raved Mr. Spoopendyke. "How are you going to fix 'em? Going to tie them on with a shoestring, like you do your bustle? Going to walk round behind me all day and hold 'em on? P'r'aps you can pull 'em up and button 'em around my neck! How d'ye suppose to fix 'em? Going to put 'm on me upside down so if they fall they'll fall up? If I had your head I'd go out to service as a file. Fix 'em, why don't ye? Why don't ye fix 'em! These trousers are getting sick at the stomach, waiting to be fixed !" And Mr. Spoopendyke shot across the room and drove under the wardrobe in search of the lost suspenders. "They must be somewhere." "Show 'em to me then !" demanded Mr. Spoopendyke. "Take a stick and point 'em out to me! Of course they're here somewhere, only just put your thumb on 'em! What have ye done with 'em? Can't ye recollect whether ye made 'em up into hatbands for the heathen like you did my dressing-gown, or whether you planted them to see if they would grow, like you did my straw hat? S'pose those suspenders have taken their girl to a picnic? What kind of housekeeping d'ye call this any how? Where's my suspenders ?' howled Mr. Spoopen- dyke, poking around in the soiled-clothes bag. "Where's those suspenders?" and he pulled the books off the shelf and rummaged around behind the case with a broom handle for a divining-rod. "Just let me buckle them tight behind," said Mrs. Spoopendyke; "the strap will hold them." "That's the scheme," shrieked Mr. Spoopendyke; "something's got to hold them! If I was as sharp as you I'd get rich hiring out for an oyster knife. All you want is to have somebody sit cross-legged on you, and come home two weeks after you're expected to be a tailor's shop! Going to find those dog-gasted suspenders between now and the next war ?" I know they were on his pants when he put them on," mused Mr. Spoopendyke, entering upon a little vin- dictive reasoning. He didn't take them off, and so they must be there now." And the good woman approached her husband with a smile. "Oh ! now, they're going to be fixed," said Mr. Spoopendyke, with a horrible grin. " P'eaps you're going to cut buttonholes in your hands and feet, and hang over my shoulder , ain't ye? Want me to put 'em on over my head, like a measly shirt with a tuck and a flounce in it, don't ye? Maybe you think those sus- penders hurried down to breakfast, so's to get the first crack at the morning paper, don't you ?" But Mrs. Spoopendyke made no response. Opening the back of her husband's fluttering skirt, she saw the missing suspenders. He had slipped them over his shoulders before assuming the muslin, and had forgotten all about them. "Smart as a whip, ain't ye," growled 'Mr. Spoopen- dyke, as he drew off his shirt and let the suspenders down. "If my head was as clear as yours I'd hire out for a church bell. You only need four lenses and a drop of rain water to be a microscope." And Spoopendyke hurried on his clothes and scuttled down-stairs to get the morning paper before his wife could make a clutch at it

THE ORATPENHALL ELECTION.—IITTENDED INQUIRY. A communication to the clerk from Mr. Henley, Local Government Board inspector, was read, and it stated that that gentleman intended to hold an inquiry into the recent election of a guardian for the township of Grappenhall on Tuesday next. The inquiry was as to the validity of cer- tain votes.—Mr. FORSTER Will It be an open inquiry ? The Cutstx : Oh, yes.

VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN.—INTERESTING DISCUSSION. The CLERK said that in reply to the inquiry be was di- reefed at the last meeting of the Board to make to the Local Government Board as to certain proposed proaecutions of Earlestown anti•vaecinators, he had received the following reply :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 21st nit. with , reference to the administration of the Vaccination Acts in ! the Warrirgton Union, and in reply I am to state that where proceedings have been taken and a penalty inflicted under' section 31 of the Vaccination Act, 1867, it is for the Guar- dians to decide whether further proceedings shall or shall not be taken in respect of the same child. It would not be in accordance with the Board's practice to express an 1 op,nion upon any particulai.case. Their views, however, 1 on the considerations which ought to be weighed by the , Guardians before giving their decision are expressed in a 1 letter which the Board addressed to the Guardians of the Evesham Union on the 17th September, 1875, of which a eapy is enclosed.- I am, sir, your obedient servant, C. N. DAL- TON, assistant secretary." The letter to the Evesham Guar- dians referred to above was dated 17th September, 1875, and was in answer to an inquiry whether the Guardians of the Evesham Union had under the Vaccination Acts any dis- cretionary powers to abstain from taking further legal pro- ceediegs against persons who had once been fined for not complying with the law by having their children vaccinated. The Local Government Board said:—" It is distinctly con- templated by atticles 16 of the Board's General Order of the 31st October, 1874, that, independently of any proceedings which may be taken against the person in default, under section 29 of the Vaccination Act, 1867, the vaccination officer shall be authorised to take proceedings against him if he continue contumacious at least once also under sec- tion 31 of that Act. Until, therefore, proceedings under the latter section have been taken in a case and a conviction obtained, the Board considered that the several means which the law provides with a view to ensura the vaccination of a child have not been used. The Board at the same time direct me to point out that by article 16 of their above-mentioned order it is provided that in any case in which a magistrate's order has been obtained, and summary proceedings have been taken under section 31 of the Vaccination Act, 1867, no further proceedings shall be taken by the vaccination officer without the express in- structions of the guardians. The intention of this provision is that the guardians should carefully consider with regard to each individual case the effect which a continuance of 1 proceedings is likely to have in procuring the vaccination of the individual child, and in insuring the observance of the ' law in the Union generally. The Board may further state that it is, on the one hand, undeniable that a repetition of 1 legal proceedings has, in numerous cases, resulted in the i vaccination of a child when such vaccination has not been I procured by the previous proceedings; and it is therefore , important, with the view of securing a proper observance of ' the law, that parents should be well assured that proceed- ings in case of non-complence with its requirements will not be lightly discontinued. On the other hand, the Board are i prepared to admit that, when in a particular case repeated prosecutions have failed in their object, it becomes neces- sary to carefully consider the question whether the continu- ance of a fruitless contest with the parent may not have a tendency to produce mischievous results, by exciting sym- pathy with the person prosecuted, and thus creating a more extendrd opposition to the law. The Board entertain no doubt that, in all cases of the kind in question, the guar- dians, having before them the preceding observa- tions, will not fail to exercise the discretionary powers confided to them in the manner best calculated to give effect to the policy of the law." —The CLERK said that before they discussed that they would perhaps permit him to remind them that it had been the practice of that Board to enforce with considerable de- termination the Vaccination Acts. They took all persons failing to comply with the Acts before the magistrates at Newton, but they never went a second time in respect to the same child. The magistrates having that in their mind put on a fine of £1 in each case, and there was an end of it. But afterwards the magistrates at Newton for some reason or other reduced the penalty to ss, and then actually reduced it to is. (Mr. Harrison: That is childishness.) He (the clerk) thought that in no case now was the penalty more than 2e. 6d. He would suggest that, as they on their part had tried to enforce these Acts, and as the magistrates, who were presumed to have an absolute knowledge of the locality, thought fit to impose only a nomioal fine, it was a question whether, when a parent had been fined once and they had distrained upon his pods and created a commo- tion in the neighbourhood in order to enforce the penelty, they should take these people in court a second time, seeing that the megistrates who could fine SI only fined is. These refusals to have children vaccinated were confined to Earles- town, and he quite agreed with the remaiks made by some one at that Board that if no further proceedings were taken that would not induce others to change their course in respect to vaccination. He believed that the fact that these people remained obstinate had no injurious effect on the rest of the people. He was of opinion that the anti-vac- cinators would remain anti-vaccinators, but be did not think their proceedings induced other people to join them. I Of course if be were wrong he would be corrected.—Mr. CLARKE: That is so.—Mr. BROWN said they had a duty to perform, and that duty they ought to perform, irrespective of the Newton magistrates. He thought the law ought to be enforced. He did not fear but that educated people, wise people, people of average mind, would adopt the wisest plan, and have their children vaccinated.
