"Gladstone ends and Castlereagh begins?' An important meeting of Unionist Liberal members of the House of Commons was held at Devonshire House, on Thursday, under the presidency of the Marqu,s of Harting- ton. Among those present were Mr. Goscoen, Mr. Cham- berlain, Sir H. James, and Mr. Heneage. Lord Hartington congratulated the meeting on the action of the Unionist Liberals in the last Parliament, which had, he said, been approved by the constituencies. The Liberal Unionists now held the balance of power instead of Mr. Parnell, and he hoped that their position would be used for the good of the country. If the Government required more time to consider their Irish policy and to elaborate their measures he thought it should be coaceded to them. Mr. Chamberlain concurred in Lord Hartington's remarks. He said be recognised his 'lordship as their leader, and he was prepared to support all his actions. The passing of a vote of shanks to Lord Hartington brought the proceedings to a close. RETIRING MINISTERS' VISIT TO OSBORNE. On Wednesday the actual transference ef the seals of office from the retiring to the newly appointed Ministers took place with all due ceremony at Osborne. The mem- bers of the out-going Liberal Cabinet assembled at Vic- toria Station, where a special train was waiting for the Ministers, who began to arrive shortly after nine. Mr. Childers, on reaching the station, took his seat in a saloon carriage. He was followed by Sir William Harcourt, who walked up the platform with Sir John Rose. Lord Rose- ben, drove up in his brougham, and soon afterwards Mr. Catnpbell-Bannernien and Sir Ughtred J. Kay-Sbuttleworth (Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster) walked down the platform, and were met by Sir William Harcourt. Earl Spencer next joined his colleagues, and in a few moments Lord Herschel! enteied the saloon. Earl Kimberley was the last to reach the station, just as the train was preparing to start. Mr. Lennox Peel, clerk to the Privy Council, accom- panied the Ministers, and Sir John Rose and Sir John Drummond Hay also proceeded by the same train, which left at half-past nine. Mr. Gladstone had already taken leave of her Majesty on Saturday, and Earl Granville is still too much of an invalid to undertake so long a journey. There was a small crowd outside the platform barriers, but no demonstration was made. The special train arrived at Portsmouth at 11-30, and the Ministers at once proceeded to the Duchess of Coenaught Isle of Wight steamer, which had been specially chartered. As the right hon. gentlemen aighted their admirers raised a hearty cheer, and there was a good deal of respectful rais- ing of hats, which was repeatedly acknowledged. The ves- sel at once steamed out of the harbour. On arrival at the Cowes Royal Landing Stage at half-past twelve several royal carriages were in waiting. On reaching Osborne House, a mile distant, the Ministers were at once admitted to their final audience of the Queen. The new Ministers commenced to arrive at Victoria Sta- tion shortly after eleven, and a special train was there pro- vided to convey them to Portsmouth, en route to Osborne, to receive their seals of office and to kiss bands on appoint- ment. Lord Salisbury was escorted up the platform by Mr. Henry Manners, his private secretary, and took a seat alone in a first-class compartment, the other Ministers bay- ing previously taken their seats in saloon carriages attached to the train. The steamer Duchess of Edinburgh conveyed them across the Solent, meeting the outgoing Ministers re- turning to Portsmouth. The latter found a special train there awaiting them, and they arrived at Victoria Station at half-past five. Lord Her- schel!, however, remained at Cowes, and the train was stopped at Epsom for the convenience of Lord Rosebery, who alighted and drove to the Durdans. The Ministers who went on to town drove away from the station without any demonstration being made.

div.p: MINISTRIES, like the beings of which they are composed, are fearfully and wonder- fully made; and the Prime Minister, whether Liberal or Tory, whether the result of his labours be ill or well received, cannot but feel glad when the job is over. Lord SALISBURY has had an exceptionally difficult task, and if he has not wholly succeeded we are not dis- posed to blame him. When the raw material is indifferent, it is impossible for the manu- factured article to be first class. It is all very well for harum-scarum politicians, like Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, to say---" Get rid of the old gang and start afresh." An old gang is not easily got rid of at any time, and the way is not made easier when there is so much about the new gang that is questionable. Lord:lSAusßußY probably thinks that it is quite a sufficient leap in the dark to make Lord R. CHURCHILL Chancellor of the Ex- chequer and Leader of the Conservative party in the House of Commons; and there is plenty of evidence that a large number of his supporters are Of the same way of think- ing. The member for South Paddington will have to alter a great deal, or he will bring discredit upon himself, upon his party, and upon the House of Commons. The Tories are indeed demoralised when they are con- strained to accept for leader an upstart who has been described by Mr. PARNELL as "a political welsher," and "the gutter sparrow of politics." It is morally wrong, and what- ever is morally wrong can never be politically right, as they will most likely find to their sorrow before many months are over. We cannot but remark that Lord RANDOLPH'S appointment is something like an insult to Lord HARTINGTON, to whom the Tories are so much indebted for their being in office at the present moment. The member for Rossendale has an instinctive abhorrence of a politician who is devoid of self-respect, and who has neither fixity of purpose nor of principle; and we are well persuaded that his alliance with the Tories, slight as it is, will not last long if it is to depend on con- tact with Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL. The admirers of the member for South Padding- ton seem to think that, because he has shown some capacity to "split the ears of the groundlings," he will be a match for the Liberal leader; but they forget that he will not now have a gallery audience, and that the gallery style will not do, night after night, in the House of Commons. Lord RANDOLPH tried a fall with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN on the question of the Birmingham riots; he selec- ted his own time and mode of attack, and it is notorious that he was worsted in the en- counter. How is he likely to fare when he grapples with a greater than Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN? He will go to pieces like the earthen pitcher against the iron pot. We have no fear for Mr. Gladstone, and, as we have no regard for Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, we shall be able to watch the struggle in the House of Commons with undisguised satisfaction. Sir RICHARD CROSS has had a difficulty in getting a place in the new Cabinet; put he has squeezed in as Secretary for India, and is to be " promoted" to the Peerage. It would seem that the new leader in the Commons would not have Sir RICHARD near him; and, so that he was got out of the way, he didn't

much care what became of him. Sir JOHN GORST is to be Under-Secretary for India ;. and, as he will remain in the House of Com- mons, he will, so far as this department is concerned, be Lord RANDOLPH'S right- hand man. Our " neutral " contemporary, while belauding Sir RICHARD CROSS in the customary fulsome style (where a Tory is con- cerned) says There has been a hitch somewhere—in fact Sir RICHARD loved the Newton Division and the Home Office, and had no ambition to be a lord." It is awful to think of the member for Newton being thus severed from his loves, and it would' seem that a t errible wrong has been done. What has Lord SALISBURY been about not to see that Sir RICHARD CROSS was a bprn Home Secretary? It is too bad to let a no- body like Mr. HENRY MATTHEWS leap into his place. As Sir RICHARD himself would say (when RICHARD'S not himself)—" We are getting somewhat mixed." But who knows? He may have his revenge; Mr• MATTHEWS is required to seek re-election at the hands of his constituents of East Birming- • ham, and its just possible that he may be rejected. He obtained his seat by the aid of Liberal voters whose chief object was to' ensure that Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill shored not become law. That object having been attained, Liberals may well ask themselves why they should be called upofl. at a bye election, to .vote for a Tory pure and simple. There is many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip. Mr. MATTHEWS may find his duties as Home Secretary will necessarily be confined to home, and then Sir RICHARD CROSS will be happy.

MR. DANIEL ADAMSON has replied in Vigorous terms to the questionable and un- provoked strictures on the Ship Canal Sche ine by Sir EDWARD WATKIN at the half-yearly meeting of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. He proceeds to shoW that, if there is a difficulty in floating the pre- sent scheme on account of the cost, tha.t.. difficulty would be enormously increased 11 they were to endeavour, as Sir EDWARD sug- gests, to construct a tidal waterway. The present project is estimated to cost eight millions at the outside, but investigations which have been made show that a tidal waterway would cost from thirty to forty millions sterling, to say nothing of such a waterway being of much less value to works built alongside the canal. Mr. ADAMSON hits Sir EDWARD pretty hard as to his rail- way management ; but this is a matter for the consideration of holders of railway stock, rather than for the general public. It is, of course, to the point to show that the chair- man of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire Railway is not quite such a great authority as he wonld make himself out to be; Mr. ADAMSON denies that he has ever said "Messrs. ROTHSCHILD had undertaken t 0 find the capital upon a commission of one per cent " ; but, admitting that he is jus- tified in giving this statement a direct con- tradiction, it is not to be denied that an impression was abroad that Messrs. ROTHS— CHILD would find the money, and this erro- neous impresssion has, in our judg- ment, had much to do with the in- difference shown by the public in the matter of taking up shares. Mr. ADAMS SON frankly admits that it was a great misfortune" that four days only were allowed to the public to subscribe; it was his convic- tion that the time was too short; but this, it seems, was a matter which Messrs. ROTHS- CHILD insisted should be left to them. A great mistake was made—a mistake which; will not be repeated, and which, it is to be hoped, is not irreparable. The Directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company are "disappointed, and to some extent dis- couraged; but they are not seriously dis- heartened nor dismayed ; " they hope to be able to go forward with and carry out the the great scheme which they have projected;- but whether they will be successful or not depends upon the response which is made by the investing public when the scheme is brought forward under new and under more auspicious circumstances. There will be a reaction after the present heavy depression; there will be a turn in the tide of public favour, and it will be for the directors to en- deavour to take advantage of that turn, and lead on to fortune.

It is very gratifying to see that the August holiday season is being more and more made use of by the advocates of temperance as an opportunity for displaying the strength of their came. Since our last issue, there have been Temperance Demonstrations at War- rington, F.arlestown, Huyton, Runcorn, and Weston; and there is every evidence that the young, at any rate, are being brought up with a full knowledge of the mischief of a traffic which has been described as more terribly de- structive than war, pestilence, and famine. Progress is being made, but it is slow pro- gress ; and we should be better satisfied if temperance men would unite to give effect to their principles during an election campaign. It is of little use preaching temperance, year in and year out, and then voting for a brewer to become a member of Parliament. Precept is a good dog, but Practice is a better. The English Church was late in the field with her temperance or- ganisations; but excellent work has been done of late years, and we look forward to a time when, uniting with leaders of other de- nominations, it will be possible to compel the Legislature to grant popular control of the liquor traffic. There is scarcely a town in the United Kingdom in which there are not far too many drink shops. The law pre- supposes that no license shall be granted un- less it is in the interest of the inhabitants ; but unfortunately the inhabitants are not consulted, and public-houses and beershops are thrust upon them to their physical, mental, and moral injury. What are called the " better :lasses " are certainly better in this respect; they take care for the most part to keep" houses for the sale of intoxicating drinks at a respectable distance from their respectable families. They have friends in court; they are hand and glove with licensing magistrates ; indeed, some of them are them- selves magistrates ; and they have sufficient regard for Number One to keep these houses from their doors. We do not quarrel with them for doing this ; they are wise in their day and generation ; but what we urge is that if a right of veto is good for them it is good for others—that, in short, the mass of the people should have power given them to protect themselves, as they do, from the evils of the drink traffic.

OTWO SAILORS BLOWN TO PIECES.—News was received at Davenport, on Monday, of a fatal accident which oc- curred on boatd 11. M S. Opal, at Sydney. A salute was being fired from the ship, when, after one of the rounds, a gun's crew omitted to sponge out the gun when fired. A charge was put in the gun, and was being rammed home, when it went off, and the two men who were serving the gun were plown away from the muzzle. One of them was instan:iy shattered to fragments, and the other died the same right.

The writ has been issued for filling the vacancy in the Newton Division ; Sir Richard Cross has prepared his farewell to the electors, and the Address of Mr. T. W. Legh, the new Tory candidate, is being printed. "The Liberal Home Ruler" is the title of a new penny paper. It advocates Home Rule and Imperial Parliamentary Federation ; the articles are well written, and, as there is room for such a journal, it ought to succeed.

The original estimates for the alterations. Sm., of the St. Helens Town Hall amounted to £5,539 ; but the total cost his reached £7,933—that is £2,396 more. These extras -----oh these extras—they are awful, irrepressible things! There are not many foremen who, like Mr. William Williamson, of the Vulcan Works, Earlestown, can say they have occupied one post for +I years. Mr. Williamson was the recipient of a handsome testimonial on Saturday last ; and he carries with him, in his retirement, the best wishes alike of masters and of men.

-- It seems that somebody has been playing tricks as to the alleged summary of the final report of the Royal Commission on Trade Depression. The Commission is still Sitting, and, though a draft report has been prepared, it is just possible that it may be subject to considerable alteration. ,

"The New House of Commons" is the title of the latest" extra" of "The Pall Mall Gazette." Its racy " mems. " about mem- bers are accompanied in many cases with por- traits ; and, besides several valuable maps, there is a complete record of the General Election of 1886. The" extra" is published at sixpence, and is absurdly cheap at the Price,

"The Daily .News was caught napping when it asserted that Lord Randolph Church- ill's appointment to the Leadership of the Tories was especially welcome to I\lr. Glad- stone. The statement was absurd on the face of it. It is not in the nature of things for Dignity to be in love with Impudence,

Mr. Chamberlain now accepts Lord Hart- Ington as his leader. It is charming thus to see him at the foot of "Rip Van Winkle ; " it is a sort of penance for his sins. It has Only to embrace " the Skeleton of the Feast" (Mr. Goschen) and then he may be said to have paid the full penalty for his "vaulting ambition."

There seems to have been a most discredit- able scramble for office amongst the Conser- vatives. Instead of waiting until they were asked, some would-be leaders have thrust themselves forward in a most repulsive way. Mr. Chaplin will have nothing, because he could not be raised to Cabinet rank; but even Lord Salisbury' can dispense with Fair Traders ; they are nowhere just now.

The contest in East Birmingham, where NIL Henry Matthews seeks re-election upon his re-appointment as Home Secretary is ae- tracting great attention. It is the straw which will show him the wind blows with the Liberal Unionists. If they are tending towards reconciliation with the . Liberal Party, they will vote for Alderman Cook, the Liberal candidate; leaving Mr. Mat- thews to look for a seat elsewhere.

Lymm is healthy as well as pretty, but the remarks of the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. l'ox) show that the death rate from con- sumption is higher than the average of the Whole country. He attributes this to the bnsanitary condition of the fustian cutting shops, and shows himself anxious to improve them. It is to be hoped the members of the ,Local Board will second his laudable efforts. 40 the fustian cutter, a pure atmosphere 'beans a longer life. Medical Officers of Health have too often to Preach to deaf ears. Dr. McDougall, the bledical officer of health for Runcorn, re- Ported, on Thursday, a nuisance at the night- fall tipping wharf, and said the matter was all the worse through children being allowed ,to convert the wharf into a recreation ground. 4Nothing was done beyond suggesting ,that the doctor should report the matter to the Realth Committee, which will in turn, and after a time, report to the Commissioners, and meantime fever may have broken out in the locality.

Warrington was considerable discussion at the warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednes- tlay, on the question of school fees. Some of the members seem to think it would be a good thing to keep a tighter hand on them ; but if they do they are likely to lose rather than gain. If parents find great. difficulty in Obtaining a grant of fees, they will be tempted to apply for relief, and thus merge into the Pauper class at a great cost to the commu- 4ity. , There is no small number of parents who have a strong aversion to applying for fees, even when they have a good case. They do riot like to be harrassed with question which are necessarily of an inquisitorial kind. They are made to feel their poverty as a crime. When will the nation rise to the occasion, nd rid itself of this burden of trouble by baking education free?

On the question of prosecution for non- vaccination the Guardians seem to be " beat- ing time." It is as well that they should .not Push matters to the extreme. It is a great deal to admit, as Mr. Harrison did, that ' "there had been children vaccinated, and bad consequences had ensued." When a ease of this kind occurs, can we wonder that .he iron enters into the soul of the parent? It is beside the mark to talk to him of the law t)f averages ; for that cannot restore his child. He jests at scars who never had a Wound."

She was the author of "The Bear Hunters," „The Boy Forresters," "The Kangaroo Hunters," " The 'astaways," and many other works, chiefly adapted for ju- teuile readers. A number of witnesses, incicding many who were in- t ted, testified tha borough police and the Glamorgan .._°tllaty Constabulary were guilty of brutal violence to- wards unoffending men and women. They were 10. gaged with a number of others in an angling competition, tmu Shepherd getting out of his depth in an attempt to OVer Rome of his tackle, Leach made a brave effort to `lie him, with the result above stated.
LOCAL NEWS.

THE WESTON POINT MAu.—The total receipts from this bazaar, welch was open for four days, amounted to £165. OPEN AIR CONCERT.—The Mill-brow Brass Bend per- formed a programme of high class music in the Market- place, Runcorn, on Wednesday night. To emenow (Sunday) sermons will be preached in Cain- den Wesleyan Chapel, Ituncorn, hy the Rev. Sidney Mees, of Shrewsbury, and in the afternoon Mr. G. Hazlehurst will • deliver an address to parents and children. WIDNES WR,LEYAN CIRCUIT.—The etev. J. Bryant. who was invited by the June quarterly meeting of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit to succeed the Rev. J. Hothersell, has been approved by the conference, and will commence his labours on the first Sunday in September. TEMPERANCE SERMON AT RUNCORN —The members of Union Tent of Rechabites and the Life Boat Crew of the Sons of Temperance attended divine service at Bethesda Congregational Chapel on Sunday afternoon. The Rev. A. P. Watson, Wesleyan minister, preached an appropriate ser- mon. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN. The anniversary ser- mons in connection with the Runcorn branch of these missions will be preached to-morrow (Sunday), at the Pub- lic Hell, Runcorn, by tee Rev. Thomas P. Bell, late cheer.. lain to the Earl of Moray. The annual excursion to Liver- pool will take place on Tuesday. RUNCORN VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP.—The F and G Com- panies of the Earl of Chester's Rifles left Runcorn on Satur- day afternoon under the command of Captain Hazlehurst and other officers for Rhyl, where the battalion has been in camp during the present week. The men presented a some- what soldierly appearance, and their departure was witnessed by crowds of spectators. WOREPEOPLES' EXCURSION FROM RUNCORN.—The men employed by the firm of Messrs. Brundrit and Co. at Run- corn and Weston were, by the generosity of their employers, enabled to pay a visit to the Liverpool International Exhibi- tion on Saturday Each workman received a couple of ti .tkets. so that be might have the company of his wife or sweetheart, and 200 persons departed from Runcorn by the 8-20 a.m. train. A most enjoyable day was spent in view- ing the countless objects of ieterest. A TRADESMAN'S TREAT AT RUNCORN.—Conforming to his annual custom, Mr. S. Coventry, tailor, of Church- street, Runcorn, gave his employes a treat on Monday. The party travelled to Llandudno by the special excursion train run by the railway company, and arriving at their destina- tion in good time spent a pleasant time amid the beautiful scenery of the Welsh mountains. The day's programme included a drive round the Great Orme's Head and an ex- cellent dinner and tea provided at Evans's Temperance Hotel. All the expenses were borne by Mr. Coventry. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fort- niehtiy meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday, at the Union Workhouse, Dutton. Mr. John Weir presided, and there were also present—the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. P. Hall, J. Stokes, T. Lewis, J. Brandreth, E. Aaron, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), J. Farrinettm (inspector of nuisances), and Dr. Adams (medi- cal officer of bealth.)—A committee was appointed to take into consideration the making of byelaws for the whole of the Union.—A certificate was granted to Mr. Peer Illidge, len., for the occupation of two new houses situate in Ship- street, Frodsham.—The Inspector of Nuisances reported that a cottage at Elelsby was still overcrowded, and it was retele7ed that proceedings be taken at once to prevent the offence. ASSAULTING A POLICE CONSTABLE AT Wnewes —At Widnes Petty Seesions, on Thursday, before Messrs. W. N. Heald and George Pilkington, Thomas Brennan, chemical labourer at the British Alkali Works, was charged on re- mand with having been drunk aad disorderly in Midwood- Street. on the 31st ult., and with assaultineand resisting P.C. Messenger whilst in the execution of his duty.—P.C. Messenger said he was on duty in Midwood-street about a quarter-past eight on the day in question, when he saw the prisoner, who was drunk and disorderly, and creating a dis- turbance. He asked him his name, but he refused to give it. With the assistance of P.C. Savory ke attempted to take the prisoner into custody, when he became very violent, kicked him several times on the legs. and bit one of his thumbs severely. They had great difficulty in getting him to the station.—P.C. Savory corroborated. —A fine of 20s and costs, in default one month, was imposed for the assault, and 5s and costs, or seven days, for the drunkenness. ODDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT DITTON.—Tbe members of the Loyal Heart of Oak Ledge, Ditton, No. 5195, of the Hale District of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, MU., held, their anniversary on Thursday. They met at the club house, the Ball Inn, Ditton, about ten o'clock, and to the number of 40 or 50, dressed in their regalia, and headed by the Ditton Brass Band, paraded the lanes of the village, afterwards attending Divine service in Ditton Church, where an appropriate sermon was preached by the Rev. C. W. Wool], vicar of the parish. An excellent dinner. which had been served by the landlord, Mr. John Hunt, was then partaken of at the Ball Inn, and was done ample justice to. After dinner the chair was occupied by P.P.G.M. John Shuttleworth, and Bro. Lewis, of the Ditton Lodge, occu- pied the vice-chair. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured and a pleasant evening was spent. The balance sheet for the year was submitted. The average worth per member is .£6 3s ld. The members on the books. December 31st. 18e4, was 95. There had been initiated during the year eight, and two had left for non-payment, making a total on the books, December 31st, 1885, of 101.

RUNCORN Co- OPERATIVE INDUSTRIAL PROVIDENT SocilsTi.—The 48th half-yearly meeting of this society was held at the Co-operative Hall, Church-street, Runcorn. on Tuesday night. Mr. Thomas Riley presided, and the ether members of the committee and officials were present. The statement of accounts showed that during the half year the total sales amounted to £32,218 14s 10d, being a de- crease of £2071 9s no on the corresponding period in last year. The profits realised, after charging all expenses, Including depreciation and interest on capital, amounted to £4.902.15s id, which, after deducting the dividend paid in excess of amount provided last year, the checks purchased, and the drapery club bonus, leaves a net disposable amount of £4,645 15s 9d. The committee recommended a dividend of 3s in the L on £29,763 lOs of grocery, drapery, and boot and shoe checks brought in, which would amount to £4,464 108 6,1 : and 2s 6d in the Lon £1.661 9s of butchery checks brought in, amounting to £132 13s Bd, leaving a balance of £4B us 7d to be carried to the reserve fund.—Mr. Ince drew attention to the steadily growing capital of the society. They would still have a capital in the bank of more than £5,000 after paying the dividend, for which they were only receiving from 1.1 to 2 per cent; while they were paying some 4 or 5 per cent to the shareholders. He was of opinion that the capital should either be reduced or they should invest the money in some way which would produce more than the ordinary book rate of interest.—Mr. Royle was opposed to any reduction of capital.—Mr. Fitzpatrick thought it would be advisable to declare a lower dividend than 3s in the Le and he moved that a dividend at the rate of 2s 9d be de- clared.—Mr. E. Aston seconded the amendment, which was lost.—After a reference by Mr. Worthington to the metal check system and the necessity for an alteration, the balance sheet was adopted.—The Secretary said that, in accordance with the instructions of the last meeting, tht whole of the fixtures, buildings, horses, lurries, carts, &c, of the society had been yalued by Mr. James Kirkham, who had certified that the total value of their property in Run- corn and Widnes was £8,872 .53.—Mr. A. Povey was re- appointed auditor.—The following members retired from the committee :—Messrs. Thomas Watson, W. Cropper, Joseph Stubbs, and W. Leatiewood. The three first men- tioned were re-appointed, and Mr. W. Whitehead took the place of Mr. Leathwood. ANNUAL EXCURSION OF MESSRS. GOSSAGE AND SONS' WORKPEOPLE.—The annual excursion arranged by Messrs. Gossage and Sons, seep manufacturers, Widnes, took place on Saturday. The workmen, who have the privilege of choosing where the annual "out" shall be spent, selected Southport for the day's pleasere, and that their decision was popular was shown by the fact that 1500 persons travelled by the two trains provided on the Cheshire Lines Railway. Southport was reached shortly after nine o'clock, and the baud of the works proceeded to the promenade playing a lively air sad accompanied by hundreds of the excursioniste. The weather was delightfully tine, and the beauties, both natural and artificial, of the watering place were viewed under most favourable circumstances. The return journey was safely accomplished by half-past nine, all apparently well-pleased with their trip. It may be stated that besides aiving each employe two tickets, so that each may enjoy himself in conjunction with his wife, the firm generously contribute towards the expenses of the men, adults receiving is 6d each, and boys is each. Accompanying the trip on Saturday were Messrs. W. Hartland, R. Corke. A. Thorpe, J. Povah, Thomas Whitley, Charles Jones, H. Rushton, Isaac Turton, John Hartland, J. Briggs, and J. Jackson. TEMPERANCE ITAIONSTRATION AT WEerox.—The annual demonstration in connection with the " Nil Desperandum " division of the order of the Sons of Temperance took place on Saturday afternoon at Weston, near Runcorn. The members met at the Wesleyan Schoolroom, and having formed in processional order they marched through the vil- lage, accompanied by the Wesleyan Brass Band. At the head wao borne the banner of the division. The charter of the division was also carried in the procession by brothers Parker and Cotterall. The rear was brought up by the members of the cadet section, whose charter was carried by Brothers Brown and Cooper. The procession stopped at the residences of the following persons, where the band Played short selections : Messrs. J. W. Kirkham, T. Ford. Ihnbebin, Griffiths, James Ford, W. Bankes. J.P., F. G. Claudet, ['rid., J. Ball, Thomas Bankee, T. Gritnths, E. Aaron, and Miss Basnett. The procession wes marshalled by Brothers Ward, Cooper, W. Norman, E. Aaron, Dnnbebin, and T. Heesom. On returning to the Weeleyan Schoolroom the members were provided with tea, the tables being presided over by Mrs Aaron, Mrs Cotterall, , Miss Griffiths, Miss Tudor, Miss Smith, Miss Ford, and Miss Danbebin. The chair was subsequently taken by Mr. Catterall, and a vote of thanks was unanimously passed on the motion of Mr. Parker, seconded by Mr. Dunbebin, to all who had contributed to the day's pleasure. An address was also delivered by Mr. T. Cooke, Grand scribe, who congratulated the Weston Division on the progress made during the past year. He spoke in eulogistic terms of the services rendered to the division by Dr. MacLennan medi- cal officer. Dr. MacLennan said he was proud of the posi- tion which the division had taken during the past year, and he earnestly hoped it would continue to make progress. Short addresses were delivered by Messrs. D. Bisbrown, T. Heesoin, and Whitehead. The members then proceeded to a field lent by Mr. W. Bankes, J.P., where the rest of the evening was pleasantly spent.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886.

AN YEW•TREE.—The old yew tree in the Runcorn Parish Churchyard has been removed from its positition. The fragments now form part of an ornamental rockery at the north-west side of the church. The tree was supposed to be 900 years old. SUDDEN DEATH AT CRONTON.—A sudden death took place at Cronton, near Widnes, on Thursday. Michael Conroy, labourer, who lodges with Mrs. Rimmer, farmer, Cronten, took suddenly ill on Wednesday night, and Dr. O'Neil was sent for and ordered him same soda water and milk. The following day he died. MR. BIRRELL's ELECTION EXFENSES.—The expenses of Mr. Augustine Birrell, the Liberal candidate at the recent election in this division, amounted to £630 18s 9.1, includ- in.: £137 Sr 9d for returning officer's expenses and £2O for Mr. Birrell's personal expenses. At the last election Mr. Muspratt's expenses totalled £719 17s BJ. Rue/coax SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held yesterday under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Present—the Key. Father Fenneliy, Messrs. Prit- chard, Imison. Handley, and Rigby (clerk.) Mr. Rooert Shaw was unanimously elected a member of the Board in the place of Mr. G. S. Hiziehurst, resigned. Mr. Handley proposed, and Rev. Father Fennelly seconded the appoint- ment. SuiclDE NEAR WIDNES.—On Thursday morning Robert Ellabv, aged 66 years, a toolmaker, who lived at Chapel- lane, bronton, near Widnes, committed suicide. He was found by his daughter-in-law hanging from a clothes line. Information was given to V.O. Durkin, who cut the body down. The deceased has not been able to follow his em- ployment for six months, and was receiving money from the Farnworth Sick Club. NATIONAL. SOCIETY OF PROFESSIONAL MUSICIANS. Miss Annie E. Chadwick, High-street, Ruacorn, has been successful in passing the advancad ex a-inination of the National Society of Professional Musicians in singing and sight reading.—Miss Milly Chadwick, of Leicester Gardens. Runcorn, has also been granted a certificate in practical music by the examiners of the same society. Both young ladies are pupils of Mr. E. France of Leigh. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Union Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday. Mr. John Weir presided, and there were also present—The Rev. J W. N. Tanner; Messrs. W. Whittaker, W. Farrell, E. Aaron, J. Stokes, T. Lewis, P. Hall, J. W. Baguley, C. Mounfield, J ,seph Smith, James Brandreth. James Parr, H Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (denuty-elerk).—There was no business of public interest. RonnEny AT MooaE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds ; a middle-aged man named Michael Murray was charged witb stealing Bs, the property of John L. Jones, of the Red i Lien Hotel, Moore. On Friday afternoon Mrs. Jones was 1 in the kitchen when she heard someone ia the bar. Upon 1 going there she Saw prisoner with his hand in the till. She , asked him to give her the money be had taken. He raised his hand and threatened to strike her, but ultimately gave I Mrs. Jones 81. Subsequently the prisoner was apprehended 1 by PC. Dutton, and alleged that he knew nothing of the theft —He was sentenced to a month's hard labour. DAMAGING A GARDEN AT DITTON.—At Widnes Petty. Sessions, on Thursday, Peter Carney, John Farley, George Hatchet], and Thomas Gill, hue, were charged with hav- ing damaged the garden of Mr. Henry Brunner, at Ditton, on the 21st ult.—Mr. Peters, solicitor, appeared to prose- Cate.—A number of boys, including the four defendants, were observed coming out of Mr. Brunner's garden, on the 21st July, and two of them, Farley and Hatchell, were caught by Mr. James Jones, who searched them and found a number of peas in their pockets. The two other defen- dants had since admitted the offence. The damage done was 25.—A fine of 2s 61, 6d damage, and costs, or seven days in default, was imposed. OLDHAM ROUGHS AT RUNCORN.—John Fletcher, a young man, was brought no at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Toes- day, charged with begging, and also with assaulting P.C. Barber.—lt appeared that on Sunday afternoon the prisoner and five other men were singing in Water-street. and asked people for alms as they passed. The officer told them he ' could not permit them to do so, and he got held of one of them, when the men surrounded him and struck him on the legs and the back of the neck.—Superintendent Holling- worth said this was a gang of men from Oldham, who went about the country singing, and there bad been many corn.. plaints.—For tagging the prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. On the charge of assault the prisoner was dis- charged. NARROW ESCAPE AT OA4TLEROCIE, RUNCORN.— On Tuesday, a little girl living with her parents in Granville- street, Runcorn. had a narrow escape from being burned to death at Castlerock. On the day named the girl, with several companions, gathered a large quantity of chips into one heap, which they ignited. The blaze caught the child's dress, which was quickly in flames. The screams of the children were heard by Mr. Peter Hindley, grocer, Lord- street, who ran to the spot immediately, tore the burning dress from the body of the child, and put out the flames. In doing so he was burned in several places about the hands. Had it not been for the prompt action of Mr. Hind- ley, the child must undoubtedly have received serious in- juries. possibly of a fatal character, as none of the children were old enough to render any aid. SMUGGLING TOBACCO AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Brown, Captain of the ts.e. Hibernia, was charged with having, on the 2nd ins:. con- cealed on his vessel 511135. of foreign cavendish tobacco with Intent to evade the payment of the duty thereon.—Mr. Mitchell, superintendent of Customs, prosecuted. The steamship arrived in the Mersey on Monday from Dieppe, and it was boarded by Mr. Garnett, Customs officer, who, after the captain had produced his stores," rummaged" his cabin. Mr. Garnett found concealed at the back of a drawer in the table the tobacco in question. The defendant ac- knowledged that the tobacco was his, and he stated that he had brought it to present to his friends.—The defendant: Yes, that's true.—The value of the tobacco with treble duty was £5 12s 91, and the defendant was fined in that amount, with 5s and costa. MASONIC PICNIC FROM RUNCORN.—The members, visi- tors, and lady friends of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons had their annual pic-nic on Wednesday, when they spent an enjoyable day at Hawkestone Park. Two special carriages I Were attached to the train leaving Runcorn at 7-40 a.m., and the party, numbering upwards of 70, arrived at Wem at 9-30. Here two large three-horse brakes were in waiting to convey the Party to Hawkestone Hotel, and they enjoyed a charming drive of four or five miles through a picturesque and pleasant country. At eleven they had luncheon, after which the party proceeded to Hawkestone Park, the seat of Lord Hill. They spent several hours in this attractive place, viewing with pleasure the various points of intetest, and returned to the hotel shortly after four o'clock, where tea was provided. The various loyal and masonic toasts were duly honoured, anel the rest of the evening was passed in an agreeable manner. Tbe party left the hotel by con- veyance at half-past nine, and arrived at Runcorn about twelve o'clock. The arrangements were under the control of Brothers W. Mellor and George Moss and gave every satisfaction, likyNES'S, for Army Bluchers, at 63 11d, great bargains. , dvt.

A" FREAK OF NATURE."—We are infOrmed that there is at present to be seen at the General Elliott Inn, Croft, a very singular" freak of nature." This is a cob about thirteen hands high, a fine and i comely animal in every respect, except that it is endowed with a pair or horns, which project from one of its feet, and, of course, give it a strange and ex- traordinary appearance. Steps are being taken, it is stated, to have this 'latest curiosity added to the unique collection of the great Barnum. GREAT FIRE AT A SHOE FACTORY.—XSO,OOO DANI- AGES.—The great boat and shoe manufactory be- longing to Messrs. Stead, Simpson, and Nephews, situate in Belgrave-gate, Leicester, was destroyed• by fire early on Saturday. The firm have over '7O branches in different towns in the kingdom, includ- ing Preston, Burnley, Oldham, Warrington, and Ashton-under-Lyne. The fire broke out before mid- night, and was not got under until nearly the whole of the vast range of bdildings had been completely gutted. The damage, which will probably emceed .£50,000, is almost wholly covered by insurance. Nothing has been ascertained with respect to the origin of the fire. The disaster has occasioned great distress in the town, as :nearly all of the two thou- sand workpeople will be thrown temporarily out of employment.

THE NEWTON COMMISSIONERS AND THE COUNTY SUSTICES.—In the House of Lords, on Friday, their lordships gave judgment in an appeal argued be- fore them a considerable time ago at the instance of the justices of Lancashire, the respondents being the Improvement Commissioners of Newton. The case may be stated thus :—ln 1855 a portion of a turnpike road from Warrington and Wigan was in- cluded within the improiement district of Newton. Thereupon that portion of the road became vested in the Improvement Commissioners, and came under their management, and the Turnpike Trustees ceased to maintain, and by reason of section 50 of the Towns Improvement Act no longer had power to do so. Section 51 of the Towns Improvement Act gave to the Commissioners large powers of Imanaging and altering the roads within their juris- diction. In 1877, the turnpike road came to an end., and the question was whether the portion of the road within the improvement district ceased to be , a turnpike road subsequent to the 31st December, 1870, within the meaning of the Highways Act, 1878. The appellants contested that it did, but the respondents insisted that it continued to be part of the turnpike road until the expiration of the trust in 1677. The judgments of the Court below were ag;ainst the appellants.—The Lord uhancellor, after referring to the Rochdale and Sheffield cases recent- ly before their lordships' house, said, having regard to the reasoning upon which the judgment in the Sheffield case proceeded, he thought it was hardly possible to distinguish that case in 'substance from that now under consideration; and, taking the Rochdale and Sheffield cases together, they appeared to him to conclude the present case against the ap- pellants. He therefore moved that the judgment appealed against be affirmed, and the appeal dis- Missed with cost.—Lord Watson, Lord Fitzgerald, and Lord Ashbourne concurred, and the appeal was accordingly dismissed with costs, and the judg- ment of the Court of Appeal affirmed.

LOCAL CASES AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.—On Mon- day Patrick Hart (20), labourer, was indicted for abusing Martha Ellen Willcock, eleven years of age, and Elizabeth Lawton, eleven years of age, at War- rington, on the 23rd May, and Mary Balmer, eleven years of age, at the same place, on the 10th June. He was found guilty of an attempt upon Willcock, and was sentenced to twenty months' hard labour. The other indictments were not proceeded with.— William Montgomery (58), labourer, was found guilty of attempting to commit a criminal assault on Mary Ellen Bowman, seven years of age, at Sut- ton, near St. Helens, on the 30th May, and sentenced to twelve months' hard labour.—Thomas Taylor (32), labourer, was acquitted of a charge of criminally assaulting Ellen Headley, at Culcheth, on the 14th May. SUICIDE AT. ASTON.—Mr. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at Aston, on Monday, on the body of Elizabeth Spruce, 65 years of age, widow of William Spruce, bricklayer, of Aston.—Elizabeth Edmund- son, of Accrington, said she had. been staying with her mother at Aston about three weeks. She left her mother's house on Saturday morning to go to a doctor's, leaving her little girl in t"the house with the deceased. Her mother seemed to be in great pain, and that was why she went for a doctor. When she returned her mother was dead. Sarah Ellen Rossbottqm, of Aston, said she had assisted to look after the de- ceased for some time past. Deceased had been gradually sinking. About 20 minutes to twelve on Saturday morning last Clara Edmuudson came for her. She said, "Will you come across? Grand- mother is bleeding." She did so, and found the deceased lying on the sofa bleeding from her throat. She breathed about three times and then died. She ' had not spoken. At times the deceased seemed "a lot bothered" in her mind.—P.C. Jackson, Preston- on-the-Hill, deposed to finding the deceased on the sofa in a leaning position. He noticed she was bleeding from the throat. There was a cut across her throat. He found the razor produced behind the sofa cushion. It was closed, but when he opened it he found blood on the blade.—The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

The wharf was in anything but a satisfac- tory condition and.it wuuld be necessary to take immediate steps to keep the wharf nrivate.—The Chairman thought it would be better for Dr. McDougall to go before the Health Committee, and make that statement. The Doctor replied • that he had no means of 'attending the Health Committee. He thought there would be no difficulty in making the yard secure by completing the fence and keeping the door locked. He was told that the nightsoil contractor was not very careful with regard to this. He could not vouch for it himself. but the contractor had been warned by the Nuisance Inspector, and it would he neces- sary to take some steps to have the matter made 'right.— The Chairman said the Board were indebted to the doctor for the very careful manner in which he had proceeded in stamping out these smallpox cases, and especially for keep- ing the knowledge of their existence from the public, be- cause in matters of this description people hoon took alarm. It was pleasing to know that the disease wag stamped out, and he was sure that similar cases in the future would be dealt with in an equalli satisfactory manner.—The doctor then retired, and at the close of the ordinary business the Chairman again pointed out the desirability of the medical officer making such statements to the Health Committee, not one member of which was present.—Mr. Imison : The doctor explained that be wee not able to meet the Health Committee.—The Chairman: We cannot have the medical officer saying he could dot see the Health Committee.—The Law Clerk said that if the doctor was notified that his at- tendance at the committee was desired he would no doubt attend. .

The results of the exaniinations for 1886 have ben re- ceived. The class in subject 111, building construction, of which Mr James Mason Frith is the teacher, began the ses- sion with 16 students, of whom 11 sat for examination, 10 of them passing successfully, viz., in the advanced stage, Messrs Thomas B Millington, William Bankes, and John A. Frith; in the elementary, Robert CJllinge, Joseph Dodds, William Coventry, Tom W Forster, Edward JJnes (George S Frith and Thomas Tench obtaining the first-class certi- ficate). In connection with the school an art class was opened in response to a widespread wish for instruction in art at an evening class. Mr George Moss, although not connected with the committee of the school, took the lead and exer- ted himself most energetically in the formation of the class by raising subscriptions for the purchase of models, &c. Messrs J T Brunuer, J Bruodrit, and R Shaw were generous subscribers. Mr W G Knight, of Hightown, Nantwich, was appointed art teacher, and the class opened with 22 students who were instructed in freehand, geometry, perspective and model drawing, second grade. The fee for the session in all the subjects was Ps. 17 students sat for examination, and the following passed successfully in freehand : Florence Mellor, George Ernest Moss, John Alfred Moss, James M. Frith in model, John Howard in perspective, H D Kitto in freehand and geometry, and Edward Lane in eeometry, perspective, and model. Mr. Lane obtained the excellent mark in geometry and perspective, which entitles him to a Queen's prize in each subject. At the examination a number of Miss Hankinson's stu- dents from her studio, Bridge-street, Runcorn, at as ex- ternal students, and the following were successful is pass- ing, viz :—Clara Taylor, model ; Samuel Rigby, freehand ; Clara Edwards, freehand and model; and William Towns, in freehand, and Jesse Kilcross in freehand and model, both obtained the highest success, their papers being marked excellent. The committee of the school consists ef the following gentlemen :—Messrs. James Pritchard, William Towns, F. J Norman, E Imison, Rev E Williams, William Handley, T D Timmins, C Dawson, W Whittaker, chairman, and Samuel Pope, secretary.

RUNCORN BOARD OF C3MMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Water- loo-road, on Thursday. Present—Mr. P. Speakman (chair- man), Messrs. Imison, Whittaker, Harris, Pritchard, White, Farrell, Linaker (law clerk). Marshall (secretary), Mc- Dougall (medical officer), and Barker (qurveyor). MEDICAL OFF/GEWS REPORT.-THE SMILIZPDX OUTBREAK.

Dr. McDoneAll reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amount to 21. Of these two were inquest cases, and of the retnaining ?..9 four were due to consumption of the bowels, two to heart disease, two two premature birth, and one each to cancer of the stomach, asthma, epilepsy, skin disease, and disease of the glands. The above 21 oeaths show au average death late for the twelve months of a little over 14 per 1,000 of the estimated populated, and, excluding the two inquest ceses, of a frac- tion over 12 per LOOO. At the last meeting of the Board communicated privately to the Authority that we had had three cases of smallpox in a house in the north-east part of the township. The affected children are now quite well, and the house has been thoroughly well disinfected and the bedding destroyed. lam glad to be able to report that there has been no extension of the dis- ease. In this ease the disease was communicated by a tramp who was taken in al a lodger on the earnest entreaty of the boy who waa the 'first member of the family tooon- tract smallpox. The tramp remained a week, leaving on Saturday, and as it turned out afterward:4. sickened of small- pox in Widnes on the Saturday night.—Dr. McDougall said he wished to -supplement his report by acknowledging the courtesy of Mr. Dickson, the nuisance inspector to the Widnes Local Board, who had given every information in his power. The doctor referred to the dificulty ex- perienced in discovering the cases of smallpox. He wished to warn people as to the class of persons they took into their hoeses. Not only did this tramp, who was about 17 years of age, convey disease to the house, but he was partly clothed and fed for a week. At the end of the week, when be received his wages from the place where he had been employed (the Mersey Brine Works) he went off with one of the boys' clothing and without paying for his board and lodging, and left this disease.

He had bad repeated complaints about it, and he considered it hie duty to visit it on sefbral occasions. He visited the place on Wednesday last and found a large quantity of nightsoil tipped on the wharf, with a large quantity of fish garbage seethinv in the hot broiling sun. Towards evening this was tipped into a boat, but the boat remained at the wharf side. He went again on Tkureday and found the same condition of affairs, only that the greater portion of the nightsoil material had been put into the boat. The Board, he thought, would agree with him that this state of things should not be allowed to exist, and if they wished to keep down the death rate to the extremely satisfactory state in which it had been for the last month it would be neces- sary for the Authority to take vigorous measures that this wharf should net be made into a mere recreation ground for children of that thickly populated neighbourhood. div.head: BANK HOLIDAY AT WIDNES.
div.p: BANK HOLIDAY AT WIDNES.

To the ordinary toiler in the chemical centre Bank Holi- day brought no c sittion of labour. The manufacture of Coda ash, bleaching powder, and ciustic proceeded as briskly as ever, and from the numerous chimneys smoke and vapour was lielOed forth, in great quantities. The trades- men, however, male a geaeral holiday, every shop and store was closed, acd the town had a deserted appearance except at the railway stations. The railway companies had made special arrangements for enabling the people to visit the various pleasure resorts in the neighbourhood, and the weather being fine; although somewhat cold, there was quite an exodus to the Liverpool " Sbipperies," Frodsham, Hale, Southport, and Manchester. On the London and North- Western Railway, between 200 and 300 members of the -Catholic League of the Cross travelled by special train to Bidston, where .they spent a most enjoyable day. The sur- rounding country was explored in waggonettes and traps, the local livery stables being very busy. ' These who staved at home had an opnortunity of Witnessing the demonstratlon of the Court Kidd Lodge 475 of the Ancient Order of For- esters. The members assembled at the .Horns Inn, Fern- worth, and, headed by the Ditton Brass, Band, walked in procession through the principal thoroughfares of Farnworth and Widnes. A beautiful new banner was borne aloft in the ,ranki. They afterwards returned to the inn, and partook Of • a substantial diaper, and passed the afternoon in the ens- -tomary fashion., The contributions to the lodge dating the year ending Dec,. 1885, amounted to £217 9a 2d; the inter- est on investments was £59 13s 9d, and thp financial dona- tions £40., The amount paid to sick members was £lB5 10s, payments to " district "L 73 3s 6d, leaving a balance in ' hand of las lid. The Lodge bolds stock in the St. Helena Corporation to the extent of £BOO, and a similar sum 13 invested with the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board, whilst £lBO Oa 83 is deposited in the Warrington Savings' Bank.

He leaves a widow and large family. EXPLOSION ON A STEAMEIL—Aa explosion of coal gas on board the German barque Teteris, in the Cardiff Docks. on Tuesday, injured six of the crew, three of whom are not expected to recover. The gas was fired by 3 lighted candle carried by one of the men. THE NEIS7 LORD-LIEUTENANT.—The Marquis of Lon- donderry and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach arrived in Dublin early on Thursday mo,ning, and at noon took the oaths as Lord-Lieutenant and Chief Secretary respectively at a Privy Council meeting held at the Castle. The progress of the new Viceroy through the streets on his way subsequently to the Phoenix Park attracted little attention. His Excel- lency left for London last evening, his state entry into Dubin being deferred for a few days.

div.head: WARRINGTON HORSE STEALING
div.p: THE WARRINGTON HORSE STEALING
CASE.

On Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Smith, at Liver- pool Assizes, Abraham Kenworthy, Isaac Smith, and John Sproston were indicted for having at Waning- ton, on the 19th July, stolen a mare, the property of John James Glover and Elizabeth Glover. Mr. Cooper, with Mr. Formby, prosecuted; Mr. Cotting- ham and Mr. Dodd defended. The particulars of the case have been already reported. Evidence having been given for the prosecution, Mr. Cottingham contended that there was no evidence of larceny at all, and submitted several cases to the judge in support of that argument.—His Lordship held that there was primafacie evidence of felony; part of the money had been paid, then the payment suddenly ceased, and the prisoners desired to appropriate the mare too.—Mr. Dodd asked did his lordship think there was any evidence against Sproston ?—His Lordship: Yes, his admission. It would have been better for him if he had said nothing.—Mr. Cotting- ham said he had a good defence to offer. There was a certain amount of trafficking about the mare, but not of such a nature as to warrant the jury in believing that Kenworthy had any criminally dis- honest intention. It was a question which ought to be settled by an action in the County Court. Mr. Dodd also contended that the sale was an out and out tran- saction, , though only part of the money - was paid, and that it was not a subject for criminal proceedings.—Mr. Cottingham called evidence •of good character on behalf of Kenworthy, who is a farmer and horse dealer, and among others Alder- man Swindells, of Oldham, gave him an excellent character.—Mr. Dodd also called evidence as to character, and showed that after the transaction Mr. Glover, Miss Glover, and one of the prisoners had drinks together .in a public-house, and Mr. Glover then stated that he had " swapped " the horse, and Miss Glover asked if he had got the money, and he said " Yes."—llis Lordship, in sum- ming up, said the evidence just called showed the truth of the aphorism that there are always two sides to a story. The fact that a grey mare which nobody owned had been left in the stables where the conversation took place about " swapping " pointed to the credibility of the story. The mare had not been owned to this day.—The jury found the prisoners guilty of conspiring.—The Judge: That has nothing to do with it. The Clerk of Arraigns: Do you find the prisoners guilty of stealing ?—The Foreman: Yes.—The prisoners were then ordered to stand down.—Sentence was deferred. —Prisoners were again brought up on Wednesday, when his Lordship said that after considering the case of the prisoners he had communicated with the Home Secretary, and until he knew the result of that communication he would admit the pri- soners out on bail in the sum of £5O each, and one surety of .£lOO each, and ordered them to come up to receive judgment when called upon. The Flo soners were released in the course of the day.—At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, a man named John Shields, of Oldham, was brought up on a charge of being concerned in the theft, and was remanded for a week.

OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

To-day the new House of Commons met for the first time at Westminster. There was a great crowd outside, and well-known members as they passed into the jealously guarded yard were ' recognised with more or less favour. Inside nothing particular happened, and the proceedings were on the whole a little lifeless. The interest 'of the occasion was greatly marred by the appearance of the Treasury Bench. This was oearly empty. Lord Randolph Churchill and all his principal colleagues in the new Ministry are just now Unseated, and dare no more walk up the floor of the House than' might an ordi- nary stranger. Mr. Peel, scarcely recognisable in mufti, sat on the corner seat below the gangway on the Opposition side, whence he was with due ceremony conducted to. the chair. Of course the Conservatives don't like this arrange- ment, in the last Parliament, when they were numerically less strong, they contemplated opposi- tion to the re-election of\ Mr. Peel, counting upon the personal animosity towards him of their then , allies, the Parnellites. They could not now by their unaided forces withstand the popular choice of the House of Commons, and their new allies, the Dissen- tient Liberals, would not lend themselves to unseat the best Speaker of modern times. So the re-elec- tion has been made unanimously. A much stronger thing is the' intimation that Mr. Courtney is to be re-elected as Chairman of Committees. This is a post, with its attachment of a. comfortable salary, which is more often made the subject of party con- flict than is the Speaker's chair. But hers again the Conservative leaders are impotent unless they could secure the assistance of Lord Hartington, and as Mr. Courtney, of all men, is a Dissentient Liberal (dissent is his chronic condition), he may be regarded as safe.

Mr. Gladstone had a strikingly enthusiastic re:i ception from the Liberals and the Irish members. During the interval since the course of the General Election was determined, the fallen lion has been , the centre of a crowd of braying asses, some of I 'whom, confident in their numbers, and assured of his final breakdown, have even presumed to kick I him. Only this morning "The Times" publishes a I column of offensive sneers at the pathetic letter in. I which the veteran statesman pleads for some modi- cum of rest. This constant stream .of obloquy can- I 'not be entirely without its depressing effect. The reception in the House of Commons this afternoon, ' therefore, was all the more welpome, and evidently ! braced the Liberal chief. He is in excellent health and spirits, and is as sure of official victory as he ; was when he entered upon the first stage of the campaign'in June last. His letter to Mr. Arnold Morley is strikingly different in its tone from the famous epistle he addressed to "My dear Granville," I now some twelve years ago. He then spoke of ad- vancing age and of a yearning for rest that com- pelled his final retirement from public life. His , letter published this morning is merely an appeal i to be relieved from a particular call upon his time s which he means deliberately to devote to recrea- tion, so that when the time comes he may be pre- pared for fresh battle. It is not necessary for Liberals to critise the con- stitution of the new Ministry. That is doneffrankly enough in the columns of the Conservative press, and still more openly in private conversation. There is scarcely an appointment in which the Conserve- tives do not find matter for contemptuous remark I or angry denunciation. In the matter of Sir Richard Cross the Peers have their special arievance. What with the Earl of Lonsdale, Lord St. Leonards, and, some others, the House of Peers, as an institution, has sufficient to put up with from within its own ranks. What it cannot stand with equanimity is having thrust Upon it the companionship of a man who is not blessed with sufficient wealth to "keep up the position." It is no discredit to Sir Richard Cross that he is what is regarded in circles he has mysteriously reached as a poor man. It is under- stood that he at first declined the peerage on these grounds, but political exigencies compelled his ac- ceptance. With six children to provide for on the peerage scale, with no means of adding to his in- come, and with no prestige to support him, the new baron should command the respectful sym- I pathy even of those who have been accustomed to, laugh at him in the House of Commons. Nothing need be said about the appointments of Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, which with the party is only less unpopular than the • nomination of Mr. Henry Matthews as Home Secretary. Mr. Johnston—he of Ballykilbeg—has discovered the hand of the 1 Jesuit in this business. Other people are content to recognise the finger of Lord Randolph Churchill. By a temarkable coincidence, both Germany and 1 France are at the present moment upon the eve of important events following on identical circum- stances. " Both their rulers are at the very gates of death, and any day may bring the intelligence that I the Imperial Throne is tenantless and the Presi- dential chair empty. In both cases extraordinary I efforts are made to minimise, the facts, or to bide them altogether. But private letters from the capitals leave no ?doubt of the condition of the two rulers. M. GrtSvy, 'living in the greater obscurity, more completely, escapes the public eye. Bu; the poor old Emperor of Germany is constantly tumbling about, as with.his indomitable spirit he insists upon walking across his room as if he were a mere chicken of seventy or eighty. These occurrences must needs be reported, and from time to time they fill a corner in the newspapers. If the Emperor lives till March next he will be ninety years of age, and is already in the more or less happy state of second childhood. He is fed every two hours with ' beef tea, jellies, and other savoury compositions which do not require the trouble of mastication, and every day Berlin is officially assured that the Emperor is in excellent health. The old man's tenacity for his position is most pathetic. He will still be Emperor, and above all a soldier. He will be dressed in his uniform, booted and spurred and helmeted, and loves above all things to be helped to , a seat near the window, where he can watch with childish joy his troops go by. As for M. GreSvy, a mere youth of seventy-nine, he for the most part sits in his chair, or hobbles round his garden wait- ing for the end. It was a cruel thing to impose upon him re-election as President. But it did not suit the interest of parties in France to join in the struggle for the Presidency at the moment M. GrOvy's first term expired. There will be a fine rumpus in France when M. GrtSvy dies. It will come in Germany, too, but may be postponed for a a year or two whilst the Crown Prince has his chance.

The Earl of Lonsdale's escapade with Miss Violet Cameron wa§ made known just on the eve of the publication of the "World,' which for a week debars Mr. Yates from the opportunity of commenting up- on it. But we may expect something next week. Lord Lonsdale, it will be remembered, is the estimable person who was instrumental in landing ; Mr. Yates for a brief period in northern latitudes, to wit. Holloway prison. Lord ' Lonsdale himself had an alternative sentence of imprisonment passed upon him in con- nection with the domestic circumstances of the Violet Cameron household. But he got off on pay- ment of. forty shillings. This will enable him to take his seat in the House of Lords to-morrow when the newly elected Speaker goes to present himself for the approval of her Majesty. If the noble lord is careful he will also be at liberty to vote on the question of Home Rule for Ireland when it comes before the House of Peers, or upon any other sub- ject affecting the welfare and prosperity of the people. Those interested in church matters will be pleased to hear that the "travelling treasurer 'S of the Violet Cameron Company is patron of forty-two livings. The present earl bears with singular ap- propriateness the family motto, Inagistratus indicat virum. ;which, being freely translated, reads, "The magistrate shows the man." Sir Charles Dilke has not, as was eagerly reported, run away to escape an indictment for perjury. He has simply gone up the river with his wife, and his address is known to all whom it may concern. I believe it was his intention to go to his place in the South of Prance. But as long as this other threat was hanging over him he has been careful to avoid anything that looked like running away. The efforts some of the Conservative papers- have made to keep the hunt going have conspicuously failed. The public mind shrinks from a restatement of the loathsome allegations, and is not untouched by the generous thought that even admitting the guilt of Sir C.Dilke the terrible punishment has not been inadequate. Beyond this is the impossibi!ity recognised in legal circles of obtaining a conviction. The law requires that in sustaining a charge of per- jury two witnesses must prove the allegations of the prosecution. It is well known that two wit- nesses cannot be found, and that is quite enough to settle the matter. The talk about its becoming a Cabinet question with the new ministry is pure nonsense. It is doubtful whether it would ever et beyond the Attorney-General. If it reached him it must be settled forthwith on the single indisputable and impassable fact indicated.
A new kind of glass ware has just been perfected i in America, and her Majesty s next week to be

Ipresented with the first service of it ever seen in this country. Like so many other .novelties in ceramic art, its invention was due to accident. An Indian was talking to the head of the American firm about the introduction of yellow glass, which is so favourite a colour with the Burmese. A was decided to adopt the tint.' I:Tranic oxide and gold were added to the alumine and other ingredients of the paste, and a fine yellow was produced. It was discovered accidentally that this yellow body. if it was suddenly chilled off and then reheated, acquired a lovely salmon tint, which died away in the canary yellow according as chill and fire were applied. Once the salmon tint was got, no subsequent visit to the furnace altered the colour. This was impor- tant, as the surface might be worked upon safely for after Artistic decoration. The service prepared. for her Majesty consists of coffee cups ami,saucers, the centres of pale yellow, and the colour _passing by imperceptible gradations into a fall salmon at the borders, the whole surface covered with raised enamel flo-Wers. The ware is called after the Indian suggester of the tint—Burmese ware.

Mr. Williamson was one who had always retained the goodwill of his employers and the men, and, while al- ways maintaining the strictest integrity, he never lost i the esteem of those under him. (Applause.) When it became known that Mr. Williamson was about to retire, it ..tvas thought a suitable occasion to mark their appreciation of him, and the presentation they had. met to make was the outcome of that feeling.— , Mr. Brettelle also spoke of the great respect in which Mr. Williamson was held, and the presetitation was then made. POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Befere Mr. John Brock. DISORDEBLEY.—For disorderly behaviour in West Bank on Saturday Jane Hardy was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

At the Old Bailey. on Wednesday, Georve Vincent Heneage Finch, aged 19, was charged with the murder of John William Bowes, by shooting him in the post office at Kentish Town, Lender]. It being found that the prisoner was insane, he wis ordered to be detained during Her Majesty's pleasure. At the same court, on Wednesday, Emil tehbenfeldt was charged with forging the acceptance of the Earl of Devon to a bill of exchange for £6OO, and was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment with hard labour.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds. A PAWNBROKBR.—Arthur Davies applied for and was granted permission to carry on the trade of a pawnbroker at 73, High-street.

PRESENTATION AT EA_RLESTOWN. On Saturday evening Mr. William Williamson, who has been for 41 years engaged as foreman at ths Vul- can Engineering Works, Earlestown, was the recipient of a handsome testimonial, which had been subscribed for by his friends and fellow workmen. The testi- monial was a valuable clock, handsomely framed, and two oil paintings, one of Mr. and one of Mrs. Wil- liamson. The presentation was made in the dining room at the works, which had been decorated for the occasion. Plants for that purpose were lent by Mr. Gooch, Mr. Bretelle, and Mr. Braham, and the rooms were decorated by Mr. Holmes, Mr. Braham, and Mr. Ferguson. Soon after six o'clock a substantial tea was partaken of, and the following ladiPs presided at the tables :—Mesdames Ca.therail, Smith, Harrison. Crawshaw, Martin, Ferguson, Pol S weetlove, Dearden, White. Knox, Silk, Hutt, Ferguson (Jun.), Tomlinson, Golshaw, Shepherd, Bate, Grundy, and Schofield. About 220 people sat down to tea. The arrangements, which were in the hands of a general committee and a small sub- committee, were well carried out. Messrs. Holmes, Braham, Smith, Eddington, Catherall, and Martin formed the sub-committee. Mr. T. 111olynenx was the caterer. After the tables had been cleared, Mr. Catherall, who presided, mentioned the absence of Mr. Gooch, who was unable to be present. Mr. Gooch told him to say that althouith he could not be there in person his heart was with them. Mr. Gooch had taken a very active part in bringing the under- taking to a successful issue, and they could not have done so well without his assistance. Ho then hoped they would all wish hearty and continued success to ' the Vulcan Foundry company. (Cheers.) Mr. Brettelle then said a few words. He was sorry to say that at the present time they were not. in the position they would like to be. The dark clouds that they heard so much of were looming over them now, but he hop.,d that they would pass by, and that there was a. bright future in store for the Vulcan Foundry Com- pany. He had been connected with the works for twelve or thirteen years, had met with many kind- nesses, and had been thoroughly happy as manager, (Cheers.) He hoped that trade would soon prelent a brighter outlook.—The Chairman then referred to the retirement of Mr. Williamson,

Hoxton-street, Bradford. writes, July 24th, 1885.—Oentlemen,—Perrnit me to attest my unsolicited 'aud humble teetimeny to the heeling and curative properties of your EXTRACT, not only in restoring the weak and debilitated but in the curing of Bphomy in its most aggravated form; not only do I speak from information, but personal observation in one special case—viz , that of a woman subjected to the above disease for upwards of twelve years; not 30 severe at -first, but as time went on the fits became MA34 frequent, until the patient was seldom a week without the recurrence, until she was reduced to sheer helplessness, and almost to a stAte of idiocy; for over th-ee years not able to do her own household work, and the family had tried anything and everything that doctors and patent medicines could do without effect; in fact, she gradually became worse, until the doctors said there was no cure, and the patient could net sur- vive long. They had tried many patent medicines, one preparatton to the amount of BT. This for a time seemed to have a little effect, and the family had hopes of a cure, but so soon as the system became used to the medicine, the medi- ates became useless and all hopes again blighted. The family, In fact, became seriously impoverished in expending mosey with hope of a cure, but all to no purpose; besides, the hus- band's health became enfeebled for want of rest tor such a length of thee that he was laid aside for long, until the family , was reduced to a sitiful condition indeed. However, as-the last effort your XTRACT was resorted to, and with surpris- ing effect! six or seven bottles regularly taken successively until the fits became less frequent and the heelth became im- proved, until the woman was enabled to attend Ler household duties; and now, though she hae not used the EXTRACT for many months, she hes not had fits for twelve months, and is now in her usual health. Any pertv writ,ng me for proof, I will gladly answer and give the full name and address of suf- ferer, and at my expense; they will most gladly reply to any inquiry, but for reasons which are justifiable, they would rather not have their name come before the public. Yet you are at perfect liberty to make what use of my statement you like, and, believe me, yours respestediy, DAVID TWOILLS. Bookseller and Stationer.
