The following wore the !Igoe, ,---Cholr contest, Mr Chas Pigot ; races, Messrs W W RoBntsad W Ford ; starters, Mr W Smith and sergeant Prise. The stewards were: Con- ctort, Messrs R Siddell, T Dale, W Taylor, J Jolley, and D Leigh ; rac.s, Messrs T Willett, G Rogers, H Gandy, J Truman, N Baker, Fernley, G Barlow, and J Lingard ; marshals, Messrs W Price, Smith, Siddall, and Prince, whilst those who gave their services at the refreshment tent were Messrs J Titehett and 8 Jones. The officers of the Union, it may be mentioned, are Mr R A Naylor, presi- dent: Mr W Roberts, chairman; and Mr Frank Williams, secretary.

At the meeting which was held towards eight o'clock in the evening in the open air in front of the grand stand Mr. R. Naylor, pree;dent of the Band of Hope Union, occupied the chair. In addressing the gathering, which was of con- siderable dimensions, Mr. NayLosa observed that it would be in no way necessary for him to make a long speech on that very interesting occasion, for he understeed they had a great host of speakers to call upon. He would, however, just congratulate the workers in connection with that Band of Hope Union upon the magnificent success which had attended their efforts that day. They had been very much favoured with fine weather, and he understood that they had bad such a procession parading the streets; of the town of Warrington as had never been known before. He under- stood that more than 3,000 Band of Hope children took pert in that procession, and he supposed that they had had on that field something like 10,000 s isitors. That spoke well for the interest boys an girls and grown-up people took in the cause of the Warrington Band of Hope Union. (Hear, hear.) That was a great undertaking, it was one in which all good people could battle and put forth every effort in order that they might he of some use in its promotion, and he was very pleased to notice that the various religious denominations in Warrington were associating so unanimously together for the purpose of doing what they possibly could do for the advancement of the cause of the Warrington Band of Hope Union. He held in his hand a letter which had been sent to him by a clergyman of the Church of England—he re- ferred to the vicar of St. Paul's. the Rev. S. Wilkinson— who would have been very pleased to be present with them that night, and he asked him (Mr. Naylor) to apologise for his non-attendance, as he had been obliged to accompany his chair, whe had had their yearly outing that day te the city of Chester. He believed, however, that they had present somewhere a number of ministers belonging to other denominations whose duty and pleasure and privilege it would be to say a few words to them en behalf of the cause of temperance. It bad been his pleasure and privi- lege to labour for the prosperity of the Band of Hope Union, or the Band of Hope movement, for the past twenty- three er twenty-four years. He had served three appren- ticeships, and it was a pleasure to him to notice the great advancement that that good cause was making at the pre- sent time, and if he happened to live another twenty-sue years he hoped that at the end if that time he should still be found a Band of Hope boy, advooating the claims of that glorious institution. (Applause.) Mr. Snail; of Runcorn, next gave a short and appropri- ate address. It was a pleasure to him, he said, to be there that night and to see so vast a number of people, and he trusted that all the people who had been in that field were total abstainers. It spoke well for Warrington io have such a turnout, but be could not help thinking that it had not- all come about in a moment. They perhaps found the secret of it when they heard that they bad had gentlemen like the, chairman working for the last twenty years. They might depend upon it that work of that kind must tell somewhere. There had been hard work in a great cause, and there had .been a determination to bring that question of total abstin- ence before the young people. It was all very well to get drunkards to become teetotallers, but it .was best to get hold rof the young. He sometimes asked his children whether it ' was better to get a leg broken and then have it well mended or to save the leg from being broken at all, and they soon told him it was best not to get the leg broken. That was Just his idea with regard to drunkenness ; it was better to prevent people from becoming drunkards than to cure them afterwards. After giving a few appropriate illustrations as to the effects of intoxicating drink, Mr. Shaw concluded by entreating all to give up habits of drinking, and he assured them that it would be better for them and their children. (Applause.) Mr. NAYLOR then anitounced that for some reason or other all the ministers who had been expected to address them had taken flight, and therefore all the speaking would have to be done by the laity. He called upon Mr. SIDDALL, who said that he had been an abstainer for 38 years, and the reason that be became an abstainer was that drink was doing for him what it had dotal for thou- sands. When a man saw that intoxicating drink was be- coming an evil it was his duty to put it away. It wee the greatest enemy he had to contend against, it would rob him of all that was good, it would" clothe a man with rage," it would put him in the Union, and it would put him in that place where hope and mercy never came.. He advised them all to take care of their hard-earned gains, and when they were old they would take care of them. When he became an abstainer he had net a penny, but to-day he was his own master and lived in his own house, and that was what every working-man ought to do. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The prizes were then distributed to the successful com- petitors in the sperts by Mr. Naylor and the very successful proceedings were brought to a Close.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMF,NT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnrssacr.

The first session of the twelfth Parliament of the Queen and the twenty-fourth of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland was opened on Thursday by Boyal Com- mission in compliance with the Royal proclamation of the 26th June last. The Royal Commissioners, who wore their ermine and scarlet robes, were the Lord Chancellor (Lord Halabury), Earl Cadegan (Lord Privy Seal), the Earl of Irldesleigh (Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs), Viscount Cranbrook (Lord President of the Council), and Lord Bra- bourne). Between thirty and forty ladies were accommodated with seats in the body of the House on the Opposition benches, and besides these' strangers a large number of ladies and gentlemen attended to witness the ceremony in the gallery. At about ten minutes after two o'clock the Lord Chan- cellor directed the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod (the lion. Sir James R. Drummond) to request the attendance of the House of Commons to hear the Royal Commission read. Fotr or five minutes having elapsed, the Gentleman Usher returned, accompanied by the Clerk of the House of Commons (Mr. Reginald Palgrave) and a large number of members of the Lower House. The Commission having been read by the Clerk of Par- liaments, in the absence of the Reading Clerk through domes- tic affliction, The LORD CHANCELLOR said We have it in command from Her Majesty to let you know that Her Majesty will as soon as the members of both Houses shall have been sworn declare the causes of her calling of this Parliament, and. it being necessary that a Sputter of the House of Commons shall be first chosen it is Her Majesty's pleasure that you, gentlemen of the House of Commons, repair to the place where you are to sit, and there proceed to the choice of some proper person to be your Speaker, and that you present such person whom you shall so choose here to-morrow at twelve o'clock for Her Majesty'a royal approbation. The members of the House of Commons having left the bar of the House of Lords to return to their own House, the Lords Commissioners retired to tbe robing-room, but almost immediately afterwards the Lord Chancellor returried and took his seat on the woolsack. _ _ _

Prayers were read by the Bishop of Southwell, after which the swearing-in of peers commenced. Their Lordships, on the motion of the Earl of Ellesmere, adjourned till 12 o'clock to-morrow (Friday). HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THUItSDAT.

The first sitting of the House of Commons was appointed to take place at two o'clock, but the first member appeared at half-past six. This was Mr. Blake, member for the Forest of Dean Division of Gloucestershire, who was the first to appear at the opening of the last Parliament. It was half-past ten before any other hon. gentleman joined him. Sir John Lubbock was among the early arrivals, along with Mr. Sidney Buxton, Mr. E. Russell, Mr. Picton, Sir E. Birkbeck, and Sir Charles Foster, who had to be assisted to his place in consequence of recent illness. At ten minutes to two Mr." Gladstone emerged from behind the Speaker's chair and took his place in the seat of the leader of the Opposition, first shaking bands with Sir E J Reed. At five minutes to two Lerd Llartington entered, and a cor- dial greeting took place between the noble lord and Mr. Gladstone, who, recognising Mr. Chamberlain for the first time, shook bands with him. Many of the Ministers bay- ing vacated their seats by accepting office. the Treasury Bench was occupied only by the subordinate members of the Government, among them being Mr. W. L. Jackson and Mr. Forwood. - - -

Shortly after two o'clock Black Rod appeared, and de- sired the attendance of members in the House of Peers to hear her Majesty's Commission read. The Clerk of the House (Mr. Palgrave) and a considerable number of mem- bers repaired thither. On their return the House proceeded to elect a Speaker. ELECTION OF SPEAKER.—Sir E. BIRIEBECK, according to previous arrangement, as indicated by the index finger of the silent Clerk at the table, arose from the middle of the third Ministerial bench, and amidst general applause from all quarters formally proposed the re-election of Mr. Peel as Speaker.—Mr. GLADSTONE. following Sir E. Birkbeck to second his proposal, was hailed with full-toned and pro- tracted cheers from his supporters above and below the gangway. He was rather hoarse, and discharged his duty with singular conciseness. As was universally felt, ex- tended praise of Mr. Peel in this instance would hare been wholly superfluous, and silence having given consent to the motion, the Speaker-elect excused himself from saying much in reply on the ground that he had been twice elected to the chair within seven months and thrice in thirty months. He took the opportunity, however, of renclving his appeal to members to observe not only the written rules, but " those conventionalities and usages which are among the proudest heritages of the House of Commons." There was not the faintest manifestation of opposition to his reappointment, and Sir E. Birkbeck crossed the floor te con:luct him to the chair. Mr. Gladstone also met the right hon. gentleman as he came down the gangway and

accompanied him past the Treasury bench to the chair,after which the ex-Premier walked round behind the chair back to his place. Mr. Peel, who was of course attired in ordi- nary morning dress, deposited his hat on the chair, and standing on the top step again express,d his acknowledgment& The Sergeant-at-Arms lifted the mace to the table, and Mr. Jackson, coming forth as tem- porary leader of the House amidst loud cheers, offere.i the Speaker-elect congratulations in a neat and effective ad- dress, which was by far the best and most lively contribu- tion to the day's placid proceedings. At the suggestion of Mr. Akers-Douglas, the House, at a quarter to three, gladly adjourned until next day, on the understanding that after the sanction of tle Crown had been given to the Speaker's election members would be sworn in batches of five and the requisite new writs issued.

SIR RICIT.ARD CROSS AND THE HOUSE OF LORDS. CONTEST IN NEWTON DIVISION. The acceptance of the office of Secretary of State for India by Sir Richard Assheton Cross, the Con- . servative member for the Newton Division of South- West Lancashire, has necessitated another election for that constituency. The additional announce- ment that he will shortly be elevated to the House of Lords has given increased interest to the forth- coming election. His appointment to office would have required his re-election or rejection—by the electors of the Division, but his elevation to the Upper Chamber means a fresh candidate, or candi- dates, for the honour of representing the. constitu- ency. This has naturally excited curicsity as to the probable contestants, and several names have been freely mentioned as likely or suitable candi- dates. Up to the present the Liberal party, we be- lieve, has taken no steps officially to adopt a candi- date, but the late candidate, Sir George Errington, Bart., who contested the seat a few weeks ago with Sir Richard Cross, has again been talked about. The retirement of Sir Richard Assheton• Crass after IS years' representation of this part of South-West Lancashire has affected opinions as to the.probable result of another struggle, and the verdict of the constituency is now considered a more open ques- tion.

In speaking of Sir Richard Cross's elevation to the House of Lords, " The Times" the other day remarked:—"Sir Richard Cross, though he may claim a creditable record in the post he formerly held at the Home Department, will bring no special knowledge to bear on the work he is about to per- form; and it must be admitted that he has of late filled but a secondary position in the councils of the Conservative party.' The London correspondent of "The Liverpool Daily Post." writing on Monday night, said The delay that has taken place in the filling up of the final places in the Cabinet shows what a great effort has been made to get rid of the .‘ old gang," and how the effort has failed. The Ministry, is to be without the services of Mr. Chaplin, who claimed and did not get Cabinet rank. The appointments finally made do much to weaken the Ministry. The idea of Sir Richard Cross as the superior officer of Lord Dufferin is too absurd. I assume, however, that his elevation to a peerage will by and. by be used with Sir Richard as constituting full payment for his services, and that he will be quietly edged out of the Ministry." Writing on Tuesday night the same correspondent says :--" The elevation of Sir Richard A. Cross, it is now well understood, was simply out of regard to Lord Ran- dolph's somewhat sensitive nervous system. He could not stand the proximity of Sir Richard, and 80 he is sent to strengthen our hereditary wisdom. I believe Sir Richard made a gallant and, as it has turned out, a successful fight. It wear the length of a declaration that he would make things pretty uncomfortable in the House of Commons for the new Administration. This appears to me, if made, a very weak and impotent threat, for Sir R. A. Cross, deprived of official position, would be of little account.'

div.head: TIIE TORY CANDIDATE.
div.p: TIIE TORY CANDIDATE.

At the early part of the week a rumour was cir- culated in the district that the Conservatives had decided to adopt Mr. William C. Gerard, eldest son of Lord Gerard, of Bryn, as their candidate, but it has been contradicted. A meeting of the Conserva- tive Council of the Division to consider the selec- tion of a candidate was held in the Town hail, Newton, on Tuesday evening. The chair was occu- pied by Mr. M. Brown-Westhead (chairman of the Council.) It was unanimously decided to ask Mr. T. Woodhouse Legh, eldest son of Mr. W. J. Legh, of Lyme Hall, Cheshire, who for some years repre- sented the East Cheshire Division in Parliament, to come forward as the Conservative candidate. The selected candidate has for some time,past been en- gaged at the British Embassy in Paris. The deci- sion of the Conservative Council was notified to him by telegram on Tuesday night, and a reply was received on Wednesday accepting the candida- ture.

div.head: LIBERAL CANDIDATE.
div.p: THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

Up to Thursday night there had been no meeting of the Liberal "300" or of the Executive to consider the selection of a candidate, but active negotiations had been in progress with the view of bringing a suitable candidate before the constituency. In the event of the re-election of Sir Richard Cross having become necessary by his acceptance of office, apart from his elevation to the House of Lords, it had been definitely decided by the Liberal party not to oppose his return, but his retirement from the repro- eentation has considerably changed the circum- stances, and it may be taken for granted that the new Conserrativ4 champion will not be allowed a walk over. On the announcement being made that Sir Richard Cross had been relegated to the Upper House, Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., and Mr. W. G. Rawlins, of Rainhill, waited upon Sir George Errington, Bart., the Liberal candidate at the last election. They asked that gentleman, whom they met at Liverpool , last Saturday, if he would consent to his name being again submitted, with others, to the Liberal "300," as one who would contest the division in case of another election. A long conversation ensued, during which Sir George Errington expressed the opinion that he did not very much care for coming before a constituency in a bye-election, but at a general election he might be agreeable to do so. Other gentlemen are being communicated with, but nothing definite.has been decided in the matter. It may be added that a meeting of the Liberal registration agents, representative of the whole of the division, was held at the Earlestown and Dis- trict Liberal Club. on Wetlnesday evening, and the prospects ot the election were considered. ARRIVAL OF THE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE.

Mr. T. Woodhouse Legh , the adopted Conserva- tive candidate for the division, who has been on his journey from Paris, arrived at Newton Bridge Sta- tion about half-past nine on Thursday night. He was accompanied by Mr. J. E. Pardey, of Newton- le-Willows, agent to the Newton estate of Mr. W. J. Legh, and among the large number of Conser- vative gentlemen and rank and file of the Tory party present were Mr. W. Y. Gooch, J.P., Mr. T. Stone, Mr. T. Pearson, Mr: W. H. Brook (election agent), Scc. The approach of the train was announ- ced by the discharge of fog signals placed upon the line outside the station, and as the candidate was observed he was loudly cheered. The pally proceeded to the Conservative Association committee-rooms, near the Town Hall, where the adopted candidate briefly addressed the crowd from one of the windows. He said he had been taken by surprise by his enthusiastic wel- come, and if they would only unite and work as they had done in the past there was not the slight- est doubt as to the result of the coming contest. At such a late hour he would not detain them, but he again thanked them for their reception. (Cheers.) J. Oath erall (chairman of the Earlestown por- tion of the Conservative Council) urgently appealed to the workers not to lack in their efforts in any respect, but to prepare for a struggle if there should be. one. (Applause,.),—The proceedings. then con- cluded.

THE COTTON TRADE.—At a meeting of the cotton spin- ners in Manchester. on Tuesday, resolutions were passed in favour of running half-time for a period of six weeks from 14th August. If two-thirds of the spinners agree to these resolutions they will be carried into eact.—The operativo weavers .4 North aod North-Eas, Lancashire have, through their committee, sent in a demand for 10, per c,,nt advance in their wages. A meeting; of the joint committee represent- ing the masters and men was held on Tuesday in this city, and after a prolonged discussion farther consideration of the question was adjourtrd to a future meeting, the date of which was not fixed.

DBA.TII ON TEE ABBE LIEZT. —This venerable musician expired at midnight on Saturday, in the city of Bavaria. Liszt was horn at Szegnird in October. 1811, consequently he was at the time of his death in his 75th year. In addi- tion te execution, Lint found time to apply himself to composition, and among his wo.its may be mentioned several Hungarian Rhapsodies for full orchestra, two ora- torios,‘• Stanislaus" and "St. Elizabeth," And an elaborate Mass known as the Gran Mass, from the fact that it was written for the consecration of the cathedral in that Hun- garian city in 1856. His compositions and transcriptions for the piano are most numerous. List was also the author of a "Life of Chopin." His remains are, at his own wiih, to be laid in the cemetery at Bayreuth,

BANK HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN. The tradesmen of Runcorn zealously observed Bank Boliday on Monday, and the men at several of the works were also at liberty. A trip to Llandudno and other Welsh pleasure resorts carried numerous passen- gers, whilst 400 were booked to Liverpool. In the afternoon the pleasures of lieleby and Overton at- tracted about 400 persems, and a considereble, number were conveyed by road lo the ancient city of Cheater. Ad-rentage was taken of the holiday by several of the friendly societies to hold demonstrations, particulars of which will be found below. FORESrEits, JUBILEE FESTIVAL. rhe Court Runcorn, No. 429 of the Ancient Order of Foriterefa celebrated its jubilee on Monday by an out-door demonetration. About 90 members met at the Hall, Devon- shire-square, where they formed in processional order, and headed by the Warrington Primitive Methodist Sunday School Band, paraded the cbief thoroughfares of the town. Walking in the front were two archers, attired in huge' skins, supported by halberd bearers. The large banner of the order was also displayed- Mr. J. Broadhurst, Asbridge-st., • and Dr. McLennan, the medical officer, Church-street, were honoured by a stoppage at their respective residences. Afterwards the procession wended its way to Halton, and then returned to the Hall, where 150 persons sat down to a "meat tea." The tables were presided over by Mesdames Broadhurst, .Tunion, Edwards, Rueleton, Saunders, W. Clarke, and W. Hoxworth ; Misses Conslanal, Ainsworth. and Turner. Subsequently a meeting was held, at which Brother Davies read an address- setting forth the nume- rous advantages possessed by members of the Order. The Chairman (Me. P: Speakman) said it was a very pleasing and happy tneering that night, for they had assem- bled together to celebrate the Sitietb anniversary of Court "Runcorn." (Applause.) If young men would only band themselves togeeher and become members of such an insti- tution, they would find that it would net only be for mutual i benefit, but also for their future welfare: (Applause.) He had watched that institution for many years—in fact, from its earliest years—and he had discovered the greatest mis- take the members had made, and that was that the members did Oct walk often enough. (Applause.) One of their rules specified how often the members should assemble for that purpose; but he was of,opinion that no army was got to- gether without recruits, and that that society would prosper in a greater degree if it was made more publicly known. Processions were one way of obtaining new members, and such societies were the rneans of young men saving their earnings. He therefore advised the youeg men of Runcorn to join that society, and was of opinion that if they did so, they wow(' have the setiefaction of knowing that they were providing for themselves in the future. (Hear, hear.) Brother Armstrong, at the request of the Chairman, ad- dressed the meeting. He said he had been a member of the Court for 49 years—(applause)—and could point to one member who bad been on their bookefor fifty years. (Ap- plause.) His purpose was to give them a short history of the rise and progress of the court during the past fifty years. from the year 1836 to 1886. That court was first opened under the dispensation of Frodsham Court (410) en June 25th, 1836, and on August 20 in the same year it was opened under their own dispensation by the District Master. The first procession took place on Mars 24th, 1837, when the court was held at the New Ihn,. and at that time 50 mem- bers and their wives sat down to a good dinner. The first death in the court was that of Brother John Leigh, on the 24th of December, 1836, when the allowance was £l2. In October of the following year he (the speaker) was proposed as a member of that court, and was initiated in November. They had only one member living now who became a mem- ber in the first year of the estalCiishment of the court, and that was Brother William Mbors. He was, there- fore, proud to tell them that they had one member who had been connected with the court for 50 years. (Cheers.) Brother Whitley stood next on the list. (Applause.) In giving a history of the Foresters' Hall, Brother Armstrong explained the difficulties the court bad to contend with, and stated that notwithstanding the draw- backs they experienced on the 24th of July, 1843, there was a procession of the members, and- or the first time they dined together in that court room, and from that period they began to feel their feet. The funeral fund was again started, and they paid to members-and members' widows the reduction they had stopped, and on the 27th December, 1851, they were able to inform, the members that the ball was out of debt—(epplause)—aed upon that occasion the members had the privilege of introducing a friend to a good knife and fork tea. (Cheers.) During the past five years £873 3s had been expended in sick allowance, and £383 for funerals, making up a total of £1,256 3s. The value of their funds and profit was £2,045-i which was equal to £l5 tier head. (Applause.) There were 136 members' names on the hooks, and the amount received from contributions was £163, and ISO from income on building, making a total of £243. After giving some general particulars of the order, the speaker said the society was governed by a High Ceurt, which was composed of delegates sent from various lodges, and Court "Runcorn "'was worth £2,045, with a member- ship of 136. (Applause.) He believed there was no society in Rimcorn in so sound a state as theirs, and he asked them to do what they could to keep up the position they had gained for themselves. (Applause..) The remainder of the evening was devoted to an enter- tainment, and some excellent songs and recitations were given by members of the Court in a praiseworthy manner, the proceedings being of a very pleasant character. SONS OF TEMPERANCE DEMONSTEATION. The members of the Lifeboat Crew Division of the Order of Sons of Temperance held their annual demonstration on Monday afternoon. The society has made great advances in the town during the past few years, and there assembled in Devonshire-square 200 adults and 140 cadets or juveniles, who were formed into processional order and paraded the town, accnmpanied by the Mill Br-ow Brass Band and the Weston Wesleyan Sunday School Brass Band. Messrs. Heesom, Jones, and Withington acted as mounted marshalls, and added considerably to the display, while the following gentlemen, who kept admirable order, were foot marshal's : Messrs. Hetherington, Cooke, S. M. Temperley, S. Hender- son, T. J. Holt, D.. Biebrown Robert Thomas, T. White, and S. Tomlinson. The beautiful banner of the society and numerous bannerettee were displayed, and added gaiety to the scene. A halt was made at the residence of Dr. Robin- son, where the Weston Band played a tune. The procession wended its way to a field off Halton-road, kindly lent by Mr. M. Sweetman, and a pleasant hour having been spent the members retuned petheeda Schoolroom, where about 400 persons sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by the following ladies :—Mesdames Eason, T. Cooke, Hetherington, Pendlebury, Gibson, Millington, Bisbrown, and F. Cooke, and the Misses Hibbert, Davidson, Martha Woodward, S. Basnett, Hill, and Piper. Subsequently a public meeting was held, when there was a large attendance. Mr. F. J. Norman presided, and on the platform were Messrs. W. Wrightman, M.W.P:, Lon- don; W. Clarke, M.W.8., Manchester; T. Cooke, G.B. ; T. Heesom, W. Heatherington, J. Withingten, D. Bistrown, John Jones, S. M. Tetnperley, Robt. Thomas, T. White, S. Henderson, W. Lee, and S. Tomlinson. Mr. W. Clarke delivered an address in which he referred to the prosperity of the order, and said they had consider- ably over 400 branches; and scattered over the United Kingdom, they had 21,309 members, with funds amounting to £70,000. They had been in existence for 37'years, and; if a page could be written to show what good had been done to sick members, the result would be something wonderful. It seemed to him that after a man signed the pledge he should join the Sons of Temperance Order, which they be- lieved to be second to none. It was not only that they re- ceived benefits when sick, but they were benefitted in their homes, and an example worthy of emulation would, be set. (Applause.) Mr. Wightman also spoke of the advantages held, by "Sons of Temperance." Mr. T. Cooke read the report of the order, which he pre- luded by congratulating the members on having turned UP in such goodly numbers. They had done the order great credit by turning out in such strong force. The order had made progress all along the line. During the year fifteen new divisions had been instituted, besides twenty-two cadet sections. They had had a net increase of 1,085 in. their membership, and an increase in funds of £6,047 13s. The Life Boat Crew division numbered 240 members, while the cadet section contained 140 juvenile members. During the year they had received from members in .contributions the sum of £303 23 51d. In sick claims they bad paid away the suer of £.234 17s. They had only paid one death c.aim of £l2. Mr. Cooke reminded the meeting that the death claims were not paid out of the funds of the division itself, but the money was drawn from the district fund. During the year they had formed a benevolent fund, for the pur- pose of assisting members who might be in distress. He was pleased to say that up to the present no call had been made upon the fund. (Applause.) The Chairman congratulated the Order upon the eminent success of the demonstration that day. He was glad that the Rechabitnt had joined them in their service on the pre- vious day and the procession that day,, and he hoped that next year they would see their way to go with them alto- gether, or that the Sons of Temperance would go with the Rechabites. (Hear, bear.), He (the chairman) was not very old, but he remembered the time when Runcorn was a very drunken place ' • and they would, remember that a cer- tain celebrated divine described Runcorn as having been given over to "drunkenness and dissent." Fourteen or fif- teen years ago that was a true description of the place. But at the present time drunkenness had diminished, and he was quite as thanklul to say that Dissent had increased. (Hear, hear.) He suggested that in future years the various temperance organisations in the town should unite for the PurP, se of having one demonstration, which, he held, should be of a purely teetotal character. (Applause.) Alluding to the advanteges.af an Order like that el the Sons of Tem- perance, the chairman said, it was worthy of note that while in a society like the Oddfellows,, the death rate was 13 per 1,0004 that of the Sons of Temperance was only 7 per 1,000. It was impossible for a person to think he cralid take drink without injuring himself. He might talk of sowing his " wild oats" and then sobering down. But if he sowed to a wind be must reap the whirl- wind. With regard be legislation, he thought the Irish question had taught teetotallers a lesson. He tkought if the leaders of the temperance movement would take a stand similar to that which Mr. Parnell took upon the Irish ques- tion, they would force it as readily to the fore as the Irish leader succeeded in pushing his matter to the fore. (Hear, hear). He thought their temperance leaders should give instructions for all temperance people to vote square for the candidate pledged to bring about temperance legislation. (Applause.) Mr. John Withington, in a short address, said he was proud to have been associated with the Rechabites that I day' The two Orders were not rivals in the field of total

abstinence, but in labouring for tbe redemption of man from drink they were real unionists. (dear, hear.) On the motion of Mr. Tempe:lE7, second by Mr. 819 brown, a vote of thanks was convoyed to the chairman for presidi.ug.

Durim-g the evening thc following Programme was pet- formed :—Vioiin solo, Master Willie Kennon ; re,citatien, Miss C. Littler; recitation, Mr. Walter Millington; Ala recitation. Master J. 'l'. Bisbrown. Th chairman also pr sented Master Willie Cooke with a book in recognition of big having proposed for membership a larger number of cadets than any ether member.
_ . The proceedings concluded with the singing of the Doxology,

'THE RECHABITE DEMONSTRATION. The members of the "Union Tent," adult, and the" celsior," juvenile, of the Independent Order of Recha-* bites held their annual demonstration on Monday. They met at the Duke of Wescrninster's Cocoa Rooms at half' past one, where they joined in..,rocessional order, and headed by the Widnes 6oap Wovit‘e Brass Band, under the conductorship of Mr. William Jannett, proceeded by way Of Greenway-road, Shaw-street. Duke's Field, and Church - street to Dr. Robinson's, where the band played a selection. The procession ists then proceeded, in conjunction with the Sons of Temperance, down Bridge-street and Halton-road, to a field kindly placed at their disposal by Brother Mat- thew Sweetman. The beautiful banners of the two sections of the Order were carried in the procession, and with these , and a number of other small- flags- and bannerettes, the proceedings presented a very pretcy appearance. Remark.' ' ably gook order was kept by Messrs. S. Lamb, Richard Evans, and James Lea, who acted as marshals.. At the bead of the procession were Brothers Dia.mend, of South. port, Past High Chief Ruler; Joseph Spruce, of Preston Brvok and George Marshall, honorary member. Alter spending the afternoon in the field the Rechabites came back by way of Bridge-street and High-street to the Co". operative Hall, where tea was provided and about 400'Pe5" sons sat down.

Is the evening a public meeting was held in the Co•oeer- ative Hall, uneer the presidency of Mr James Pritchard, who was supported by the following gentlemen :—Mr. Dia- mond, of Southport ; Mr. Joseph Spruce, of Preston Brook ; the Rev. E. Williams, and Meesre. James Lea (secretary), J• C. Warburton, Richard Evans, drc. The Chairman, after a few preliminary. observations, said _ so far as he could understand the workings of the Rechae bites, they embraced two very important practices, one of total abstinence, and the other the benefits that accrued frorn the benefit society. He thought any eause which promoted two such important principles was deserving and worthy ef all support and encouragement, and of every success—(aV plause)—and be trusted that they would go forward in in. creaeing numbers, in power, and in influence in the town - (Hear, hear.) He presumed that they gained their title from the Independent Rechabites that were mentioned in Scripture. Certainly they did set forth a very noble es' ample of adherence to principle, and he trusted that they in the present day, the modern Recbabitesovould also stand forth to expound their principles and adhere to them with equal tenacity to what the Independent Rechabites did in years gone by,. and that they in the town of Runcorn would do all they could to wipe off that-stain of drink which was upon this country's fair fame and hollow. (A1)- pl Anse.) The Secretary then read his report of tbe adult eocietl'• from which it appeared that the number otmembers on the books on the rat January, 18e5,.was 131, and there had been admitted during the year 34, making a total of 165. TWO had died during the year, and six had. left from other causes, thus bringing the number at the end of' December 10 157, which showed a net increase for the year of 28. During the present year they had initiated 10 ' and lost two, giving a nett increase of eight, which, plus 157, gave a total of 165 ordinary members, with two honorary members The nett increase to the present was 34. (Applause) The average age at 31st December, 1885 was 28 years. The benefit fund at 31st December,lBB4, was £276 is 6p, management fund £l4 15s 61, total £290 17s OP. On the 31st- December, 1885, the benefit fund was £31415s sp, and the manage- ment fund £/455, total £329 Oe SP. At March of the present year the benefit fund was £3OB 23 3p, and the management fund £l3 18s al, total £3220s Bd. The aver.- age sick pay for members for 1885 was 9e 9P, and for the past nine years 65 9P. The worth per member on the 31et December, 1885, was £2 is 11d. Mr. Richard Evans then read the report of the juvenile branch, prefacing it by the remark that they were gill go- ing onward and upward. That was their motto, and through the past year it had been put inpractice.. Twelve months ago, in June, 1885, they had on the books 107; members. During 1886 they had 117, and with five who had entered the lodge that day, it meek, a total of 122, or an increase since June, 1885, of 15. They bad also an increase ill fueds. In Ante, 1885, they had £2l is ; and in June, 1886. £26 Is 4d. (Applause.) Addresses were delivered by Mr. Spruce and Mr. Dia- mond. During the evening an entertainment was taken part in by the following :—Miss Wormsley, Masters Walter Hague, Henry Hart, George West, and St. JOhn's Church choir.

TER IMPORTANT CONSIDERATION. A_ I- A most linportant consideration for all at this seaston of the year is how best to rid the system of tt e diseases induced by the trials of winter In many cases,it seems as though tbe seeds of consumption had been planted in the system by the trying weather we have gone through. The symptoms may' have commenced with a sllgh; cold, a little sore throat wail hoarseness, then come, perhaps, a feeling of weakness, or chil- liness, accrmpanied or followed by aching of the limbs; noir and again a hot, dry, feeling of the skin; gen-rat feverishness; tightness in the chest, with difficulty of breathing ; a MOD cough, short and dry. then soma expeotorAtion ; the weakness incresees, and friends become anxious. _ .

In other cases various forms of Liver or Kidney Complaints are develop-d ; tbe lassitude becomes nervous weakness; tbe sleep Is uneasy, and troubled by unpleasant dreams; and the patient, instead of waking refreshed, gets ,rip with a teeliag of weight and anguor, and every action seems a burden. Fire broke out on Monday evening in the,urnieroom of the Olive Mount Mill, Burnley, and a considerable portion of the building was pracfcally destroyed before the out.. break was subdu,d. The damage is estimated at about £7,000, and 250 operatives will be temporarily deprived of em ployment. SIIOCEIN-G ACC3DENT AT' PLY3,IOI:ITH.—On Monday after- noon, an Oddfellows' Ate was being held at the Drill Hall. Plymouth. In the midst of a foot-race a rush was made for. a raised platform, which suddenly gave way. When tboo struggling mass of people had been extr:c,ated, it was found,. that of-three sisters named Coombe two bad been killed and,' one dreadfully crushed,and that several other persons had been iejared. SIIOCKING MURDER. OF A POLICB Oaaricaß NEAR BAEVO" LEL—Dodsworth, a naining village about two miles front Barnsley, wason Saturday evening the scene of a shocking murder. James Maisphy, a collier, who has been repeatedli before the Barnsley Bench, deliberately shot Police•constable Austwick, who wan stationed in the sane village, causing his death about two hours afterwards. The decease, wh° was a very intelligent man, was educated at Thopp Arch College, near Tadcaster. He was one of the finest officers in the West Riding Constabulary,, standing Oft 4in,sand be- ing of commanding appearance. So far as can :ae ascer' tamed, the motive for the crime seems to lie in the fact that on Friday tne deceased had occasion to serve a summons erl Murphy for drunkenness, for which offence he was te. appear before the Barnsley Bench on Wednesday. As soon' as the gun was fired Austwiek fell to the ground, bleedin profusely. He was taken up and carried to h:s own house,. where a doctor attended him. Although sensible to the last, he never fairly rallied, and he died al half-past one- o'clock on Sunday morning. He was able to narrate tbe circumstances which led to his death. He 'ewes widow and five children. Murphy, in addition to 418 conviction recorded against him at tha instance of his Ile' Urn, has been repeatedly fined by the Barnsley Bench various offences. He has served five years for housebreak- ing at Batley. Murphy is a married man, and has children. The wound caused by the gunshot was tbre inches in diameter —An inquest was held at Barnsley 0e Monday. Evidence was given that Murphy had times threatened to take the life of the constable. div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

A difficult mis.sion--Submission. The nicest things in summer hats—Pretty girls. Highland drover, trying unsuccessfully to divide a flock of sheep: " Roth, hoch, ta stupid brutes, tere's no Wan o' them wur gang two roads at wan timel'l An editor who has reached the advanced age of ninety attributes his long life and excellent health to the fact that he never expected to please everybody and never. tried to do so. Customer, in restaurant : "See here, Mr. Proprietor This steak is so tough I can scarcely cut it." Proprietor: "We will make all right, sir. Here, waiter, just bring this gentleman another knife !" A writer says, "In great emergencies woman is a silent power among men." She is a power at all times ; undoubtedly a great power in emeigencies, but a silent power !—the writer is certainly not a married man. "You'll be glad to hear, John," said a farmer to his shepherd one day, "that the University of St. Andrew's has made our minister a doctor." "I am naeway sur- prised at that," said the shepherd. "Mair than twenty years syne he cured my wife o' a colic. I think he should hae been made a doctor lang syne!" A BEAUTIFUL ExemPLE.—They were sailing in the little boat together, and she said, "Are we running be- fore the wind now, George?" "No, my darling! said he, "our boat is hugging* the shore." "Ah !" she ex- claimed, "what a beautiful example we have here." THE COLOURED Momna's SOLICITUDE.—Passing along a side street some days ago I sa,W an ebon black woman standing in a doorway gesticulating with energy as she called to an equally black barefooted urchin of some eleven years. "You, George Washington! you come right along here and put yer shoes on, else folks'll take yer to be an Irish chile. Do you hear now? move right smart and don't you never go into the street with yer bare feet." Old Wigglesworth, who is somewhat irascible' called for a glass of milk and a bottle of soda water at lunch. "Look here, waiter !" he said angrily. "Here's a cow's hair floating in this milk." 'Well, sir," the waiter I answered, rubbing his hands softly together," you would not expect to find a horse-hair in milk, would you, sir ?" TILE MINISTER REBUKED.—A little girl, 3 years old, attended church for the first time with her older sister. During the sermon she heard the minister mention the name of God several times, and acted as if she knew he was doing something wrong. At last she could stand it no longer. The next time he said it she rose in her seat, and, pointing her chubby finger at him, she said, in im- pressive tones, "Man, 'top Your swearin' The following is said to be an authentic anecdote of Charles Darwin. It refers to his old age—the period when he was bringing out his books on the habits of plants. His health was failing, and an old family ser- vant—a woman—overhe,aring his daughter express some anxiety about his condition, sought to reassure her by all right, madam, hif saying, "Hi believe master'd be 'e only 'id somethin' to hoccupy 'is mind; sometimes 'e stands in the conservatory from mornin' till night just a-lookin at the flowers. Hif 'e only 'ad somethin' to do, 'e'd be hevver so much better, hi'm sure I." RUNNING No RISKS.—" Now, Johnnie, go' and kiss your little sweetheart, and make it up," said Johnnie's mother. "No, I won't !" "Go and tell her how niuch you love her, and how sorry 'you are." "No, I won't! Pa says he got into a breach of promise cae by tellin' a girl that, and had to marry the old thing. I won't run any risks, I won't!" One of the' most amusing incidents of the general election of 1885 occurred at a meeting held at Cheadle in support of Sir William Cunliffe Brooks. A very eager but very decent Irishman announced that he wished to ask Sir William a question, which he accordingly pro- ceeded to do. The question was this, "What grounds have you for the statement made by you that a large number of the Irish voters are illiterate ?" The chair- man told him that, if he would write down the question and send it up to the platform with the other questions, it would be answered. The Irishman, however, objected to do this, and, being asked why he objected, said at , last, amid roars of laughter, " Shure thin I can't write!"
Why is a man who keeps his eyes shut like an illiterate schoolmaster ?—Because he keeps his pupils in dark-

ness. "NEVER AFORE !"—The house of a well-known member of society in Porchester Terrace is exactly two miles one thousand seven hundred and fifty-nine yards from the Carlton Club. This gentleman so constantly drives from his house to the Carlton in a cab, and so invariably gives the cabman the exact eighteenpence, which is the legal fare, that he is known to the cabdrivers of his neigh- bourhood as "the worst job in London." A few days ago, however, he drove the distance, and, being in a , cheerful temper, he for once gave the cabman an extra, sixpence. The cabman looked at the unwonted two ' shillings, but said not a word, and prepared to drive away. "Why, you ungrateful rascal," said his fare, "I have given you an extra sixpence, and you never even say "Thank you' !" "Would you like to know the reason why ?" asked the cabman, pulli "Yes, I should," returned his fare. "Then, sir,-it is this. I've druv yo a good many years, and I never see a hextra sixpence from you afore. And when I did see it, s'help me, it took my breath away !" The mind of man loves to substitute something in- telligible for that which is unintelligible, just as English sailors changed Bellerophon, which had for them no meaning, into Bully Ruffian, which convey-ed a definite idea. So an English boy, remarks a writer in a monthly contemporary, seeing no sense in the word " y-cleped," makes Milton state that "in Heaven yelped Euphrosyne." The same tendency urged another boy to say, "Find out some uncouth swell," in the place of the usual reading "cell." A third described some one as "a man three feet high." It appeared, upon inquiry, that this person had been called by the master a "freebooter ;" this word, conveying no idea, had been altered by the boy to "three-footer," and this had by him been expressed more elegantly in words quoted above. Painful recol- lections must have led another to describe a "weeping birch" as "a birch that makes you weep ;" while expe- riences of another kind made his friend define "eating cares" as "troubles because you are tired of eating," the triumvirate being completed by one who said that "spoiler's hand" meant "father's hand," because he spoils you.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

• An ordinary meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday evening. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), presiding; Alder- men Burgess, Holmes, Chandley, Webster; Councillors Broadbent, Brown, ,utton, Ashton, Whittle, Greenall, Hut- chinson, W. Pierpoint, Jolley, Dixon, Bolton, Wright, Roberts; Brook (town clerk), Paterson (gas manager), and Chcrley (borough treaturer). WATCH COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the members of the police force be provided with the serge tunics, and that the order for these tunics be given to Messrs. Smith and Co., of Derby, at Sc 6d elch. On the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman WnsTrza, the minutes were confirmed.
NINANCI. The Finance Committee's minutes, which contained various orders for payment of accounts, were confirmed. on he motion of Alderman liomatts, seconded by Councillor Bzowx.

STREET IMPROVEMENT, &C. The minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee contained a recommendation that the following plans be approved :—Plan of new store, dining room, stable, and loft in Lythgoes-lane for Mr. John Platt; twenty cet- tages in Battersby-lane for Mr. John Appleton; abed at 34, Lythgoes-lane, for Mr. Joseph Oakes; alterations to house in Sues-street for Mr. H. Ferguson; new offices at Bank Quay for Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons; 17 houses in York- street and a new street off York-street, for Mr. Joseph Twiss. The minutes also coatained the following letter : The Cheshire Lines Committee, Secretary's Office, Man- chester, June Sed, 1816. My dear sir,—l broaght before the Committee at their last meeting the question of the giving up of the piece of land for widening Bewsey-etreet. Warring- ton, and I am desired to inform you that while tfie Com- mittee think they should receive some payment for that valuable piece of land, still they think the argument you use is not without weight, and therefore they agree to the proposition made by you, that upon the condition of our giving up the piece of land in question. the Corporation will, at their own expense, widen. pave, die., the street, and make no claim for Rowe-street, which is proposed to be ab- sorbed by the Committee, and that they also consent to the crossing over of Winwick-street with the additional bridge in accordance with the plans for which we are seeking powers in the bill of the present session of Parliament.— Yours very truly, Edward Ross, secretary. W. H. Brooh, Esq., town clerk, Warrington. The Improvement Commit- tee considered that the terms of this letter were satisfactory, and recommended that they be agreed to. Councillor BBOADBBNT moved, and Councillor BUTTON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman WEBSTER asked if any steps were being taken for the widening of Friar's-gate, Or whether it was to remain a narrow street. Councillor HuTCRINSON also desired to be informed on this point. Councillor BROADDSNT said the committee had had that question under consideration within the last few days almost It was thought when the arrangements for the im- provement of Bridge-street were made that it was not worth while sacrificing much land for the widening of Friar's- gate, because it was thought that under no circumstances could it ever be an impartant street, and it was thought also that the proper side to widen Friar's-gate would be the upper side, that was to say the side nearest Market-gate. But the borough surveyor had prepared a plan for widen- ing Friar's-gate from the position of the old district bank to Bridge-street, and he (Councillor Broadbent) thought the committee had decided to still further increase the width, thus making 1.1, narrow part of Friaes-gate which abuts on Bridge-street about as whir... nearly so, as the widest part. The committee had decided to widen it at the month as ' much as possible without sacrificing too much of the valu- able land they had at their disposal. He also called the attention of the Council to the minute referring to the very satisfactory arrangement that had been made with the Cheshire Lines Committee. Alderman BURGESS said he should like to make one sug- gestion, and that was that instead of considering the widen- ing of Friar's-gate, which he thought would be found not be so grand an improvernen,t as they might expect, they I might continue the line of St. Austin's-lane through into Bridge-street, and so make a good street from Bridge-street to Bank Quay. Alderman VVEESTBR considered that ultimately the street would be an important one. The minutes were then confirmed. e SANITARY COMITITTBE.—STRBET WATERING. The Sanitary Committee's minutes contained a resolution that the Warrington Waterworks Company be required to fix hydrants for street watering purposes on their mains at the following places :—ln Knutsford-road, opposite entrance to Old Warps; in Knutsford-road, near the Cheshire Cheese Inn ; on Wilderspool Causeway, near Miss Picton's house. And also a resolution that the tender of Mr. Jacob Sankey for the purchase of all manure made at the Cor- poration stables for the next 12 months, at 6s per ton, be accepted. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, referred to the minute relative to hydrants for street watering. At present, he said, the water for watering the two very important thoroughfares, Latchford Causeway and Wilierspool Causeway bad to be carted from the hy- drant in Wharf-street, off Mersey-street. Gentlemen pre- sent would very easily see that carting water from Mersey- street ever the bridge, and down to the Cheshire Cheese, and up towards Wilderspool, must be attended with a very large expenditure, a great deal of which might be avoided if they could have the water nearer at hand. The resident public on those thoroughfares bad a right to complain in summer time when the roads were covered with dust, and in the next place the roads being macadamised they suffered from the want of moisture to keep the binding material together, and that applied to Wilderspeol Causeway, whore the wind blew away the dust, which was really the binding material, and as a consequence the road became all loose on the surface and wasted away with great rapidity. He believed that the county surveyor had been over here on this very subject, and be complained of the condition of the road; and he (Alderman Burgess) did not think that their present satisfactory arrangement with the county as to that road should be disturbed. Alderman Burgess then read the following letter, signed by Mr. John Ross, secretary of the Warrington Waterworks Company, relative to the matter : " Warrington water. Dear Sir,—In reply to yours of the 30th ult., according to agreement your requirements for street watering in Knutsford-road were not to exceed 300 gallons per hour at opposite entrance to Old Warps, and 300 gallons per hour at 'neat the Cheshire Cheese Inn.' A three-quarter-inch pipe will in each case suffice to pass these quantities. Under the same agreement your requirements at Miss Picton's were for 1,800 gallons per day; but as the disused main by which you could draw 10,800 gallons per hour near St. James'-street, runs along the river side at the back of Miss Picton's, you could apply the full power of that main to street watering purposes, the connection with which and a pipe to Wilderspool-road would cost £3O or £4O. If you take the water carts to the river side. Say by the foundry, the cost of coenectioa will be about £l5. A cheap river side connection could be made per the company's river discharge pipe; but unfortunately this pipe is 165 yards from the Black Lion, and 240 yards from the foundry in Croes-street. A similar cheap connection could be made per company's river discharge pipe at the River View corner. At any of these points the carts could be loaded:in less than one minute's time; but the distances off the) main road would form a constant expense in the way of idle travel. I shall be glad to point out to you the river side mains, as also the discharge pipes above referred to. With reference to the tin. pipe, which would only give 300 gallons per hour, he thought that was rather like trifling with the question. There would be an hour wasted in load- ing a cart, and the money that would be run away with in the shape of horse hire would be very considerable. (Hear, hear.) He doubted whether they could not get better terms with the company, but if it was found that the committee had not carried out that work, do not let the Latchford people suppose that their interest had been lost sight of. (Hear, hear.) Councillor SuTTON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor DIXON asked if John Holland had been dis- charged from the Longford Works, or had left. Alderman CHANDLE'Y asked if Alderman Burgess would explain whether the Corporation bore the cost of whatever hydrants were put up.

Alderman BURGESS said, in reply to Alderman Chandlev's question, that whatever they might require from the Water- wotks Company they would have to p.y for. (Hear, hear.) With regard to Councillor Dixon's question, he believed that John Holland hail left the Long tord Works, but as to whether he had discharged himself, or had been discharged he could not a.iv. if Councillor Dixon wished it, he would ascertain whether Holland had been discharged or

not. • Councillor DixoN said he should be glad if Alderman Burgess would do that. The minutes were then cenfirmed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that the borough sur- veyor bad laid upon the table a plan of the borough, showing the whole of the sewerage system, and that a resolution had been passed that the same should be laid before the Coun- cil at its next meeting, and that it be an instruction that the plan be constantly kept up, showing any extension or alteration of any building, sewer, or private drain. Councillor BROWN moved, and Councillor ASHTON sec- onded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor ROBERTS asked if it would be possible to have a regular systematic flushing of drains in Friar's-green, Stanley-street, and Museum-street and that neighbourhood. The stench committed from the grid-holes at times was simply horrible, and was, he believed, entirely owing to the drains being so near the river. There was very little fall and consequently the refuse that the drains were more or less filled with was lying stagnant and emitted vapours of the snost disagreeable and dangerous character. Be thought that it was quite time that whoever was responsible should have their atter), ion called to that fact. Alderman BURGESS said what Councillor Roberts com- plained of had already been attended to. The Sanitary Com- mittee had undertaken the carrying of it out irrespective of the Paving Committee, and had given instructions to the borough surveyor thih there should be the requisite amount of flushing in the neighbourhood of the town referred to. But they must bear in mind that all these luxuries had to be paid for, and in the end there was a cossiderable total arising from the use of water with that freedom which he thought it ought to be used. Councillor WHITTLE said that that nuisance would not arise but for Alderman Burgess's tallow works at Friars'- green. (Laughter.) If he had not been chairman of the COnimittee they Would nt)t have been allowed to retrain there. Councillor SUTTON: What has that to do with Bank Quay. Councillor WHITTLE: Shut up. (Laughter.) The minutes were then confirmed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. Alderman WEBSTER, in proposing the adoption of the minutes of this committee drew attention to the report of the inspector that 102 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 98 cases for 235 children. The number of parents, he said, who found themselves unable to pay school fees seemed to be increasing seriously, and was evidence of the great distress prevalent in various parts of the town. Councillor &attars- seconded the resolution, reworking that he was sorry to have to endorse what Alderman Web- ster said in reference to the school attendance cases.

The minutes were coufirmed. fuesiom.LIBILARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee stated that the visitors to the Museum in June numbered 2,316, the books issued in reading room 1,276, and those issued to subscribers 1,436. Several gifts bad been received. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Alderman WEBSTNR, seconded by Councillor W. PIERPoncr.

CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The report of this committee was adopted on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor WHITTLE. It con- tained a report of the Registrar, that the intermeuts for tbe past five weeks were :—Adults 23, minors 29, stillborn and premature 7 ; and for the corresponding period last year : Adults 28, minors 19, and stillborn and premature 9. The receipts for the past four weeks were £59 9s bd, and for the corresponding period last year £55 4s 6d. TOWN HALL, PARE, AND BATES COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee, which were confirmed on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor 13ourow, reported that the income from the Baths for the past four weeks was £35 lOs 101, and for the corresponding period last year £33 lOs 10d. The committee also recommended that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to have the aviary in the gardens repaired and put into proper order; and that the tender of Messrs N. Greening and Sat's. Limited, for the repair of the aviary in the gardens at £36 7s 6d be ac- cepted.

MARKETS COMMITTBE. This committee recommended that the tender of Mr. William Wareing for the painting and whitewashing, &e., at the Markets be accepted; and that the tender of Mr. Thomas Oakes, the cleaning and preparing of the iron work on the Market roofs be accepted. The total income from the Markets for the past four weeks had been £266 is sd. Alderman CHAXnutv proposed, and Councillor GREENALL seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON asked what was the amount of the tenders referred to in the minutes; he thought that was in- formation that should have been furnished. Alderman CHANDLEY said that it was not usual, nor desirable, to furnish the amount of tenders, but Councillor Bolton could if he wished obtain the information at Mr. Chorlev's office. Councillor ROBERTS thought that Councillor Bolton bad raised a very proper question. The prices at which tenders were accepted by some committees were published to the Council, but in the case of other committees the figures were omitted. There should be one standing rule, either to publish or not to publish them. The Paving and Sewerage Committee invariably published the figures. Councillor BOLTON moved as an amendment that the minutes be -confirmed with the exception of that portion referring to the tenders, but the amendment was not seconded. The minutes were then confirmed. GAS OOMMITTEB.

The minutes of this committee, which were net of in- terest, were proposed for adoption by Alderman Hoom, and the motion WAS seconded by Councillor WRIGHT. Councillor DixoN asked where the £20,000 that it was said had been received from the gasworks had gone, and, in reply, Alderman HOLMES said that if Councillor Dixon would refer to the financial statement he would find the in- formation he desired. £20;000 had been paid off since the works were pm chased. The minutes were passed. PROPOSED PURCHASE OF THE WATERWORKS.

The General Purposes Committee recommended "that the Mayor, Aldermen Davies, Crosfield, Holmes, Webster, and Burgess be re-appointed a committee to make overtures to the Warrington Waterworks Company as to the purchase of their undertaking, and that they be requested to resume their negotiations and report to this committee." The MAYOR proposed the adoption of the committee's minutes. At every Council meeting, he said, they were more and more convinced how desirable it was that they should have control of the water. The present arrangements were of a most unsatisfactory character, and were scarcely creditable to the town.

Alderman BURGESS seconded the proposition. Councillor BOLTON: Are any of the gentlemen on the committee shareholders in the waterworks company? I think, if they are, they should retire. Alderman BURGESS: I think Alderman Davies has a share. Councillor POLTON I think he ought to retire. Alderman WEBSTER said that whatever Alderman Davies's interest in the waterworks might be, his interest in that borough would far outstrip it, and he was sure that he (Alderman Davies) would give most cordial advice to the committee.

Councillor JOLLEY said that the question of Councillor Bolton was a pertinent one. He did not for one moment doubt the honour of the gentlemen whom it was proposed should be appointed, but thought that, as a matter of pu in- ciple, anyone who was a shareholder had no right to repre- sent the Council in negotiating a purchase. He then called for the exercise of great caution in undertaking such a ne- gotiation, as the gentlemen who were to take it in hand, though good business men, were not technically acquainted with the matter, and might thus be.placed at a disadvan- tage. • After a little farther discussion, the MAYOR said that whatever the committee did would be subject to the appro- val of the Council, and the minutes were then passed. This was all the business before the meeting.

div.head: PRLSCOT MAN AWARDED £4OO
div.p: A PRLSCOT MAN AWARDED £4OO

DAMAGES. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, the case of Prescott against the London and North-Western Railway Company came on for hearing. The plain- tiff, a watch manufacturer' living at Stanley-crescent, Prescot, sought to recover damages for injuries ens- tamed on board one of the company's boats. Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Thomas Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pope, Q.C., and Mr. Moore were for the defendants.—ln opening the case, Mr. Addison, Q.O , said he thought that there would be no doubt that the plaintiff had sustained some injuries, and that he was entitled to some corepensatioe. He stated the circumstances under which the plaintiff received the in- juries whilst returning from Ireland in June, 1885, in one of the defendants' steamers, the Banshee. The ship ran upon the rocks near Holyhead, and plaintiff, who at the time happened to be in the starboard part of the ship look- ing out of the port-hole, was suddenly thrown forward upon his left shoulder, was jerked forward again, and some lug- gage which was piled up behind him, came tumbling down upon him. Ile felt but little injury then, and proceeded home, where he became exceedingly ill, suffering from severe pains. Dr. Hall, his medical adviser, was called in, and in January other doctors visited him. He had not, however, got well, and it was doubt- ful as to whether he would get thorobighlv well again.— The plaintiff then gave evidence and stated that after the occurrence though feeling unwell, he proceeded to Liver- pool, and occurrence, there to Prescot. When at home he became so unwell that a medical man was called in, and he bad been more or less ill ever since, being at the present time I very ill. In crossemarnination plaintiff said that he had lost two stones in weight since the accident. Be suffered Ifrom pains in the stomach, which he thought was wind, and. ' seat for his medical attendant. In reply to further ques- tions he said : I feel as though somebody had struck me across the shoulder with a stick, and as though a locomo- tive had gone against me. (Laughter.)—Mr. Pope: I sup- pose the locomotive buffer must have gone against you. (Laughter.) Although you suffer from pain in the back, you appear to be upright? Plaintiff: I was always up- right. (Loud laughter.) I feel pains in my foot and legs, and sometimes as though a ballet bad gone into my foot, or a 561 b weight had fallen upop me.—Mr. Pope: Dear me! That's rather like gout. elocomotive in your back, and bullets in your foot. (Loud laughter.)—A porter at the Prescot Railway Station was called, and stated that. he noticed that the plaintiff, when he reached Prescot on the morning after the accident, was unwell; and the plaintiff's wife stated that when he came home she applied hot fomen- tations to the back and ironed him. (Laughter.) Since that time he had never been able to dress himself, nor had he been able to work at all.—Dr. H. F. Hall, of Prescot, stated that he had attended the plaintiff for some twenty years. During that period he had noticed some symptoms which made him believe that he suffered from cengestion of the kidney, and treated him for that complaint, he be- ing well when his treatment terminated. When, after the accident, he was called in, he found the plain- tiff suffering from aches and pains, whieh he attributed to shock. It was, in his opinion, doubtful as to whether he would be well again.—Dr. Lowndes was also called, and stated that he found the plaintiff was still suffer- ing from fright and nervous shock.—Dr. Paull, lecturer on jurisprudence at the theiversity College, also gave evidence on behalf of the plaintiff, stating that the exposure and the shock would have a tendency to reproduce the complaint the plaintiff had been suffering from befere.—This being the plaintiff's case, Mr. Pope said he did not intend to call any witness.—Mr. Addison having summed up, Mr. Pope ad- dressed the jury on the question of damages. He did not dispute that the plaintiff had sustained BOMB injury, but contended that it did not wholly arise from the accident. He asked the jury to give the plaintiff £75 for expenses, and £2OO as compensation for the injuries he had received. —Mr. Addison: We want more.—The jury returned a ver- dict for the plaintiff, damages £4OO.
