AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. There were pre- sent Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P. (chairman), the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Jolley, Forster, W. Houghton, Woods, K. 'shall, John Houghton, R. OwAn ; S. Sutton (clef k), J. C. Sutton (clerk to the Guardians), W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and Rawlings (inspector) MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPorcr.—Dr. Sephton reported , that toe number of biiths in the district during the past rcomth was 38, deaths 11; death rate from all Causes was equal to 10 1 per 1000, against 13.8 the corresponding month of last year. Tne death rate from zvmotic diseases (seven principal) was equal to nil agtinst *4 per 1,000, the average rate of the lea three months, and *9 the cerrespond- ing month of last year.—The Chairman: That itovery Bads- I ',teeny, Dr. Septiton.—Dr.Sepleton: Very satisfactory. SCRVEYOR.'S REPORT.—Mr. Owe reported that during the month inspections had been made of Mr. Hindley's house, Padgate ; Mr. John Jackson's houses, Penketh ; Mr. J. Davies' house and outbuildings, Hullinfare ; Lord Winmarleigh'e cottages and farms, itivon ; Mrs Ashbrook's house, Orford ; additions to Wesleyan Schools, Padgate ; and Mr. Jos. Bissell's houses, Price-street, off Lovely-lane. The following plans for buildings were eutonitted and might be approved as being in accordance with the bye- laws : For the trustees of the New School Char :1, Burton- wood ; plats of chapel and schoolroom to be erected at Burtonwood ; Mr. James Craven, additions to house at Rixton. Lovely-lane drainage district :He had aFcertained positions where two sewers would be required. During thel month he would obtain estimates and lay them before them at their neat meeting. Lodge-lane, Bewsey :He had to re- port to them that this drain was almost completed, and thatl he should require the connectionsof the house proper,y to be made a oece. so that the nuisance arising from the ditch at the roadside might cease.—The report was adopted. RESIGNATION OF AN OFFICER.—A let:er Was read from Mr. Bawling, inspector of nuisances, tendering the resignation of his office, which he bad held for up- wards of thirteen years, haviog been appointed by the Rawtenstail Local Board to the office of in- Spector of nuisance of their district. He wished to take that opportunity of thankieg all those members of the Authority wko had at all times endeavoured to assist and support him in the discharge of his duty; and also to thank their clerk, medical officer, and all the officers of the War- rington Uoion, with whom he had worked amicably for 17/ years. The Clerk mentioned that he also had a letter from the clerk of the Bawtenstall Local Board asking that Mr. R.rwlings might be allowed to go to his new sphere. at as early a moment as they could possibly allow blue—The CHAIRMAN said Mr Rawling's letter was a very proper one, and showed a proper feeling towards the Authority and its officers. If Mr. Bawling must go he would carry with him their appreciation of the very devoted services be bad reniered to the Autherity. (hear, hear.)—On the motion of Mr. FORSTER, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, the resignation was ace...n.ed, and on the motion of Mr. JR. HotromoN, seconded by Mr. KiLsaaLL, it was decided to advertise for a nuisance inspector, to be paid £BO a year and be provided with a uniform. This was all the business.

div.head: DIOCESAN MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DIOCESAN MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday, the anniversary of the Warrington institution for daughters and widows of clergy in the dioese of Liverpool and Chester and the arch- deaconries of Manchester and Blackburn was held at the Institution buildings at Warrington. Lord Egerton of Tatton presided, and amongst those present were the Bishop of Chester, Lord Winmar- leigh, Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., the Dean of Ches- ter, Archdeacons Gore and Bardsley, Canons Hop- wood, Maclure. Stowell, Greenall, Hergn, Upperton, Fielden, Dodd, Robin, Blencowe, Livingstone, and Clarke; the Revs. G. London, William Quekett, D. Ellison, G. W. Reynolds, P. M. Herford, Garven, and Holme ; Messrs. E. Greenall, J. C. Parr, H. D. Corbett, J. Allen, W. Beamont, J. Tinsley, John White, Sze., Sze.— Canon tiaausaLL read an annual report which stated thar two teheeter and one Manchester widows had been assisted to the amount of £3O since the annual grants were made in August last. Four of the pensioners (two widows, one frem Liverpool and one from Manchester. and two orphans, one from Chester and one from Manchester) had died, and the revnes of three widows and one orphan had been withdrawn frore rlJ' list during the year. Tilers were fourteen new ap- plicante—t we widows and one orphan from the Chester dis- trict, two widows and two orphans from lYtanchester diocese, and three widows and four orphans from Liverpool diocese. The number of the applicant, now on the list were—Chester, two widows and six orphans; Liverpool, twelve widows and six orphaes; Mance ester. three widows and nineteen orphans, making a total of 104 applicants-73 widows and 31 orphans. Six free scholars in the Clergy Danghters' School had been pad for during the year by the parent society at the rate of £45 each, the total amount paid being £270. One of the six hail ceased to be a free scholar, and the remaining five— two from Chester and three from Mauchester—now asked for a renewal of their grants. Tnere were three applicants for the vacincy—one from Chester and two from Liver- pool. The meeting would be asked to sanction pensions, donation?, and payments to the Clergy Daughters' School to the amount of £2.390. The committee were obliged last year to withhold donations to the amount of £l5O and the whole of the bonuses. They had re- • ceived many urgent appeals for the renewal of those donations this year, but in the face of the still diminishing income and so many new applicants it seemed! impossible to do so, much less to give any bonuses. The committee were sorry to add that this year again they have been ohlieed to reduce the doeations to the amount of £lBO. There was again no legacy to report. The special donations amounted to £67 lie, and the remaining portion of the income was derived as follows :—From interest on ' invested capital and bank interest, £677; offertories, £636; ' snhscriptions, £846; grants from the unappropriated funds of the Chester and Liverpool Fieance Association.% £lO4 ; making a total of £2,331, or £94 less than the previous year. Tile amount received from offertories was £7l less ! this year than last. That, added to the £42 deficiency last last year, showed a falling off in two years of £ll3. The ! subscriptions were £5 13s less this year than last. The corn- mittee deeply regretted that these two important sources of inc rme showed so serious a diminution. If they continued to fall (AI as they had done during the last two years the c ommittee would be under the painful necessity of declin- ing all fresh applications, and they asked for renewed sup- ! port. In conclusion the report referred to the loss sustained ' in the death of the Bishop of Manchester.—The re- port was adopted without discussion.— The report of ' the Clergy Daughters' School, which was also adopted, stated that it was in a flourishing condition. Eleven pupils had been admitted, eight having left during the year, 63 remaining on the books—nine from Chester diocese, 32 from Manchester, 20 from Liverpool, and two extra- liocesan. Thirteen of those were orphans. The disepline of the school was excellent, and the conduct: of the girls as a whole had been good. There had been very 1 little sickness of a serious character during the year, and the Committee were thankful to say that there had not been ' one ease of infectious disease. By strict economy the debt 1 on the echool had been diminisbe.d, but the present income was not sufficient to meet the increased exp,.n.e of pa 7ing the stipend of a clerical principal The Committee urgently appealed to parents who had daughters in the school and to the cleray and laity of the three diecess to use their in- fluence to secure additional offerteries and subscriptions. ! A rho for a joint chapel for the school and training! college had been prepared and approved, and as soon as ; the necessary funds were provided the building would be ' proceeded with. •The training college authorities had set apart r•. legacy of £5OO •for the purpose, and altogether rather more than £BOO had been secured. The building would cost £l2OO, and the total cost, with fittings and other necessary expenses, would p.ob %Hy be £4500. The Committ es confidently commended the school to continued support. Other businees was transacted, and afterwards the Bishop of Chester preached the annual sermon in the Parish Church --In the afternoon luncheon was served in the dining hall at the in- stitution.—Lord Egerton of Tatton presided, and most of those who attended the business meeting, as ass a num- ber of ladies, were present —The Chairman pronosed the 1131,1a1 loyal toasts.—Lord Win m;trlerlh propos, d the healths of the Bishops of the three dioceses—Liverpool, Chester, and Manchester." All these bishops, he said, were deeply interested in the success of that meeting, and two of them had on various occasions exercised all the influence their position gave them in promoting its welfare. (Hear, hear.) The third had not yet come among them, but, from the charnter the present Bishop of Manchester bore in the minds of the people, he was convinced that when he did come among them they would find him acting as his col- leagues, the other bishops, had done.—The Bishop of Ches- ter (Dr. Stubbs) briefly replied to the toast.—The Chairman , proposed "The Clergy Instiution." The institution, he said, was an admirable one, serving in a most excellent way,' the really pressing need of the clergy of the three dioceses. It only required cordial co-operation and assistance to make it a thorough success. He was sorry that during the last year or two there had been a falling of in the funds. and that there was a question of diminishing some of the allowances, but he trusted that the want might be remedied by a more earnest advocacy of the claims of the institution thronehout the dioceses. In such matters the clergy had legitim,te claims on the laity, and that should be made known and understood. There should be no false delicacy on the part of the clergy in asking for assistance for the in- ' stiAltion, and he hoped that their claim, would be made more widely known.—Archeeacon Bardsh•yr gave the health of tbe" Lay Friends," coupling with it the name of Lord Winmerleigh.—Lord Winnaarleigh briefly replied —Sir Gil- bert Greenall, Bart., gave "The health of the Chairman," wee, after replying, proposed "The Town and Trade of Warrington," to which the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman H meson) responded. " The health of the .Secretary " (Canon Greenall) was also honoured, and the meeting then sepnrate.d.
The title by which Sir Thomas Brassey in sa in the House of Lords will be Lord Brassey of Bulkeley, and Sir Arthur Bide will become Lord Burton. C 0 ,

There is a very decided improvement in Mr. Ruskin's condition. He is now so much better that bulletins will only be issued periodically. EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT.—On Friday afternoon, a rumour was circulated that an accident had occurred at the Peasley Cross Collieries, belonging to Messrs. Bourne and Robinson, that a number of men bad been killed, and that others were cut off from the shaft by a fall of roof. The rumour bad its origin, it has since transpired, in an attempt to deceive the police. During the morning a woman named Elizabeth Wareing, had been bound over to keep the peace for assiulting a neighbour. As sureties were not forthcom- inz, she was placed in the cells. During the day a woman of the defendant's acquaintance entered the po-lice-station and said there had been an alarming accident, that Mrs. Wareines son was killed, and that the body had been brought home. Superint,ndent Johnston immediately despatched an officer to the Paisley Cross Collieries to ascertain the extent of the disaster, but as nothing unusual had occurred, the officer was sent to see if the dead body of Mrs. Ware- ing's son had been taken home. This was also found to be incorrect. As soon, however, as the woman was told that an accident had happened, and that her son was killed, she was seized with an epileptic fit, from which she did not re- cover for a considerable time. The woman who originated the cruel rumour was afterwards seen. She aPpeared to oe sorry for what she had done, and said she did not know what had possessed her.to do it, except to get Mrs. Wareing out of custody.

div.head: ptttro to the (Editor. THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.
div.p: ptttro to the (Editor. THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.

Sir,—May I ask the committee that was formed a few weeks ago to take up this question, what are they doing about It? Surely the recent election has not exbansted all their energy, nor, it is hoped, have they allowed the obsta- cles they met with to crash them. I think the agitation ought to commence again, and Mr. Beamont be made to see that he must move either one way or anotber..—Yonrs,
BOOKWORM.
THE FAIR TRADE CRAZE.

Sir,—Mav I call the attention of your Tory and Fair Trading readers to a few extracts taken from an abridged copy of the final report of the Trade Commission lately ap- pointed by the Tory Government to inquire into the causes of the supposed diminution in our trading returns? Very little consolation, I am afraid, will be found in the full re- port for those of your readers who placed faith in the large results expected to accrue from their appointment, and those electors of Warrington who believed in the Tory statements respecting the disadvantages of Free Trade and the ruin to which the Liberal party were fast hastening the countty, will no doubt regret baying voted for Sir Gilbert Greenall. Anyone who follows the various char-es in our commercial relations with foreign countries would be aware of the in- accuracy of these statements, but so repeatedly were they made that it seemed useless to deny them. All Liberals will be pleased with the report, inasmuch as it refatee the meins used by the Tories to win the November elections. The greatest influences at work for the Tories last Novem- ber were Fair Trade and the Irish vote. Already Lord Car- narvon and Mr. Parnell have explained. Will the final re- port of the Trade Commission justify the other influence? I think not.

The abridged copy from which I quote is communicated by the Central News authorities, and announces that "The Cornmissioaers do not find any evidence of depression of trade, so far as deprceeiuti 19 ltsen to mean the reettlction of trading operations. On the contrary, they find that the volume of British trade has continued to increase more and more than commensurately with the growth of the popula- tion, and that the general industrial condition of the coun- try is satisfactory." The Commissioners will report that "there has been anapnusuallY long period of over produc- tion, due mainly "fo the vast increase of wealth in the country, and the competition arising from a superabundance of capital." No fiscal alterations are suggested, nor will there he anything to report pointing to Fair Trade, protec- tive duties, or reciprocity as remedies. Can there be a more complete answer or exposure of the highfiown adventaxe of Fair Trade. etc. Surely after this no more will be written respecting a return to protective duties. Further comment is quite unnecessary.—Yours, W.

div.head: EARLESTOWN ANIT-VACCINATORS.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN ANIT-VACCINATORS.

Sir,—lf I were wishful to point out the most bigoted of all bigots I could imagine I should Wet' to that enlightened (?) and mind-illuminated (?) sect, the anti-vaccinators of Earlestown. Their fanatical zeal to override and thwart the just execution of the law on every possible occasion knows no bounds, and like the blind led by the blind they are led on by those whom I should have thought age would have taught to seek more honourable and lawful ends. I well remember the miserable attempts made to thwart the just execution upon their goods and chattels by the officers of justice on the fined anti-vaccinators being unwilling—or shall I say unable ?—to pay the fines and costs, much too small, imposed upon them. The deserved ridicule showered upon them on that occasion was shown more in sorrow than in anger; and I venture to think that in spite of their spas- modic and frantic efforts, the whole paper structure of" anti- vaccination" will shortly be ,scattered to the winds, unless better means are adopted to bring it into popular sympathy. These observations are caused by reading your account of the discussion on anti-vaccination at the meeting of the Board of Guardians of the Warrington Union which ap- peared in the "Examiner."

I see that friends Clarke and Ratcliffe—two brilliant and representative champions of that beclouded portion of the Warn i ',won Union, Earlestown—have again been airing their favourite topics of no prosecutions for failing to have child- ren vaccinated. What trash and nonsense this is! Away • with it. The bare suggestion of such a course, coming from respectable tradesmen and heads of families, is enough to make me wonder if 1 am in this Christian country of Eng- land. I speak now as a matter of principle. Granting, for the sake of argument to our friends John Clarke and George Ratcliffe, that the anti-vaccinators are conscien- tiously of opinion they are in the right in not having their children vaccinated, I would ask, does that constitute a justification for them to break the law and deliberately set it at defiance? Certainly not. If they believe so, then I would ask, why not apply the same principle all round ? Why should not a publican who conscientiously believes that a working-man should be served with a glass of beer on Sunday forenoon be allowed to sell it to him? Perhaps Messrs. Clarke and Ratcliffe will tell us ? Just as in the case of the anti-vaccinators, the publican would be acting upon his "conscientious principles." Again, supposing a revo- lutionist who believed that he was designed by God to have a due proportion of this world's goods should come to the premises and property of Messrs. Clarke and Co., and forci- bly help himself to what he "conscientiously " thought himself entitled, surely Meters. Clarke and Co. could not consistently object. I might go on multiplying instances without number, but the absurdity of the propositions of iMr. Clarke and the other anti-vaccinators is manifest to everybody. It a la, exists it should he obeyed by all and every class. If people are to be allowed to thwart the aims of jus- , tice because of conscientious scruples, this country—the ,1 symbol of all that is free—will soon become chaotic and without any system at all. Therefore let the anti-vaccina- tors suffer for the consequences of their sins of omission, and I have no doubt the public generally will say they have only lead meted out to them the punishment due to all law-breakers—Yours, &c., Warrington. August 3rd, 1888.
JUSTICE.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 7, 1886.
PRESCOL
CRICKET.—On Saturday last a cricket match was played between Liverpool and Prawn, the result being in favour of the visitors.

_ BANK HOLIDAY.—Monday and Tuesday were observed as a general holiday by the townspeople, most of the shops being closed both days. Many people availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting Blackpool and Southport, and the Liverpool Exhibition, the weather being all that couldl be desired.

AN OLD OBFENDBIL—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Jane Mulhearn, was summoned for being drunk ard disorderly in Beaconsfield-street, Prescot. on the 20th ult. The defendant, who did not appeAr, and had been 26 times previously convicted, was committed to prison for a month with hard labour.

A " RINGLBADRIC FlNED.—Thomas Lloyd was sum• moned at the Petty Sessions on Tuesday for being drunk and disorderly in Ellam's Court, Prescot, on the 19tn ult. The defendant did not appear. Superintendent Barker stated there had been a great deal of disturbance during the last fortnight about Ellam's Court, and the defendant was one of the ringleaders.—A fine of lOs and costs was in- flicted.

"A GOOD CrrAnacren."— Befere Messrs, F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sesaions, on Tues- day, Henry Byrne was summoned for being drunk and dis- orderly in Cross-street, Prescot, on the 26th ult. upt. Barker stated that since 1879 the defendant had had a good character, but prior to that time there were a great many convictions recorded against him.—The Chairman : Yeu see the benefit of a good character. We shall only fine you 5s and costs, and I hope it will be seven years before we again see you here. THE STONE THROWING NIIISANCB.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earki and W. L. Evans, Thomas Jones, Christopher Garritty,William Holdcroft, and William Molyneux pleaded guilty to a charge of throwing stones on the highway on the 18th ult. P.C. Burton stated that about eigbt o'clock on the Sunday night in question the boys were throwing stones in Scott's Barn-lane, Whiston. A good many people were returning from church, and several complaints of the stone- throwing were made. The Chairman said stone throwing was a most dangerous practice, and each defendant woula have to pay a fine of 2s 6d and costs. RIDING WITHOUT REINS.—At the Prescot Petty Ses- sions on Tuesday, Elias P.awlinson was summoned for riding on his waggon. drawn by two horses, without reins, at Knowsley, on the 24th tilt, and was fined 5s and costs.— James Maudalev, for riding on the shafts of his cart with- out reins, at Rainbill, was fined 2s 61 and costs.—George Sumner was fined 7s 6d and costs for riding on a harry, drawn by two horses, at Tarboek on the 24th ult. Supt. Barker described the defendant as a drunken lazy carter.— Uriah Upton. for being asleep in a dray drawn by two horses and laden wi.b beer barrels, at Knowsley on the 22nd nit., was fined fis 6d and costs.—A fine of 70 6d and costs was also imposed on Thomas Taylor for leaving his horse and cart without anyone in charge near the Eagle and Child, Huyton, on the 21st ult. A RAMIE= SERVANT ng TROURLIL-A t the Pres- cot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans, Sarah Regan, 17 years of age, was brought up for stealing a winsey skirt, petticoat, and bodice, together of the value of 2s, the property of Michael Con- nor, of the Forester's Arms beerhouse, Rainhill. Mrs Mary Connor stated that the prisoner had been in her employ as a servant up to June last, when she left. She missed the articles named after the prisoner had left, and she gave in- formation. She stated that she did not wish to press the charge against the prisoner, who had expressed her sorrow for what she bad done. She had been her servant for two years, and she never had hnevionslv to complain about her. Superinterdent Barker said the prisoner had been in cus- tody a week upon that charge, and it was her first appear- ance. The Bench hoped it would be a warning to her and discharged her with a caution. A SHOP•DOOR ROBBERY.—At the Petty Sessions on Tues- day, before Mr. F. W. Earle and W. L. Evans, Jane Gill, a young woman, was cnarged kvith stealing a dozen pairs of men's socks. value 6s 6d, from the door of the shop occupied by Mr. William Jone„ pawnbroker, Eceleston-street, on the previous Tuesday. Thomas Hatton (assistant) stated that from what he was told he followed the prisoner, who was walkint, away from the shop, and saw she had some- thing bulky under her shawl. He found they were the socks produced. Mrs. Alice Moss deposed to having seen the prisoner take the goods from a nail at the shop door. Prisoner pleaded guilty. Superintendent Barker said the I prisoner had been 27 times previously convicted, and des- cribed her as a travelling thief. He was informed she had just come out of prison on the day upon which she was ap- prehended on the present charge.—The Bench committed her for three months with hard labour. A RurtswAY HUSBAND AND FATHER. Before Mr. F. W. Earle and Mr. W. L. Evans, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a sand labourer, formerly living at St. Helens, was charged under a warrant with deserting his wife and two children, arel leaving them chargeable to the Prescot Union. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, prosecuted. 11e stated that on the 17th May application for relief was received from the prisoner's wife and her two children, one aged four year's, and another eight months. Up to the middle of May prisoner had worked at Mr. Brier's, sand merchant, and was in constant and good employment, which he left without any reason. When apprehended he was working for market gardeners in Cheshire. The cast of maintaining his wife and family had been EIS 12s, and he had on two occasions previously been convicted for similar offences.—Mr. C. M. Stuart, relieving officer, gave evidence to the foregoing effect, and the magistrates committed the prisoner for three months with hard labour. PRE!COT HIGHWAY BOARD—The monthly meeting was held at the office of the clerk, Prescot, on Tuesday forenoan, when there were present Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman), Tyrer, Sumner, Lowe, Goldsworth (surveyor), and Cowherd (assistant clerk).—Expenditure : The .Surveyor reported that his expenditure during the four weeks ending July 29th had been as follows: Bold £l5 31 6d, Knowsley £l3 105 11-0, Bainhill £6 12s 6d, Whiston £23 18s 2d, team labour £lB 7s lid, new materials £67 15s 2d, incidentals £22 19s sid, total £l6B Ts 101d.—Telephones at Rainhill: The Surveyor read a letter from Mr. A. R. Claxton, manager for the Lan- cashire and Cheshire Telephone Company, who submitted plans showing the route the company were prepared to adopt in substitution of the St. James's-load line of poles at I Rainhill, but on making the offer to Mr. Owen they found that be was not willing to give them any facilities for connecting Rainhill Constabulary Office, although they only asked for three or four poles between Church-road and the Rainhill Police Office. In offering to take down more than one mile of poles and erect a like quantity on privabs property they were doing all they possibly couldrto meet the objections which had been raised, and as they had net been met in their endeavours they must ncei throw them- selves upon the Board with the hope of obtaining consent for the poles to remain as now erected, and they would by' that means be able to complete their line to Widnes. They had already erected poles and wires between Rainhill and Widnes, of which they could not make any use until they were able to complete their route at Rainhill.—Mr. Lowe said Mr. Owen appeared to heithe principal objector, and it was upon that gentleman's account that an alternative route had been taken. He thought for the sake of public conve- nience Mr. Owen ought to give way.—The Chairman ob- served that he thought the Rainhill people bad peculiar no- tions about telegraph and telephone poles, and he suggested the clerk should write in reply to the letter that that Board had no objection to the erection of the poles.—Mr. Lowe suggested that in the meantime Mr. Owen should be written to upon the subject. He thought the ratepayers should know the reason why the poles were sot erected.—This sug- gestion was adopted.—There was no other public business.

Chairman did not think anything further could be done in 1 the matter until the Local Government Board had been heard from.—The Clerk explained that the woman had been atten- ded at the Providence Hospital by the Union medical offi- cer, and she was afterwards removed to her father's home when she was found suffering from infectious di- sease. The hospital at St. Helm. s was closed against her. The Guardians had done everything they possibly could in the matter, but the public health had not been protected, and he had medical authority that the fever was spreading. He could also go further and say that the fever arose in consequence of defective ashpit arrangements, so that it would appear the local authority was at fault. The quegtion now arose—was the hospital at St. Helens to be used for the parpose for which it had been erected. The Guardians were willing to relieve destitution, but it was no part of their duty to attend to the health of the district. He thought the case was becoming a public scandal and d:sgraceful.—The Chairman said there was no doubt about tbat.—The chairman's suggestion to leave the matter over, awaiting the Local Government Board's answer, was adopted.

WORKHOUSE ALTERATIONS.—The following tenders had been received for contemplated alterations to the bakehouse and drying-room at the Workhouse :—Messrs. G. W.izbom and Son. 29, Kirkland-street, St. Helens, £455; Mr. John LUC3S, Prescot, £491 ; Mr. Peter Taylor, Prescot, £517 ; and Mr. Thomas Roberts, North-road, St. Helens, £487. On the motion of Mr. W. Birchall, seconded by Mr. Middlehurst, the first-named, vs the lowest, was accepted. THE MILK SUPPLY.—Several members expressed dissat- isfaction with the present milk supply to the workhouse, and the subject was referred to the Visiting Committee, and it was decided to ask the milk cantractor to appear before that committee.

THE WIDNES MEDICAL OFFicnit.—The Rev. Father Finegan give notice that on that day month he would move the reappointment of Dr. Cooper as the medical officer for the Widnes district of the Union. This was the principal business.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Presoot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present Mr. J. Lowe (chairman), the Rays. T. Chambers and T. Finegan, Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Jackson, W. Birchall, W. Gerrard, J. Buckley, J. Fisher, J. W. Wareing, W. G. Ashton, J. Whalley, W. Middlehurst, E. Syder, J. Burchall, J. Ranson, J. Renwright, T. Heald, W. B. Longton, J. Leatherbarrow, P. Longten, T. Eatock, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

RELIEF RETURNS.—Mr. Hale, the workhouse maeter, re- ported there were 464 inmates in the workhouse, 462 last week, and 403 in the corresponding week of last year. Du- ring the week 71 vagrants had been relieved.
MR. BARTON'S SALARY.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board anorovin of the increase of £2O per annum in the salary of Mr. 0. M. Barton, relieving officer.

THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE AT LIVERPOOL.— The Clerk read a circular letter in reference to the forthcoming Poor Law Union Conference at Liverpool, and the Rev. 'l'. Ehambers gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that a deputation be appointed from that Board as the representatives of the Union to attend the conference. THE POOR RATE —The Clerk reported the receipt of a precept from the county justices reouiring the Guardians to pay, on or before the 30th inst., £7066 Os 2d for the pur- poses of covnty expenditure for the ensuing six months. He observed it was a very large item. and the cost of the constabulary for the county division amounted to £4119 94. He wished the press to take note of the fact that the poor rate, so-called, included changes other than the actual cost of relieving the poor. The whole of the charges were out of the poor rate, and besides the £4119 for the Present police, the general constabulary expenses were £514, so that about £4600, out of £7OOO was for police purposes alone.— Councillor Fisher: And collected as poor rates?— The Clerk: Yes.

THE GUARDIANS AND ST. HELENS CORPCRATION.—Tbe Clerk read a letter from Mr. Brevris, town clerk of St. Helens, dated the 28th July, drawing attention to the case of a woman named Mary Ann Thompson. at present suffer- ing from an infections disease. The letter continued— " She is in receipt of parish relief and lodged in a house at Greenbank, St, Helens, in which, having regard to its accommodation and general surroundings, it is impossible she can receive proper treatment. The medical officer (Dr. McNicoll) states that it is undoubtedly a case in which he should ask the relieving officer to remove for proper treat- ment to the hospital at Whiston, were it not for the fact that the relieving officers have received instruc- tions from the clerk to the Guardians not to send any eases of infections diseases from St. Helens to the Workhouse Hospital, and his tequest would not be complied with. The committee are of opinion that in a destitute ease like the above it devolves upon the poor law aethorities to provide accommodation for the due and pre- cer treatment of the case. lam sending a copy of this letter to the Local Government Board by tonight' s post."—The

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

RUSH/SEARING at Lymm commences to-day (Satnrdayl, and will be continued next week. A considerable number of shooting galleries, swings, and ether accessories to a fair have already arrived, greatly to the delight of the juvenile portion of the community. LTISIM AS A PLEASURE RESORT.—Lymm was visited on Monday by a large number of pleasure seekers. Early in the day omnibuses arrived in quick succession, and towards noon the resources of the various publicans were taxed to the utmost, to find accommodation for the late arrivals. The day was tine. Many of the visitors were attracted by the beautiful walk alongside the dam, and other places of in- terest were the Parish Church, the Cress, and the Stocks. TRAP ACCIDENT—ShortIy after eleven o'clock on Satur- day evening a person named Richard Holcroft, a farmer and cattle dealer, of Lymrn, met with an accident when driving on Wilderspool-road, Warrington. His horse and trap, driven, it is said, at a rather rapid pace. collided with a 'bus that was coming from the direction of Stockton Heath. Mr. Holcroft was pitched out of the trap, and received in- juries to Ws head. He was removed to a house in the vicinity, and was afterwards taken home. One of the shafts of the trap was broken off.

div.head: LYMM /LOWER SHOW.
div.p: LYMM /LOWER SHOW.

The fourth annual flower show for the parishes of Lymm (with Statham), Oughtrington, The!wall, High Legh, and Warburton, was opened yesterday in the Park at Lymm Hall. The show comprised a tent for the exhibition of plants, vegetables, <ix., one that contained exhibits of art and manufactures, and in a third was a bee exhibition which excited some attention. The weather was not very bright. The president of the show is the Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A., Mr. R. Dutton the hon. treasurer, and Mr. J. Smith the hon. secretary. The largest tent was devoted to plants, vegetables, and fruit, the exhibits being'ranged at the side. In the centre were placed a number of foliage and fl,wering plants, which had been lent for view by Messrs. J. C. Dewtaurst, W. Battersbv, Stubbs, J. G. Dewhurst, Mrs. Crosfield, and Mrs. Grandy. Among the exhibitors in the second tent a number of machines of the Singer Com- pany occupied a prominent place. They were under the charge of Mr. C. Crank, from the Warrington branch in Lyme-street. Mr. J. Smith (Lymm) exhibited decorations, Mr. D. Brown (Lymm) specimens of furniture, and Mr. W. Harkes (Mere, Cheshire,) a novel easy chair with a framework made of horns. The prizes for a forthcoming' athletic meeting were also placed in this tent, which in addition contained specimens of needlework, fancy and otherwise, paietings on silk and in oil, models, and many other articles connected with art and industry. The fol- lowing people took prizes and awards, some of them obtain- ing distinction in several classes e--J Herman (gardener to Mrs King), Levi Clare (gardener to the R3V W Guest), Mrs Grundy, Mrs Battersby, G Brown, T Bolt, M instanley, J Sharpies, T Calton, T Braman, Chamberlain, J Brooker, F Brad burn, W Ellison, J Whitlow, H Burgess, Mrs Stahl, P Clare, J Lowndea, T H Marsh, T Ardern, T Whitfield, VT Bates, J Kerfoot, W Hatton, E Mort, Astall, Atkimson, Mrs Clare, J Knowles, T Nash, E Hazlehurst, H Clare, W Wheeler, F J Lee, H Simpson, T Heaton, A Smith, Mrs E Crosfield, T P Williamson, H 'Warburton, H Broo- ker, H Bradburn, S Bradburn, S Clare, L Smith, G Pigott, P Brazendale, F Barrow, M Winstanley, Jae Knowles, Mrs Burgess, II Holt, B Brooker, M Skillieg, M Rawlinson, T Mort, H Gibbon, W Holt, El Gibbs, King, Bennett, Miss Battersby, H C Evans, L Clare and J Clare, jun., E Davies, J' Whitelegge, Clark, A Donald, J Appleton. C Cbantler, 8 Gregson, M Oulton, H Hegg, M Chorley, Maggie Skilling, Ann Volt, Mary Ann Smith, T Moody, A Heathcote .Jane Brooks, M E and A Whitelegge, E Welford, M Chander, A Kirk, Rouse, Leah. E Entwistle, E A Morris, A Kirk, E Sharpies, Clarke, E M and A Moe- ton, F Wilson, W Platt, and J Smith. Mesdames Jackson, Leather, Hajton, Burrows, and Heywood took prizes for bread.

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, Lymm, on Thursday evening. There were present the chairman (Mr. Cameron), Messrs. Gibbon, Woolley, Appleton, Hall, Forster, Brazendale, Thomason, Ridgway (clerk), and Dr. Fox (medical officer). MEDICAL OFFxcEres REPOILT.—Dr. Fox presented a re- port to the Board, in which he stated it would be within the remembrance of the Board that the annual death rate calcu- lated upon the mortality of the first quarter of the year was exactly 10 per 1,000. During the second quarter the number of deaths registered from all causes and at all ages, was 16; and the death rate was increased to the still very low figure of 13.3 per LOCO. In both quarters of the year not a single death had been occasioned by any of the sym- otic or infectious order of diseases. Ten out of the 16, deaths et all ages were at the opposite ends of the scale of life; viz., six, or 37'5 per cent of aged persons; and four or 25 per cent of infants under the first year of age. All the cutting shops had been visited, and a schedule was presented cf their sanitary condition. Gener- ally it might be pronounced that their sanitary condition was not satisfactory. There was too little attention given to cleanliness and to means of ventilation. It seemed to be a prevailing impression that any four walls with a roof and floor will serve for a cutting shop. This was not true. Any person engaging in that department of industry was bound to conform in all respects to the requirement of the Act controlling employers of labour of this character. On account of the amount of dust given off in the maniptela- tion of fustian, the point of most essential importance to be attended to was adequate means of ventilation, capable or carrying off the fleffy particles which filled the atmosphere of the room. He was told in many instances that to open a window was an occasion of draught. This was equivalent to an admission that the room was unfit for occupation as a cutting shop, no ether means of ventilation being avail- able. In these cases the duty of the Board was to close such places as out of conformity with the requirements of the Act. General cleanliness was another important mat- ter which it was within the scope of every employer to give every attention to. For the comfort of employers with small capital he might say that as it was possible for the best designed and constructed places to be a nuisance if r.eglected and badly attended to, so on the other hand, it was possible for smaller and improvised domestic apart- mente used as cutting shops to be rendered suit- able and unobjectionable if ventilation and clean- liness be diligently studied and observed. A prize might be given to the cutting shop maintained in the best order for one year. He had a fund from which he should be glad to devote .C 5 for this purpose.—Sorno discus- sion took place with respect to this report, in the course of which Dr. Fax remarked that the death rate in Lymm from consumption fur the last eight years was higher than the general death rate throughout the country, and there was no other cause for that than the want of ventilation in the fustian shops. The matter of dealing with the sanitary condition of fustian shops was ultimately referred to the Sanitary Committee. RESIGNATION OF Mn. DEWITDRST.—The minutes of a special meeting of the Board were read, and stated that Mr. J. D. Dewhurst had tendered his resignation as a member of the Board, and that the resignation had been accepted. The question of the appointment of a successor was consequently considered, and Mr. Brazendale moved, and Mr. Hall seconded, that Mr. F. Holt be elected to fill the vacancy.— Mr. Woolley moved, and Mr. Forster seconded, an amend- ment that Mr. Rogers,. who was a member of the Board up to the time of the last election, be elected.—On being put to the vote the amendment was carried by five votes ta, two. This was the principal business.
An explosion occurred on board a dredger in the har- bour of Dieppe on Saturday morning, by which four parsons were killed and three injured.

A TICIETLESS RAILWAY PASSENGEIL—Before Mr. H. S. Hall and Alderman J. Harrison at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Thomas Davies, a young man, living at Sutton, was charged with travelling without a ticket fran Warrington to St. Helens Junction on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Lucas, stationmaster at St. Helens Junction, said that on Sunday afternoon on the arrival of a train at the station, he saw the defendant alight from a third-class carriage. He walked behind a waiting-room and witness sent a ticket-col- lector who asked him for his ticket. He said he had not come by train, and alleged he was going to Liverpool. He was removed to the booking office and asked to book to Liverpool, but he then said he did not care about goiag. He was told he had come by train, and he then said ho had no money. He was given into custody, and the sum of £2 9.! Vid was fnund in his possession.—rrisoner, wbQ pleaded guilty, was fined 20s and costs.

WANDERING CIIILDIZEN.—Lizzie Kelly, five years of are, who lives in Wellington-road, Liverpool, has been on a visit to Mr. Corrin, 17, Higher Parr-street, St. Helens, and on Monday morning she went out, taking Ida Corrin, two and a half years old, with her. As they did not return during the day; the greatest anxiety was felt, and the police were informed, with the result that the children were on nesday night found at Stubshaw Cross, Ashton-in-Maker- field, they having wandered about nine miles from home. COLLIERY FATATATT.--On Wednesday iifternoon, Jolla Wynne, eighteen years of age, who lived with his brother on Park-road, St. Helens, and was employed as a lashir-on of waggons in the Havannah Colliery, belonging to Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., was killed in the pit. Deceased had finished work and shrted along the balance brow towards the shaft. Soon afterwards his lifeless body was foand between two waggons. His neck was broken, and he had been fear- fully crushed in the bowels, it is not definitely known how deceased got into the position in which he waa found. An inquest will be held.

THE EARLESTOWN DIMEVIITS Cram—This club, which has been in existence about four months, is making satisfactory progress, and there are already aboye 40 good members. A special gonfral meeting, well attended, was held at the Welcome Coffee Palace, Market-street, Earles- town, on Wednesday evening. and Mr. John Makin (presi- dent), occupied the chair The chairman alluded to the position of the club, and commented upon the good progress it had made. The secretary (Mr. S. Wightngan) having re- signed, Mr. John Clarke, jun., of 15, Bridge-street, was eleoted in his place. The committee was directed to draw ap a form of rules, and submit them to, a future general meeting. UNFRIENDLY NEIGHBOURS.— A.t the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, William Appleton was summoned for using threatening language to a married woman, named Jane Taylor, a neighbour. Mrs. Taylor said she kept same fowls, and on the 11th July the defendant and his wife turned some pigs into the yard. These pigs chased th,e hens and she asked her husband to fetoh the hens in. Defendant then used abusive language, and holding a stick in his hand, said he would lay her down a corpse. Colonel McCorquodale (who presided) said: You are neighbours, and we hope you .will try to live well together. The case is not sufficiently serious for us to decide, but we hope you will endeavour to live on proper term in filo future.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

One thousand men and boys at Castle Eden Colliery, Durham, struck work on Friday for an advance of wages. A Lloyd's telegram from Ismalia on Friday morning says the steamer Orion, which grounded on Thursday, has floated and proceeded.
Circagr.—Australians (first innings) 194; Gloucester, three wickets for 164. In the second innings Dr. Grace and Townsend not out.
During the rioting at Belfast, on Tbarsday night, two well-known Belfast pressmen were set upon by a crowd at Peter's-hill Barracks and severely beaten.

The Duke and Duchess of Connaught will proceed to the Mediterranean in a few days for a cruise Ira the Duke of Edinburgh's yacht Burprisennow preparing for sea. The Irish party intend to move an amendment on the Ad- dress, calling upon the Government to take steps to secure the revision of rents and the prevention of evictions. On Friday Prince Albert Victor presented the colours to the East Kent Regiment, at Dover, complimenting the regi- ment on its brilliant services, and expressing the pleasure it gave him to perform the ceremony. THE KING OF PORTITGIL.—The Royal yacht Victoria and Albert. with King Louis of Portugal on board, arrived at Cowes on Friday morning. The King was conveyed in a pinnace from the Royal yacht to Trinity Pier, whence he was driven to Osborne House.

In connection with the Ministerial banquet at the Man- sion House next Wednesday, it is a matter of curiosity that Alderman Staples has been the only Lord Mayor in the whole history of the Corporation of London who has held office during three separate Administrations. A MOTHER AND LIMO KDSLED NEAR SOTITHPORT.-00 Thursday evening a shocking accident occurred on the Lan- cashire and Yorkshire Railway, near Southport, whereby two persona lost their lives. The victims are Mrs. Hesketh and her child, the wifa and daughter of John Hesketb, a poiatsman employed at Bescar-lane Station. FATAL PIT ACCIDENT: Two MEN KILLED.—A fall of roof took place on Thursday at Mr. Stroogitharm's lime- stone pit at Bushell, Staffordshire, by which two men were killed. One man, named White,. was crushed to death oa the spot, and a man named Smith W. 48 so fearfully injured that he died soon after admission to Walsall Cottage Hos- pital.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT A RAILWAY STATION.—On Friday morning a shocking accident occurred at Trentham Railway Station, near Stoke. An elderly woman, named Sarah Johnson, was crossing the line to see a friend off by train to Stafford, when the train for Lichfield knocked her down and killed her and her grandchild four years of age, whom she bad in her arms. Both bodies were terribly mutilated, the woman being decapitated. THE COOKSON' DIVORCE CASE.—lin the Divorce Court, on Friday morning, Sir James Hannon and a special jury re- sumed the hearing of the suit of Cookson v. Cookson and Finlayson, in which the petitioner is Mr. Joseph Cookson, a hemp merchant and waste manufacturer, Manchester, and the co-respondent, the Bev. Arthur R. Morrison Finlayson, formerly organising secretary to the Liverpool district of the Colonial and Continental Church Society.—The Rev. Arthur Robert Morrison Finlayson,. the co-respondent, de- posed that he was an ordained priest of the Church of Eng- land. In the advertisements he did not intend to justify tbe use of the words "pet " and '4 love." They were in- serted in an " allegorical sense." (Laughter.) He got a telegram from the respondent that her husband had met her at the hotel instead of witness. He only went to express sympathy with her. The advertisements in the " Christian World " were not intended to be seen by Mr. Cookson —Mr. Inderwick : Why did you give the man Simmons any money P—Witness : Because I knew that Lord Stanley of Alderley was very pArticulrr abcut trespassers, and I gave him money so that my name and address should not be taken.—ln the result the jury found for the petitioner, and assessed damages at £l,ooo.—HiteLordship granted a decree nisi with costs.

div.p: THE ENGLISH COMMERCIAL TREATY WITH SPAIN.
MADRID. FRIDAY.—The text of the Treaty of Commerce, 'concluded between England and Spain, is officially published to-day.

THE DIFFICULTY IN BURMAH. SWEEPING MILITARY' CHANGES. CALCUTTA, FRIDAY.—Tn consequence of the continned unsatisfactory state of affairs in Burmab, it has been de- cided to make sweeping changes in the composition and disposition of the troops and in the superior commands. All the troops both in Upper mid in Lower Bnrmah will be placed under the command of Lieutenant-General Sir Her- bert Macpherson, at present Commander-in-Chief at Madras. Reinforcements to the extent of 5-io3omen will be dispatched to Burmah early in the cold season. On their arrival ex- tensive military operations will be undertaken. In regard to the civil administration, additional police will be sent from India, and the whole country will be scoured with a view to extinguishing dacoity.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE 011 LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE 011 LORDS.

The House of Lords met at twelve o'clockewhen the Queen's assent was given to the Commons' selection of Speaker. There was only a small attendance of peers. The Commons were summoned, and the Speaker's election con- firmed. The Speaker then claimed on behalf of the Com- mons their undoubted ;ights and privileges, which the Lord Chaneellor intimated her Majesty was ready to grant. The ceremony then concluded, and the Commons withdrew. A number of lords afterwards took the oaths, and the House adjourned until four o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE APPOINTMENT OF SPEAKER.

At noon a large gathering of members had assembled on the floor of the House of Cbrnmons, when the cry of "Speaker" sent them to their seats. The Speaker-elect im- mediately entered and took the chair, and the Mace being on the table, the Howie was constituted. The right hon. gentleman wore a bob wig and court dress, his gown full- bottomed wig being reserved until the Queen's approval of. his election. A few minutes later the Black Rod appeared and summoned members to the other House. hi delivering his message the Speaker allowed a curious lapse of memory by using the formulary desiring, the attendance of the Com- mons in tie Lords to hear the Royal Assent given "to Acts agreed upon by both Houses," instead of "to the choice of Speaker." A smile illuminated every contenance, while some members could not repress a momentary titter. On returning to the Commons the Speaker donned his gown and wig, and, taking the chair, announced their choice of himself as Speaker had been approved by the Queen. TAKING THE OATH.—Members then proceeded to take the oath in groups of five, begiesning with the Ministers and Privy Councillors present. The first group consisted of Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Moiley, Sir John Gorst, Mr. Beres- ford Hope, and Mr. Akers-Douglas. Then followed Mr. Jackson, Sir John Mowbray, Sir James Fergusson, Sir Henry James, and Mr. Campbell-Bannerman. 'The third group consisted of Mr. Trorwood, Mr. Heneage, Baron de Worms, Mr. Henry Fowler, and Mr. Arnold Morley, the baron taking the Hebrew oath with his hat on. Everything in the nature of unseemly pressure to get forward in the early groups was met with shoots of "order," and as the ceremony proceeded as fast as the roll could he subscribed, the wisdom of the Speaker's new rules of procedure was generally admitted. In all nearly three hundred members, have taken the oath.

THE VACtiNCIES.-At four o'clock the Speaker was sum- moned to the House of Peers, an 4 on the right hon. gentle- moo's return he informed the House that her Majesty had commanded that several vacancies that had occurred in the House should he filled up in order that, after a short recess, it might be in a position, to consider the grave and serious motions that would be laid before it. Wris were then issued for South Paddington, West Bristol, Strand, East Birmingham. the Melton Division of Leiaeo. tershire, Ealing, 2ublin University, Cambridge University, Isle of Wight, East Manchester. the Walton Division of Liverpool. Brighton, Hampstead, St. Andrews Univenity, Butethire• the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire lutes hire. Lincoln, Lindsay Division, Tower Hamlets, St. George's' Division, Plymouth, North-East Devon, Croydon, Wigtown- shire, Marylebone, East Sheffield, Eocleshall Division, West Down, Middlesex (Enfield Division), and Lewesharn„ The Housoadjourned at a quarter to fire until Monday at two o'clock.

FALL OF HOUSES AT WARRINGTON. TWO PERSONS INJURED. Yesterday afternoon an alarming accident oc- curred at Warrington, by which two persons were injured—one of them seriously. Four dwelling- houses in Catherine-street, numbered 104, 106, 108, and 110, suddenly collapse with a great crash, to the consternation of the people living in the neighbour- hood. Fortunately the houses were not occupied, or the consequences would have been far more serious than what they are. Some of the houses in the street, and in proximity to scene of the accident, are, however, occupied, and the peOple living in them experienced gceat alarm. The houses fell in at about 2-15 in the afternoon A woman named Selina Lyons, the wife of a puddler named James Lyons, who lives at 102, Pierpoint-street, was, with her two children, near to the houses at the time of their collapse. She perceived that the houses ap- peared to be falling and, in trying to get her chil- dren out of danger she was injured on the shoulder A girl named Mary Rogers, eight years of age, toe daughter of Wm Rogers, a puddler, who lives at 100, Pierpoint-street, was seri- ously injured, and was at once conveyed to the Infirmary, which is not very far distant. She was taken there by her father, and a woman named Robinson, who lives close by.. The girl was badly injured about the head, and was apparently in a cri- tical state. Catherine-street is situated a short dis- tance beyond Bewsey Bridge, and close to Bewsey forge. Pierpoint-street, where the two injured. people live, is also close to Catherine-street. On the. news of the accident being circulated, many peo- ple went to view the ruins, and several constables I were on duty in the neighbourhood during the even- ing. The property belongs ton Blackburn Building Society, who have advanced money on it, and who have a local agent. It is described as having been for some considerable time in a very dilapidated condition, some of the walls having large holes in them. The houses were also, minus doors and windows. Several people who, know the neigh- bourhood have' since the occurrence said that they had expected some such accident would licippen, and that, as there was nothing to prevent children getting into the houses to play, the result might be serious. Soon after the fall of the prverty informa- tion was taken to the police station, and P.S. Shaw went to the street, and afterwards reported on the matter. Yesterday afternoon information was given to. a borough constable of thefact that during the last fortnight doors and windowframes had been carried away from the houses in question. Measures will doubtless be at once taken twenettre the safety of the rest of the houses that are empty. Already some walls that were in a dangerous condition have been razed to the ground. On. inquiry at the Infirmary early this morning it was ascertained that the injuredl girl was up to that; time. doing well.
